bal.0.shloka1: Of letters, of the hosts of meanings, of rasas (the moods of poetry) and of metres too,
and of all that is auspicious: to Sarasvatī and Gaṇeśa, the two who make them, I bow.
bal.0.shloka2: I bow to Bhavānī and Śaṅkara, the embodiments of faith and trust,
without whom even the siddhas cannot see God seated within their own hearts.
bal.0.shloka3: I bow to the eternal guru, who is all knowledge and has the form of Śaṅkara,
in whose shelter even the crooked moon is honoured everywhere.
bal.0.shloka4: The two who roam the holy forest of the virtues of Sītā and Rāma,
rich in pure realised knowledge, the lord of poets and the lord of monkeys, Vālmīki and Hanumān: to them I bow.
bal.0.shloka5: She who brings about the birth, the upholding and the dissolution of the world, who takes away afflictions,
and who brings every good: to Sītā, the beloved of Śrī Rāma, I bow.
bal.0.shloka6: Under whose māyā (his power of illusion) the whole universe lies, with Brahmā and the other gods and the demons;
by whose being all this seems real, as a rope is taken for a snake;
whose feet are the one boat for those who long to cross the ocean of worldly existence:
to him I bow, the Lord who is beyond every cause, Śrī Hari, called Rāma.
bal.0.shloka7: What agrees with the many Purāṇas, the Vedas and the Āgamas,
what is told in the Rāmāyaṇa, and something taken from elsewhere too:
for the joy of his own heart, Tulasīdāsa sets out this story of Śrī Rāma
as a most lovely composition in the common tongue.
bal.0.so1: He on whose remembrance success comes, the lord of the gaṇas, whose face is that of a noble elephant:
may he, Gaṇeśa, the store of wisdom and home of auspicious virtues, show me his grace.
bal.0.so2: By whose grace the mute become eloquent and the lame climb the high and pathless mountain:
may that compassionate one, who burns away all the impurity of the Kali age, melt with mercy for me.
bal.0.so3: Dark as the blue lotus, with eyes like the fresh red lotus:
may he who ever rests on the ocean of milk make my heart his home.
bal.0.so4: His body white as the kunda flower and the moon, the consort of Umā, the home of compassion,
who loves the lowly: may Śiva, the destroyer of Kāma, show his grace.
bal.0.so5: The guru, the ocean of mercy, Śrī Hari in human form: I bow to his lotus feet,
and his words are a flood of sunbeams upon the thick darkness of great delusion.
bal.1.cau1: I bow to the pollen of the guru's lotus feet, lovely, fragrant and full of the sap of love.
It is a fine powder of the herb of nectar, which quells the whole family of the ills of worldly existence.
bal.1.cau2: It is the pure sacred ash on the body of the virtuous, who are as Śiva, and it gives birth to lovely blessings and joy.
It wipes the dirt from the fair mirror of the devotee's mind; worn as a mark on the brow, it brings the whole host of virtues under one's sway.
bal.1.cau3: The light of the gems that are the nails of the revered guru's feet: as soon as one remembers it, divine sight dawns in the heart.
That radiance destroys the darkness of delusion; great is the fortune of the one in whose heart it comes.
bal.1.cau4: Then the pure eyes of the heart open, and the faults and sorrows of the night of worldly existence fade away.
The gems and rubies of Śrī Rāma's deeds come into view, hidden or open, wherever each lies and in whatever mine.
bal.1.do1: Just as seekers, adepts and the wise, with the magic collyrium on their eyes,
see with ease the many treasures hidden in mountains, forests and the earth.
bal.2.cau1: The dust of the guru's feet is a collyrium, soft and lovely, nectar to the eyes, which destroys every defect of sight.
With it I clear the eyes of discernment and tell the deeds of Śrī Rāma, which set one free from worldly existence.
bal.2.cau2: First I bow to the feet of the Brahmins, the gods on earth, who take away every doubt born of delusion.
Then with love and gentle words I salute the company of the good, the mine of every virtue.
bal.2.cau3: The life of the saints is auspicious, like the life of cotton, whose fruit is juiceless, white and full of guṇa (thread, and virtue).
Bearing pain itself, it covers the holes (the faults) of others, and so it has won in the world a fame worthy of reverence.
bal.2.cau4: The company of the saints, full of joy and blessing, is Prayāga, the king of holy places, moving about the world.
In it devotion to Śrī Rāma is the stream of the Gaṅgā, and the spreading of thought on Brahman is the Sarasvatī.
bal.2.cau5: The teaching on action, full of what is enjoined and what is forbidden, which takes away the impurity of the Kali age, is named the Yamunā, daughter of the Sun.
The stories of Hari and Hara shine as the Triveṇī, the meeting of the streams, and to hear them brings every joy and blessing.
bal.2.cau6: Unshaken faith in one's own dharma is its undying banyan, and good deeds are the retinue of that king of holy places.
All may reach it with ease, on any day and in any land, and when it is served with reverence it puts an end to affliction.
bal.2.cau7: This king of holy places is beyond words and beyond this world; it gives its fruit at once, and its power is plain to see.
bal.2.do2: Those who hear of it and understand, and with a glad heart bathe in it in deep love,
gain the four fruits of life (dharma, wealth, desire and liberation) while still in this body: such a Prayāga is the company of the saints.
bal.3.cau1: The fruit of bathing in it is seen at once: crows become cuckoos, and herons too become swans.
Let no one wonder at hearing this; the glory of the company of the good is no secret.
bal.3.cau2: Vālmīki, Nārada and Agastya, the pot-born, have each told with their own lips what befell them.
Of all the many beings in the world, those of the water, the land and the air, inert and conscious alike,
bal.3.cau3: the wisdom, fame, blessed end, prosperity and goodness that any has gained, at any time, by any means, in any place,
is to be known as the power of the company of the good: there is no other way, in the world or in the Veda.
bal.3.cau4: Without the company of the good there is no discernment, and without Śrī Rāma's grace that company is not easily found.
The company of the good is the root of joy and blessing; it is the fruit and the fulfilment, and all spiritual practices are but the flowers.
bal.3.cau5: Even the wicked are reformed when they find the company of the good, as base metal becomes fine gold at the touch of the philosopher's stone.
And if by fate the good fall into bad company, they keep to their own virtue, like the gem in a serpent's hood.
bal.3.cau6: The speech of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva, of poets and the learned, falters when it tries to tell the glory of the saints.
How then can I tell it, any more than a seller of greens can tell the many virtues of gems?
bal.3.do3क: I bow to the saints, whose minds are even, to whom no one is friend and no one foe,
as a lovely flower held in cupped hands gives its fragrance equally to both hands.
bal.3.do3ख: The saints are simple of heart and wish the world well; knowing this nature and love of theirs, I pray:
hear this child's prayer, be gracious, and grant me love for the feet of Śrī Rāma.
bal.4.cau1: Next I bow in all sincerity to the host of the wicked, who without any cause turn against even those who are kind to them,
for whom the loss of another's good is their gain, who rejoice when others are ruined and grieve when they prosper.
bal.4.cau2: To the full moon of the glory of Hari and Hara they are Rāhu; at ruining the work of others they are warriors like Sahasrabāhu.
They look on others' faults with a thousand eyes, and their minds are a fly in the ghee of others' good.
bal.4.cau3: In fierceness they are fire, in anger Yama, lord of the buffalo; in the wealth of sin and vice they are as rich as Kubera.
Their rising is like the rising of Ketu, the comet, a blow to the welfare of all; like Kumbhakarṇa, they are best left asleep.
bal.4.cau4: To spoil the work of others they will give up even their own bodies, as hailstones crush the crops and melt away.
I bow to the wicked as to Śeṣa, for in their wrath they recount the faults of others with a thousand mouths.
bal.4.cau5: Again I bow to them as to King Pṛthu, for they hear the sins of others with ten thousand ears.
Then I entreat them as I would Indra: wine (surā) is ever good and dear to them, as the army of the gods (surānīka) is dear to Indra.
bal.4.cau6: To them the thunderbolt of harsh words is ever dear, and with a thousand eyes they look upon the faults of others.
bal.4.do4: Whether one is neutral, a foe or a friend, the wicked burn on hearing of his good: such is their way.
Knowing this, this servant joins both his hands and makes his plea to them with love.
bal.5.cau1: I have made my plea from my side, but they will not fail in their part.
Rear crows with all the love you may: will crows ever give up eating flesh?
bal.5.cau2: I bow to the feet of both the saint and the wicked; both give pain, yet a difference between them is told.
The one takes away our life when he parts from us; the other gives us bitter pain when he meets us.
bal.5.cau3: Both are born together in the world, yet like the lotus and the leech they differ in their nature.
The good are like nectar and the wicked like wine; both have one father, the unfathomable ocean of the world.
bal.5.cau4: The good and the bad, each by their own deeds, win the wealth of good name and of ill repute.
Nectar, the moon, the Gaṅgā and the saint; and poison, fire, the Karmanāśā, river of the Kali age's impurity, and the hunter:
bal.5.cau5: the virtues and the vices of these everyone knows, yet whatever pleases a man is what seems good to him.
bal.5.do5: The good take up only goodness, and the base take up baseness.
Nectar is praised for giving immortality, and poison is praised for bringing death.
bal.6.cau1: The tale of the sins and vices of the wicked and the tale of the virtues of the good are both oceans, boundless and unfathomable.
So I have described some of their virtues and faults, for without knowing them one can neither take up the one nor give up the other.
bal.6.cau2: The good and the bad were all made by the Creator; the Vedas have counted up their virtues and faults and set them apart.
The Vedas, the Itihāsas and the Purāṇas say that the Creator's world is a mixture of virtues and vices.
bal.6.cau3: Sorrow and joy, sin and merit, day and night, the good and the wicked, noble birth and low birth,
demons and gods, the high and the low, nectar and poison, a good life and death,
bal.6.cau4: māyā and Brahman, the soul and the Lord of the world, prosperity and poverty, the pauper and the king,
Kāśī and Magadha, the Gaṅgā and the Karmanāśā, Marwar and Malwa, the Brahmin and the slayer of cows,
bal.6.cau5: heaven and hell, attachment and dispassion: in all of these the Vedas and the scriptures have drawn the line between virtue and fault.
bal.6.do6: The Creator made this universe, inert and conscious, full of virtues and faults.
The saints, like swans, take the milk of virtue and leave behind the water of fault.
bal.7.cau1: When the Creator grants such discernment, the mind leaves the faults aside and takes delight in the virtues.
Yet through the overpowering force of time, inborn nature and past deeds, even the good, under the sway of Prakṛti, fall short of goodness.
bal.7.cau2: As the devotees of Hari set that lapse right, crushing sorrow and fault and granting spotless fame,
so the wicked too do good when they find good company; but their unclean nature, which company does not touch, is not wiped away.
bal.7.cau3: Seeing their fine garb, the world worships even those who are cheats, by the power of the garb.
But in the end they are found out, and the disguise does not hold to the last, as with Kālanemi, Rāvaṇa and Rāhu.
bal.7.cau4: Even in an unsightly form the good are honoured, as Jāmbavān and Hanumān are honoured in the world.
Bad company brings loss and good company gain; in the world and in the Veda alike, this is known to everyone.
bal.7.cau5: In the wind's company dust climbs to the sky; in the company of water, which runs low, it sinks into the mud.
Parrots and mynas in the home of the good remember Śrī Rāma; those in the home of the wicked count out abuse after abuse.
bal.7.cau6: In bad company smoke turns to soot; the same smoke, made into fine ink, is used to write the Purāṇas.
And joined with water, fire and wind, that same smoke becomes a cloud, the giver of life to the world.
bal.7.do7क: Planets, medicines, water, wind and cloth, as they meet a bad or a good conjunction,
become bad or good things in the world; people of discernment see this.
bal.7.do7ख: Both fortnights hold light and darkness in equal measure, yet the Creator gave them different names.
Taking one to waste the moon and the other to feed it, the world gave fame to the one that feeds and ill fame to the one that wastes.
bal.7.do7ग: Knowing all the beings of the world, inert and sentient, as many as there are, to be full of Śrī Rāma,
I ever bow to the lotus feet of them all with both palms joined.
bal.7.do7घ: Gods, dānavas, humans, nāgas, birds, ghosts, ancestors, gandharvas,
kinnaras and demons, I bow to you all; now be gracious to me, all of you.
bal.8.cau1: The beings that dwell in water, on land and in the sky are born from four sources and are of eighty-four lakh kinds;
knowing the whole world to be full of Sītā and Śrī Rāma, I bow to it with both palms joined.
bal.8.cau2: You who are mines of grace, know me too for your servant, and all of you together, setting guile aside, be kind to me.
I have no faith in the strength of my own wit; that is why I make this humble plea to all.
bal.8.cau3: I long to tell the tale of Śrī Rāma's virtues; my understanding is small, and his deeds are fathomless.
Not one means or resource for it occurs to me; my mind and wit are paupers, but my ambition is a king's.
bal.8.cau4: My wit is very low, my longing high and noble; I want nectar, though in this world I cannot come by even buttermilk.
The good will forgive my presumption and listen with attention to the prattle of a child.
bal.8.cau5: When a child says something in lisping words, its father and mother listen with delight.
The cruel, the crooked and the evil-minded will laugh, those who wear the faults of others as their jewels.
bal.8.cau6: Who does not find his own verse pleasing, whether it is rich in flavour or utterly insipid?
Those who rejoice to hear the poetry of others, such noble people are not many in the world.
bal.8.cau7: Brother, many people in the world are like lakes and rivers, which swell with their own flood when they get water.
Rare is the good person who is like the ocean, which swells when it sees the moon full.
bal.8.do8: My fortune is small and my longing great, but I hold to one trust:
all the good will find joy in hearing it, and the wicked will mock it.
bal.9.cau1: The jeers of the wicked will do me good. Crows call the sweet-voiced cuckoo harsh.
Herons laugh at swans and frogs at the cātaka birds; just so the unclean, wicked ones laugh at pure speech.
bal.9.cau2: Those who neither savour poetry nor love Śrī Rāma's feet will find in this, too, the pleasure of the comic mood.
The verse is in the common tongue and my wit is simple; it deserves laughter, and there is no blame in laughing at it.
bal.9.cau3: Those who have neither love for the Lord's feet nor sound understanding will find the story flat when they hear it.
Those who love the feet of Hari and Hara, and whose minds are not given to perverse argument, will find Śrī Rāma's story sweet.
bal.9.cau4: Knowing in their hearts that it is graced with devotion to Śrī Rāma, the good will listen to it and praise it with kind words.
I am no poet, nor clever with words; I lack every art and all learning.
bal.9.cau5: Letters and their meanings, figures of speech of many kinds, metres and compositions in many forms,
the boundless kinds of feeling and of rasa, and the faults and merits of poetry, are of many sorts.
bal.9.cau6: Of these skills of poetic judgement I have not one; this is the truth, and I put it in writing on a blank page.
bal.9.do9: My verse is devoid of every merit, but it has one merit the whole world knows.
Weighing that, the wise, whose discernment is pure, will listen to it.
bal.10.cau1: In it is the bountiful name of Śrī Rāma, utterly holy, the essence of the Purāṇas and the Vedas,
the home of all that is auspicious and remover of all that is not, which Śiva, the foe of Tripura, repeats together with Umā.
bal.10.cau2: However wonderful a poem made by a fine poet may be, without the name of Śrī Rāma it too lacks grace,
as a lovely moon-faced woman, adorned in every way, does not look graceful without clothes.
bal.10.cau3: And the words of a poor poet, devoid of every merit, when they know them to be marked with Śrī Rāma's name and glory,
the wise recite and hear with reverence; for saints, like the bee, take in what is good.
bal.10.cau4: Though there is not a single poetic flavour in it, Śrī Rāma's glory is plain to see in it.
This is the hope that has come to my mind: who has not won greatness from good company?
bal.10.cau5: Even smoke gives up its natural acridness and grows fragrant in the company of aloe-wood.
My verse is rough, but the matter it tells is good: the story of Śrī Rāma, which brings blessing to the world.
bal.10.cha1: Says Tulasīdāsa: the story of Śrī Rāma brings blessing and removes the impurity of the Kali age.
The river of my poetry runs a winding course, as a river of holy water does.
Joined with the Lord's fair fame, this verse will become good and win the hearts of the good.
Even the ash of the cremation ground, once on the body of Śiva, is lovely and purifying to call to mind.
bal.10.do10क: Through its bond with Śrī Rāma's glory my verse will be very dear to all.
Does anyone weigh what the wood is? Through its link with Mount Malaya, home of sandalwood, it is revered.
bal.10.do10ख: A cow may be dark, yet its milk is white and very wholesome, and all drink it.
The speech is rustic, but it tells the glory of Sītā and Śrī Rāma, and the wise sing it and listen to it.
bal.11.cau1: The beauty that gems, rubies and pearls have does not show on a serpent's head, a mountain or an elephant's head.
On a king's crown and a young woman's body they all gain greater splendour.
bal.11.cau2: In the same way, the wise say, a good poet's verse is born in one place and finds its beauty in another.
Drawn by devotion, Sarasvatī leaves the abode of Brahmā and comes running as soon as she is called to mind.
bal.11.cau3: Unless she is bathed in the lake of Śrī Rāma's deeds, that weariness of hers does not go, though millions of remedies are tried.
Weighing this in their hearts, poets and scholars sing the glory of Śrī Hari, which takes away the stain of the Kali age.
bal.11.cau4: When she is made to sing the praises of ordinary worldly people, the goddess of speech beats her head and is filled with regret.
The wise say the heart is like the ocean, the intellect like the oyster shell and Sarasvatī like the Svāti star.
bal.11.cau5: If the fine water of thought rains into it, the poems become lovely pearls.
bal.11.do11: Pierced with skill, those pearls are then strung on the fine thread of Śrī Rāma's deeds,
and the good wear them on their pure hearts, where their beauty is deep love.
bal.12.cau1: Those born in the terrible age of Kali, crows in their deeds and swans in their dress,
who walk the wrong road, forsaking the way of the Vedas, bodies of deceit and vessels of the Kali age's filth,
bal.12.cau2: cheats who call themselves devotees of Śrī Rāma, slaves of gold, anger and lust:
among them, in all the world, my name stands first, a brazen rogue who flies the flag of dharma for show, foremost in worldly schemes.
bal.12.cau3: Were I to tell all my faults, the tale would grow so long that I would never reach its end.
So I have told only a very few; the wise will understand from a little.
bal.12.cau4: Understanding my pleas in their many forms, no one who hears the story will find fault.
If, after all this, any still harbour doubts, they are duller than I am and poorer in understanding.
bal.12.cau5: I am no poet, nor do I claim to be clever; I sing Śrī Rāma's virtues as far as my understanding goes.
Where are the boundless deeds of Śrī Rāma, and where is my mind, sunk in worldly life!
bal.12.cau6: Tell me, before a wind that blows away mountains such as Meru, what does a tuft of cotton count for?
When I think of Śrī Rāma's boundless greatness, my mind quails at the telling of the story.
bal.12.do12: Sarasvatī, Śeṣa, Śiva, Brahmā, the Āgamas, the Vedas and the Purāṇas
sing his virtues without end, saying neti, neti, not this, not this.
bal.13.cau1: All know the Lord's greatness to be such, yet no one has held back from telling of it.
For this the Veda has set down a reason: it has told in many ways of the power of worship.
bal.13.cau2: The One, free of desire, without form or name, unborn, being, consciousness and bliss, the supreme abode,
the all-pervading Lord whose form is the universe, has taken a body and done many deeds.
bal.13.cau3: He did this only for the good of his devotees, supremely compassionate as he is, and loving to all who bow before him.
He holds his devotee as his own, with great affection, and on one to whom he has shown mercy he has never turned in anger.
bal.13.cau4: Śrī Rāma restores what was lost and cherishes the poor; he is a guileless and mighty master.
Knowing this, the wise tell the glory of Śrī Hari and make their own speech holy and fruitful.
bal.13.cau5: On the strength of that, bowing my head at Śrī Rāma's feet, I shall tell the tale of his virtues.
The sages sang the fame of Śrī Hari before me; brother, to walk their road is easy for me.
bal.13.do13: If kings have bridges built over great rivers that are vast beyond measure,
even the tiniest ant climbs onto them and crosses to the far side without effort.
bal.14.cau1: Having in this way shown my mind its strength, I will compose the lovely story of Śrī Rāma.
Vyāsa and many other eminent poets have reverently told the fair fame of Śrī Hari.
bal.14.cau2: I salute their lotus feet: may they fulfil all my wishes.
I bow to the poets of the Kali age who have described the host of Śrī Rāma's virtues.
bal.14.cau3: The most skilful poets of the Prākṛta tongue, who have told the deeds of Śrī Hari in the common speech,
those who have been, who are, and who will be hereafter: to them all I bow, setting aside all guile.
bal.14.cau4: Be pleased, and grant me this boon: that my verse be honoured in the company of the good.
A work the wise do not esteem is labour wasted, spent by childish poets.
bal.14.cau5: Fame, poetry and prosperity are good only when, like the Gaṅgā, they do good to all.
Śrī Rāma's fame is fair and my verse is rough; such is the mismatch, and this is my misgiving.
bal.14.cau6: By your grace even that becomes easy for me: stitching in silk looks lovely even on sackcloth.
bal.14.do14क: Poetry that is simple and sings of spotless fame is the only kind the wise esteem,
the kind which even an enemy, forgetting his natural enmity, praises when he hears it.
bal.14.do14ख: Such poetry does not come without a pure mind, and the strength of my mind is very slight.
Be gracious, so that I may tell Śrī Hari's glory; again and again I entreat you.
bal.14.do14ग: Poets and learned ones, lovely swans of the Mānasa lake of Śrī Rāma's deeds,
hear a child's plea, see his keen delight, and be gracious to me.
bal.14.so14घ: I salute the lotus feet of Vālmīki, the sage by whom the Rāmāyaṇa was made,
a work that tells of Khara (khara, harsh) yet is very tender and lovely, and is free of fault (doṣa) yet tells of Dūṣaṇa (dūṣaṇa, fault).
bal.14.so14ङ: I salute all four Vedas, who are like a ship on the ocean of worldly existence,
and who never, even in a dream, tire of telling the spotless fame of Śrī Rāma.
bal.14.so14च: I salute the dust of the feet of Brahmā, who made the ocean of worldly existence,
from which the saints came forth as nectar, the moon and the wish-granting cow, and the wicked as poison and wine.
bal.14.do14छ: Saluting the feet of the gods, the Brahmins, the wise and the planets, I say with joined palms:
Be pleased, and fulfil all my fair wishes.
bal.15.cau1: Again I salute Sarasvatī and the Gaṅgā, a holy pair whose ways enchant the mind.
One, the Gaṅgā, takes away sin when one bathes in her and drinks of her; the other, Sarasvatī, takes away want of discernment through speaking and hearing.
bal.15.cau2: Maheśa and Bhavānī, my guru, father and mother, friends of the lowly, givers every day: to them I bow.
Servant, master and friend of Sītā's lord, they are in every way the selfless well-wishers of Tulasīdāsa.
bal.15.cau3: Seeing the Kali age, Śiva and Girijā, for the good of the world, created the whole web of Śābara spells,
whose letters are ill-matched, with no sense and no japa; yet by the might of Maheśa their power is plain to see.
bal.15.cau4: That lord of Umā, being kind to me, will make this story a root of joy and blessing.
Remembering Śivā and Śiva and receiving their grace, I tell the deeds of Śrī Rāma with an eager heart.
bal.15.cau5: By Śiva's grace my verse shines like a lovely night joined with the moon and its host of stars.
Those who tell and hear this story with love, with understanding and with attention,
bal.15.cau6: will come to love Śrī Rāma's feet, be free of the impurity of the Kali age, and have a share in great blessing.
bal.15.do15: If the grace of Śiva and Gaurī is upon me both in dream and in truth,
then may all I have said of the power of verse in the common tongue come true.
bal.16.cau1: I salute the most holy city of Avadh, and the river Sarayū that destroys the impurity of the Kali age.
Then I bow to the men and women of that city, on whom the Lord's affection is far from small.
bal.16.cau2: The Lord destroyed the mass of sins of those who slandered Sītā, and he freed those townspeople of sorrow and settled them in his own realm.
I salute Kausalyā, the eastern quarter, whose fame has spread through all the world,
bal.16.cau3: from which Śrī Rāma rose like a lovely moon, a joy to the world and frost to the lotuses that are the wicked.
King Daśaratha with all his queens, whom I hold to be the very form of merit and blessing,
bal.16.cau4: I bow to them in deed, mind and word: knowing me the servant of your son, be gracious to me.
By creating them the Creator became great; they, Śrī Rāma's father and mother, are the very limit of glory.
bal.16.so16: I salute the king of Avadh, whose love for Śrī Rāma's feet was true,
who, on being parted from the Lord compassionate to the lowly, gave up his dear body like a blade of grass.
bal.17.cau1: I bow to Videha, King Janaka, with his household, who held a deep love for Śrī Rāma's feet.
He kept it hidden within his yoga and his enjoyments, but at the sight of Śrī Rāma it came to light.
bal.17.cau2: First I bow to the feet of Bharata, whose rules and vows are beyond telling,
and whose mind, like an enamoured bee, never leaves the side of Śrī Rāma's lotus feet.
bal.17.cau3: I salute the lotus feet of Lakṣmaṇa, cool, lovely and a joy to devotees,
whose fame became like the staff of the spotless banner of Śrī Rāma's glory.
bal.17.cau4: The thousand-headed Śeṣa, the cause of the world, who came down to rid the earth of fear:
may he, the son of Sumitrā, ocean of mercy and mine of virtues, always look kindly on me.
bal.17.cau5: I bow to the lotus feet of Śatrughna, brave, gentle, and the follower of Bharata.
I make my plea to the great hero Hanumān, whose fame Śrī Rāma himself has told.
bal.17.so17: I bow to Hanumān, son of the Wind, a fire to the forest of the wicked, full of wisdom.
In the house of his heart Śrī Rāma dwells, holding his bow and arrows.
bal.18.cau1: Sugrīva, king of the monkeys, Jāmbavān, king of the bears, Vibhīṣaṇa, king of the demons, and the host of monkeys led by Aṅgada:
I salute the lovely feet of them all, who found Śrī Rāma even in lowly bodies.
bal.18.cau2: All who worship the feet of Śrī Rāma, birds and beasts, gods and men, and the asuras with them:
I salute the lotus feet of them all, who are Śrī Rāma's servants without any desire.
bal.18.cau3: Śuka, Sanaka and his brothers, the devotee-sage Nārada, and all the great sages versed in realised knowledge:
to all of them I bow, my head laid on the ground. O lords of sages, know me as your servant and be gracious.
bal.18.cau4: Jānakī, daughter of Janaka and mother of the world, is exceedingly dear to the Lord, the treasury of compassion.
I pray to her two lotus feet, that by her grace I may gain a pure mind.
bal.18.cau5: Then in mind, word and deed I salute the lotus feet of Śrī Rāma, who is able in all things,
the lotus-eyed, bearing bow and arrows, who breaks the troubles of his devotees and gives them joy.
bal.18.do18: Like speech and its meaning, like water and its wave, they are spoken of as different, yet are not different:
I salute the feet of Sītā and Śrī Rāma, to whom the afflicted are supremely dear.
bal.19.cau1: I salute the name Rāma of Śrī Rāma, the cause of fire, the sun and the moon.
It is Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva in one, the life of the Vedas; beyond all qualities, beyond compare, and a treasury of virtues.
bal.19.cau2: It is the great mantra that Maheśa repeats, and which he teaches in Kāśī as the means of liberation.
Gaṇeśa knows its glory: it is by the power of this Name that he is worshipped first.
bal.19.cau3: The first poet, Vālmīki, knows the might of the Name: he became pure by repeating it reversed.
Hearing Śiva say it is equal to a thousand names, Bhavānī repeated it and took her meal with her beloved.
bal.19.cau4: Seeing this love in her heart, Śiva rejoiced, and made her, the ornament of women, his own ornament.
Śiva knows the Name's power well; through it the deadly Kālakūṭa poison gave him the fruit of nectar.
bal.19.do19: Tulasīdāsa says: devotion to Śrī Rāma is the rainy season, and true devotees are the rice;
the two fine letters of the name Rāma are the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada.
bal.20.cau1: Both letters are sweet and charming, the eyes of the alphabet and the life of devotees,
easy to remember, a joy to everyone, gain in this world and a support that carries one through in the next.
bal.20.cau2: Lovely to speak, to hear and to remember, they are as dear to Tulasīdāsa as Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Described letter by letter, the love seems divided; yet like Brahman and the soul they are companions by nature,
bal.20.cau3: good brothers like Nara and Nārāyaṇa, sustainers of the world and above all protectors of devotees.
They are the lovely ear-ornaments of the noble lady Devotion, and, for the good of the world, a spotless moon and sun.
bal.20.cau4: They are like the taste and the contentment of the nectar of liberation, like the Tortoise and Śeṣa who uphold the earth,
like bees to the lovely lotus of the devotee's mind, and to the tongue as Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma were to Yaśodā.
bal.20.do20: See: over all the letters, one is the royal umbrella and the other the crest-jewel;
Tulasīdāsa says: so the two letters of Śrī Rāma's name shine.
bal.21.cau1: To the understanding, the Name and the one named are alike, and their love for each other is that of a master and the one who follows him.
Name and form are the two defining adjuncts of the Lord, beyond telling and without beginning, grasped by right understanding.
bal.21.cau2: To say which is greater and which smaller is an offence; hearing of their qualities, the good will see the difference.
Forms are seen to depend on the name: without the name there is no knowing the form.
bal.21.cau3: Even a particular form lying in the palm of one's hand is not recognised without knowing its name.
Remember the name, even without seeing the form, and the form comes into the heart with a special love.
bal.21.cau4: The ways of name and form are a tale beyond telling; to understand it is a joy, but it cannot be described.
Between the Lord without qualities and the Lord with qualities, the Name is a true witness, a skilled interpreter who makes each known.
bal.21.do21: Set the jewel-lamp of Rāma's name on your tongue, the threshold of the door,
if, says Tulasīdāsa, you want light both within and without.
bal.22.cau1: Yogīs, set apart by dispassion from the world that Brahmā has spread out, chant the Name with the tongue and stay awake,
and taste the incomparable bliss of Brahman, which is beyond words and free from all ill, and has neither name nor form.
bal.22.cau2: Those who wish to know the deep and hidden truth also come to know it by chanting the Name with the tongue.
Seekers chant the Name with their minds absorbed in it, and become siddhas, gaining aṇimā and the other powers.
bal.22.cau3: When people in great distress chant the Name, their dire troubles vanish and they become happy.
In the world the devotees of Śrī Rāma are of four kinds, and all four are virtuous, sinless and noble.
bal.22.cau4: For all four of these wise ones the Name is their support, and of them the one who knows is especially dear to the Lord.
In all four ages and in all four Vedas the Name has power, in Kali above all, for in it there is no other means.
bal.22.do22: Those who have no desire of any kind and are steeped in the sweetness of devotion to Śrī Rāma
have also made their minds the fish in the lake of nectar that is pure love for the Name.
bal.23.cau1: Without attributes and with attributes: these are the two forms of Brahman, both beyond words, unfathomable, without beginning and without equal.
In my view the Name is greater than both, for by its own strength it has brought both under its sway.
bal.23.cau2: Let the good not take this for boldness on the part of their servant; I speak of the faith, the love and the longing of my heart.
One fire lies hidden in the wood and one is seen by the eye; the two forms of Brahman are to be understood as being like this fire.
bal.23.cau3: Both are hard to reach, and the Name makes both easy to reach; that is why I have called the Name greater than Brahman and than Śrī Rāma.
Brahman is all-pervading, one and imperishable; it is being and consciousness, a dense mass of bliss.
bal.23.cau4: Though such a Lord, free from all change, dwells in the heart, every being in the world is wretched and unhappy.
Through knowing the Name truly and striving with the Name, that Lord too becomes manifest, as a jewel's worth comes to light when it is tested.
bal.23.do23: In this way the Name is greater than the Lord without attributes, and its power is boundless.
By my own reasoning I say that the Name is greater even than Śrī Rāma.
bal.24.cau1: For the good of his devotees Śrī Rāma took a human body, and by bearing hardship he made the good happy;
but devotees who chant the Name with love become, with no effort, a home of joy and blessing.
bal.24.cau2: Śrī Rāma set free one woman, Ahalyā, the wife of an ascetic, but the Name has set right the evil minds of millions of the wicked.
For the good of the sage Viśvāmitra, Śrī Rāma made an end of Tāṭakā, the daughter of Suketu, with her son and her army;
bal.24.cau3: but the Name destroys the evil hopes of its servants, with their faults and sorrows, as the sun destroys the night.
Śrī Rāma himself broke the bow of Bhava (Śiva), but the glory of the Name breaks the fear of bhava, worldly existence.
bal.24.cau4: The Lord made the Daṇḍaka forest lovely, but the Name has made the minds of countless people pure.
Śrī Rāma crushed the hosts of demons, but the Name uproots all the sins of Kali.
bal.24.do24: Śrī Rāma gave the blessed state to his good servants Śabarī and the vulture Jaṭāyu;
but the Name has saved countless wicked ones, and the tale of its virtues is known in the Vedas.
bal.25.cau1: Śrī Rāma kept two, Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa, under his protection, as everyone knows;
but the Name has shown favour to many of the humble, and this great fame of the Name shines in the world and in the Vedas.
bal.25.cau2: Śrī Rāma brought together an army of bears and monkeys and laboured hard to build the bridge;
but when the Name is taken, oceans of worldly existence dry up. Good people, consider this in your minds.
bal.25.cau3: Śrī Rāma slew Rāvaṇa in battle with all his house, and with Sītā he set foot in his own city.
Śrī Rāma became king with Avadh as his capital, and gods and sages sing his virtues in noble words.
bal.25.cau4: But a servant who lovingly remembers the Name conquers the mighty army of delusion without any toil,
and goes about immersed in love, in a joy of his own; by the grace of the Name he knows no care even in a dream.
bal.25.do25: Thus the Name is greater than both Brahman and Śrī Rāma, and gives boons even to those who give boons.
Śiva knew this in his heart, and from the hundred crore verses of Rāma's story he took the Name for himself.
bal.26.cau1: By the grace of the Name Śiva is imperishable, and though his trappings are inauspicious, he is a mass of all that is auspicious.
Śuka, Sanaka and his brothers, the siddhas, sages and yogīs enjoy the bliss of Brahman by the grace of the Name.
bal.26.cau2: Nārada knew the glory of the Name; the world holds Hari dear, and Nārada himself is dear to Hari and to Hara.
Because Prahlāda chanted the Name, the Lord showed him grace, and he became the crest-jewel of devotees.
bal.26.cau3: Dhruva, in his hurt, chanted the name of Hari, and won a place unmoving and beyond compare.
By remembering the holy Name, Hanumān, son of the Wind, has kept Śrī Rāma in his power.
bal.26.cau4: The fallen Ajāmila, the elephant Gajendra and the courtesan were set free by the power of the name of Hari.
How far can I go in telling the greatness of the Name? Even Śrī Rāma cannot sing the virtues of the Name.
bal.26.do26: The name of Śrī Rāma is a wish-fulfilling tree in the age of Kali, a home of all welfare;
by remembering it Tulasīdāsa, who was like hemp, has become like the holy tulasī.
bal.27.cau1: In all four ages, in all three times and in all three worlds, beings have been freed from sorrow by chanting the Name.
This is the view of the Vedas, the Purāṇas and the saints: the fruit of all good deeds is love for Śrī Rāma.
bal.27.cau2: In the first age the Lord is pleased by meditation, in the second by the rites of sacrifice, and in Dvāpara by worship.
But Kali is nothing but impurity, the very root of impurity; in it the minds of people are fish in an ocean of sin.
bal.27.cau3: In this fearsome time the Name is a wish-fulfilling tree, and remembering it ends all the entanglements of the world.
In the age of Kali the name of Rāma grants what one desires; it is a friend for the world to come and father and mother in this one.
bal.27.cau4: In Kali there is neither the way of works nor devotion nor discernment; the name of Rāma is the one support.
Kali is Kālanemi, a storehouse of deceit; the Name is Hanumān, wise and mighty.
bal.27.do27: The name of Rāma is the Man-Lion, and the age of Kali is Hiraṇyakaśipu;
the Name will crush that tormentor of the gods and protect those who chant it, as Prahlāda was protected.
bal.28.cau1: Whether it is chanted with love or with ill will, in anger or in idleness, the Name brings blessing in all ten directions.
With that Name in my remembrance, and my head bowed to Śrī Rāma, I compose the tale of Śrī Rāma's virtues.
bal.28.cau2: He will put right what has gone wrong with me in every way, he whose grace is never sated with showing grace.
Śrī Rāma so good a master, and a bad servant like me! Yet the treasury of mercy has looked to his own nature and cherished me.
bal.28.cau3: In the world and in the Vedas alike, this is the way of a good master: as he hears a humble plea, he knows the love in it.
Rich or poor, of village or town, learned or foolish, of ill repute or renowned,
bal.28.cau4: good poet or bad, all men and women praise the king, each as far as their understanding goes;
and a king who is good, wise and gentle, born of a portion of God and supremely kind,
bal.28.cau5: listens and honours them all with kind words, knowing each one's words, devotion, humility and state.
Such is the nature of earthly kings; the king of Kosala is the crest-jewel of those who know.
bal.28.cau6: Śrī Rāma is won by pure love alone; but who in the world is as dull and as impure of mind as I am?
bal.28.do28क: Yet compassionate Śrī Rāma will honour the love and the longing of this wicked servant,
he who made ships of stones and wise counsellors of monkeys and bears.
bal.28.do28ख: I too am called his servant, and everyone says so, and Śrī Rāma bears the ridicule
that so great a master as the Lord of Sītā has so poor a servant as Tulasīdāsa.
bal.29.cau1: Very great are my boldness and my fault; even hell, hearing of my sins, has wrinkled its nose.
Seeing this, I shrink with a fear of my own making; yet Śrī Rāma has never given it a thought, even in a dream.
bal.29.cau2: Hearing it, looking, and searching with an attentive mind and eye, my Master praised my devotion and my understanding.
Though a thing may be spoiled in the telling, if it is good in the heart, Śrī Rāma is pleased, knowing his servant's heart.
bal.29.cau3: The Lord's mind does not keep a fault once committed, but he recalls the heart's good a hundred times.
The very sin for which he killed Vāli as a hunter kills, that same misdeed Sugrīva committed afterwards.
bal.29.cau4: That same was the deed of Vibhīṣaṇa, yet Śrī Rāma did not hold it in his heart even in a dream.
Śrī Rāma honoured them both when he met Bharata, and praised them in the royal court.
bal.29.do29क: The Lord sat under the trees and the monkeys on the branches, yet even such as they he made equal to himself.
Tulasīdāsa says: nowhere is there a master like Śrī Rāma, a treasury of goodness.
bal.29.do29ख: O Rāma, by your goodness it goes well with everyone.
If this is always true, then it will go well with Tulasī too.
bal.29.do29ग: Having told my own merits and faults in this way, and once more bowed my head to all,
I describe the bright glory of Śrī Rāma, by hearing which the sins of Kali perish.
bal.30.cau1: The lovely story which Yājñavalkya told to Bharadvāja, best of sages,
that same dialogue I shall tell in full; let all good people listen to it with delight.
bal.30.cau2: Śiva composed this lovely story and then graciously told it to Umā.
That same story Śiva gave to Kākabhuśuṇḍi, knowing him for a devotee of Śrī Rāma and one fit to receive it.
bal.30.cau3: From him Yājñavalkya then received it, and he in turn sang it to Bharadvāja.
These listeners and speakers are alike in goodness, see all with an equal eye, and know the play of Hari.
bal.30.cau4: By their own knowledge they know the three times like an Indian gooseberry lying in the palm of the hand.
Other wise devotees of Hari also tell it, hear it and understand it in many ways.
bal.30.do30क: I too then heard that story from my own guru at Sūkarakṣetra;
but I did not understand it as it is, for I was a child then and knew very little.
bal.30.do30ख: The listener and the speaker are treasuries of knowledge, and the story of Śrī Rāma is deep;
how could I understand it, a dull soul, seized by the impurity of Kali and utterly deluded?
bal.31.cau1: Even so, my guru told it again and again, and I understood something of it, as far as my mind allowed.
That I shall set in the common tongue, so that my own mind may come to understand it.
bal.31.cau2: Such strength of intellect and discernment as I have, so far shall I tell it, as Śrī Hari moves me in my heart.
I make this story, which takes away my own doubt, delusion and error, a boat to cross the river of worldly existence.
bal.31.cau3: The story of Rāma is rest for the wise, a delight to all people, and the destroyer of the sins of the Kali age.
The story of Rāma is a peahen to the serpent of the Kali age, and the kindling-wood (araṇi) that brings forth the fire of discernment.
bal.31.cau4: The story of Rāma is the wish-granting cow in the Kali age, and a lovely life-giving herb for good people.
It is a river of nectar on the face of the earth, the breaker of fear, a serpent to the frogs of error.
bal.31.cau5: Like Pārvatī, the mountain's daughter, it destroys the hells as she destroys the armies of demons, and works the good of the saints, who are the race of the gods.
To the ocean of the assembly of saints it is like Lakṣmī, and in bearing the weight of the universe it is like the steadfast earth.
bal.31.cau6: In the world it is like the Yamunā, blackening the faces of Yama's messengers, and for the liberation of living beings it is Kāśī, as it were.
It is dear to Śrī Rāma like the purifying tulasī, and to Tulasīdāsa it is like Hulasī, his mother, who wished him well from her heart.
bal.31.cau7: It is like the daughter of Mount Mekala, the Narmadā, dear to Śiva, and it is a heap of every success, happiness and wealth.
To the host of virtues it is like Aditi, mother of the gods, and it is like the very height of devotion and love for Śrī Rāma.
bal.31.do31: The story of Rāma is the Mandākinī river, and the lovely mind is Citrakūṭa hill;
Tulasīdāsa says: fair love is the forest in which Sītā and Śrī Rāma wander at play.
bal.32.cau1: The deeds of Śrī Rāma are a lovely wish-fulfilling gem, the fair adornment of the lady that is the good sense of the saints.
The host of Śrī Rāma's virtues is the welfare of the world, the giver of liberation, wealth, dharma and the Lord's abode.
bal.32.cau2: They are the true teachers of knowledge, dispassion and yoga, and the physicians of the gods for the dread disease of worldly existence.
They are mother and father of love for Sītā and Śrī Rāma, and the seed of every vow, every dharma and every observance.
bal.32.cau3: They allay sin, anguish and grief, and are the loving protectors of this world and the next.
To reflection, the king, they are minister and mighty warrior, and to the boundless ocean of greed they are Agastya, the sage born of a pot.
bal.32.cau4: In the forest of the devotees' minds they are lion cubs to the herds of elephants that are desire, anger and the impurities of the Kali age.
They are guests worshipped by Śiva, the foe of Tripura, and most dear to him, and wish-granting clouds over the forest fire of poverty.
bal.32.cau5: To the serpent of the objects of sense they are the charm and the great gem, and they wipe away the hard ill-fortune written on the forehead.
Like the rays of the sun they take away the darkness of delusion, and as clouds nourish the paddy, they nourish the servants of the Lord.
bal.32.cau6: Like the finest tree of heaven they give what is desired; like Hari and Hara they are easy to reach and give joy to those who serve them.
They are like the stars in the autumn sky of good poets' minds, and like life's treasure to the devotees of Śrī Rāma.
bal.32.cau7: They are like the abundant joys that are the fruit of all good deeds, and like saints who seek the good of the world without guile.
They are like swans on the Mānasa lake of the servants' minds, and like the rows of waves of the purifying Gaṅgā.
bal.32.do32क: Wrong paths, false reasoning, evil conduct, and the deceit, pretence and hypocrisy of the Kali age,
the host of Śrī Rāma's virtues burns them all, as a fierce fire burns fuel.
bal.32.do32ख: The deeds of Śrī Rāma, like the rays of the full moon, give joy to all,
but to the hearts of the good, who are the night-lotuses and the cakora birds, they are a special blessing and a great gain.
bal.33.cau1: How Bhavānī asked her question, and in what way Śaṅkara explained and answered it,
all of it, with its reasons, I shall sing and tell, shaping the story into a wondrous composition.
bal.33.cau2: Whoever has not heard this story before should not wonder at it on hearing it.
The wise who hear this story beyond the world do not wonder at it, for they know
bal.33.cau3: that the story of Rāma has no bounds in the world: such is the conviction in their minds.
Śrī Rāma has descended in many ways, and the Rāmāyaṇas are a thousand million, without end.
bal.33.cau4: In the different aeons the great sages have sung the lovely deeds of Śrī Hari in many ways.
Bearing this in mind, do not doubt, but hear the story with reverence and love.
bal.33.do33: Śrī Rāma is endless, endless are his virtues, and the spread of his story is boundless;
those whose thoughts are pure will not wonder on hearing it.
bal.34.cau1: Having thus set all doubts aside, and placing on my head the dust of my guru's lotus feet,
I again entreat everyone with joined palms, so that no fault may touch me as I tell the story.
bal.34.cau2: Now, bowing my head with reverence to Śiva, I tell the clear tale of Śrī Rāma's virtues.
In the year Saṁvat sixteen hundred and thirty-one, with my head at Śrī Hari's feet, I compose this story.
bal.34.cau3: On the ninth day of the month of Caitra, a Tuesday, this story came to light in the city of Ayodhyā.
On the day the Vedas celebrate as the day of Śrī Rāma's birth, all the places of pilgrimage come there.
bal.34.cau4: Demons, nāgas, birds, men, sages and gods come and serve Śrī Rāma.
The wise hold the great festival of his birth and sing the lovely fame of Śrī Rāma.
bal.34.do34: Crowds of good people bathe in the holy water of the Sarayū,
and, meditating in their hearts on his lovely dark form, repeat the name of Rāma.
bal.35.cau1: Seeing this river, touching it, bathing in it and drinking its water take away sin, say the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
The river is holy; its glory is so boundless that even Sarasvatī, of spotless mind, cannot tell it.
bal.35.cau2: This lovely city gives Śrī Rāma's own abode; it is known in all the worlds and is supremely purifying.
The world holds countless beings of the four kinds of birth; for those who leave the body in Ayodhyā, worldly existence is no more.
bal.35.cau3: Knowing the city to be lovely in every way, the giver of every success and a mine of blessings,
I began this spotless story, on hearing which desire, pride and hypocrisy perish.
bal.35.cau4: Its name is Rāmacaritamānasa (the Mānasa lake of Śrī Rāma's deeds); one finds rest the moment one's ears hear it.
The elephant of the mind is burning in the forest fire of the objects of sense; if it falls into this lake, it becomes happy.
bal.35.cau5: This Rāmacaritamānasa, dear to sages, lovely and holy, was composed by Śiva.
It crushes the threefold faults, sorrows and poverty, and destroys the evil ways of the Kali age and all its sins.
bal.35.cau6: Śiva composed it and kept it in his own mānasa, his mind, and when the right moment came, he told it to Pārvatī.
That is why Śiva, looking into his heart, joyfully gave it the fine name Rāmacaritamānasa.
bal.35.cau7: That same joyful, lovely story I now tell; good people, listen with reverence and with your whole mind.
bal.35.do35: What this Mānasa is like, how it came to be, and why it spread through the world:
all that I now tell, remembering Umā and Śiva.
bal.36.cau1: By Śiva's grace good sense welled up in the heart, and Tulasīdāsa became the poet of the Rāmacaritamānasa.
He makes it as lovely as his understanding allows; good people, listen with attentive minds and set it right.
bal.36.cau2: Good sense is the land, and the heart a deep hollow in it; the Vedas and Purāṇas are the ocean, and the saints the clouds.
They rain down the fine water of Śrī Rāma's fair fame, sweet, lovely and full of blessing.
bal.36.cau3: The Lord's play in his embodied form, which they tell at length, is the clearness of this water, which washes away impurity;
and loving devotion, which cannot be described, is its sweetness and its pleasant coolness.
bal.36.cau4: That water does good to the paddy of good deeds, and it is the very life of the devotees of Śrī Rāma.
Fallen on the ground of the intellect, that holy water gathered and flowed, lovely, along the channel of the ears;
bal.36.cau5: it filled the fine Mānasa lake and settled there in a good place, and, growing old, became pleasant, cool, delightful and lovely.
bal.36.do36: The very lovely and excellent dialogues, composed with careful thought,
are the four charming bathing-places of this holy and lovely lake.
bal.37.cau1: Its seven books are the lovely steps, and the mind delights to see them with the eye of knowledge.
The glory of Śrī Rāma, beyond attributes and beyond all bounds, which I shall describe, is the unfathomable depth of this fine water.
bal.37.cau2: The fame of Śrī Rāma and Sītā is its nectar-like water, and the similes are the charming play of its waves.
The lovely caupāīs are its thick lotus leaves, and the turns of poetic skill its fair shells that hold fine pearls.
bal.37.cau3: The chanda, soraṭhā and lovely dohā verses are its clusters of many-coloured lotuses,
and the matchless meaning, fine sentiment and fine diction are their pollen, nectar and fragrance.
bal.37.cau4: Heaps of good deeds are its lovely rows of bees, and knowledge, dispassion and reflection its swans.
The suggestion, the oblique turns, the qualities and the kinds of poetry are its many sorts of charming fish.
bal.37.cau5: The four aims of life, wealth, dharma, desire and the rest, and knowledge and realised knowledge, which I shall tell after reflection,
the nine rasas, japa, austerity, yoga and dispassion: all these are the lovely creatures of the water in this lake.
bal.37.cau6: The songs in praise of the virtuous, of the saints and of the Name are like the many kinds of water-birds.
The assembly of saints is the mango grove on all four sides, and faith is said to be like the season of spring.
bal.37.cau7: The exposition of devotion in its many forms, and forgiveness, compassion and self-restraint are its bowers of creepers;
tranquillity, the yamas and the niyamas are their flowers, knowledge their fruit, and love for Śrī Hari's feet the juice of that fruit, as the Vedas declare.
bal.37.cau8: The many other stories and episodes are its parrots, cuckoos and birds of many colours.
bal.37.do37: The thrill of rapture is its gardens, orchards and woods, and joy the sporting of its lovely birds.
The good mind is the gardener, who waters them with the water of love from lovely eyes.
bal.38.cau1: Those who sing this story with care are the skilled guardians of this lake.
The men and women who always hear it with reverence are the noblest of gods, those entitled to this Mānasa.
bal.38.cau2: The very wicked, given to sense-pleasures, are the herons and crows; the unfortunate ones do not go near this lake.
Here there are none of the many savoury tales of sense-pleasure, which are like snails, frogs and water-weed.
bal.38.cau3: For that reason the poor lustful crows and cranes lose heart on the way here.
Coming to this lake is very hard; without Śrī Rāma's grace no one can reach it.
bal.38.cau4: Hard, evil company is the fearsome wrong road, and the words of such company are the tigers, lions and snakes.
The work of the household and its many entanglements are the vast mountains, very hard to cross.
bal.38.cau5: The many trackless forests are delusion, pride and vanity, and the fearsome rivers are sophistries of every kind.
bal.38.do38: For those who lack faith, the provisions for the road, and have not the company of saints,
and to whom Śrī Rāma is not dear, this Mānasa is very hard to reach.
bal.39.cau1: If someone does take the pains to get there, as soon as he arrives sleep comes over him like a fit of ague.
The bitter cold of dullness grips his heart, and though he has come, the unfortunate one cannot bathe.
bal.39.cau2: He can neither bathe in the lake nor drink from it, and he comes back still carrying his pride.
And if anyone then comes to ask him, he answers him by running down the lake.
bal.39.cau3: None of these obstacles trouble the one on whom Śrī Rāma looks with special grace.
He alone bathes in the lake with reverence and is not burnt by the threefold affliction, great and terrible as it is.
bal.39.cau4: Those who have a true love for Śrī Rāma's feet never leave this lake.
Brother, whoever wishes to bathe in this lake should keep the company of the good (satsaṅga) with all his heart.
bal.39.cau5: Seeing such a Mānasa with the eye of the mind, the poet's intellect plunged into it and became pure.
Joy and eagerness rose in his heart, and love and delight surged up in a flood.
bal.39.cau6: From it flowed the lovely river of poetry, full of the water of Śrī Rāma's spotless fame.
Its name is Sarayū, the root of all that is auspicious; the ways of the world and of the Veda are its two fair banks.
bal.39.cau7: This holy river, daughter of the fair Mānasa, tears up by the roots the grass and trees of the impurities of the Kali age.
bal.39.do39: The gatherings of listeners of three kinds are the towns, villages and cities on its two banks;
the assembly of saints is the matchless Avadh, root of all that is auspicious.
bal.40.cau1: Devotion to Śrī Rāma is the Gaṅgā, and the lovely Sarayū of fair fame went and joined it.
The holy fame of Śrī Rāma and his younger brother Lakṣmaṇa in battle joined it as the lovely great river Son.
bal.40.cau2: Between the two the stream of the divine river of devotion shines, together with true dispassion and reflection.
This meeting of three streams, which strikes terror into the threefold affliction, flows on towards the ocean of Śrī Rāma's own being.
bal.40.cau3: Rising in the Mānasa and joined with the Gaṅgā, it will purify the minds of the good who hear it.
The varied episodes of the story here and there are like the woods and gardens along each of its banks.
bal.40.cau4: The guests at the wedding of Umā and Maheśa are its countless water creatures of many kinds.
The joy and rejoicing at the birth of Śrī Rāma are the charm of its whirlpools and waves.
bal.40.do40: The childhood deeds of the four brothers are its many lotuses of many colours.
The merits of the king, the queens and the household are its bees and water-birds.
bal.41.cau1: The lovely story of Sītā's svayaṃvara (her choosing of a husband) is the beauty that spreads over this fair river.
The boats on the river are the many shrewd questions, and the skilled boatmen the wise answers.
bal.41.cau2: The talk that people have with one another after hearing it is the company of travellers that graces the river.
Its fierce current is the wrath of Paraśurāma, lord of the Bhṛgus, and its firmly built bathing steps are Śrī Rāma's noble words.
bal.41.cau3: The festivities of the wedding of Śrī Rāma and his younger brothers are the river's auspicious flood, a joy to everyone.
Those who rejoice and thrill as they tell it and hear it are the virtuous who bathe in it with glad hearts.
bal.41.cau4: The auspicious preparations for Śrī Rāma's coronation are like the crowds that gather on a festival day.
The moss upon it is Kaikeyī's evil thinking, and its fruit was the heavy calamity that fell.
bal.41.do41: Bharata's story is the japa and sacrifice that quell all the countless calamities.
The telling of the sins of the Kali age and the failings of the wicked is the scum of the water, the herons and the crows.
bal.42.cau1: This river of fame is lovely in all six seasons; at every time it is fair and greatly purifying.
Its frost season (hemanta) is the marriage of Śiva and the daughter of the Himālaya, and its pleasant late winter (śiśira) the festival of the Lord's birth.
bal.42.cau2: The wedding pageant of Śrī Rāma that I shall describe is the king of seasons, spring, full of joy and blessing.
The unbearable summer is Śrī Rāma's going to the forest, and the story of the journey is its fierce sun and scorching wind.
bal.42.cau3: The rainy season is the fierce war with the demons, a great blessing to the rice crop that is the race of the gods.
The happiness, the humility and the greatness of Śrī Rāma's reign are the clear, pleasant and lovely autumn.
bal.42.cau4: The tale of the virtues of Sītā, crown of faithful wives, is the pure and matchless quality of its water.
Bharata's nature is its perfect coolness, ever the same and beyond all describing.
bal.42.do42: The four brothers' glances at one another, their talk and their meetings, their mutual love and laughter,
and the true brotherhood among them are the sweetness and fragrance of the water.
bal.43.cau1: My distress, my pleading and my lowliness are the pleasing lightness of this good water, and there is no little of it.
This wondrous water does good merely by being heard, and takes away the thirst of longing and the impurity of the mind.
bal.43.cau2: It nourishes pure love for Śrī Rāma and takes away all the sins and the dejection of the Kali age.
It dries up the weariness of worldly existence, satisfies contentment itself, and quells sin, sorrow, poverty and faults.
bal.43.cau3: It destroys desire, anger, pride and delusion, and increases pure discernment and dispassion.
Bathing in it and drinking it with reverence wipes sin and anguish from the heart.
bal.43.cau4: Those who have not washed their minds in this water are cowards whom the Kali age has cheated.
Like thirsty deer that see the water made by the sun's rays, a mirage, those beings will wander about in misery.
bal.43.do43क: Having counted, as far as his understanding goes, the many virtues of this good water, and bathed his mind in it,
the poet, remembering Bhavānī and Śaṅkara, tells the lovely story.
bal.43.do43ख: Now, holding the lotus feet of Śrī Rāma in my heart and receiving his grace,
I tell the beautiful dialogue at the meeting of the two great sages.
bal.44.cau1: The sage Bharadvāja lives at Prayāga; he has the deepest love for Śrī Rāma's feet.
An ascetic, a treasury of calm, self-restraint and compassion, he is supremely wise in the way to the highest good.
bal.44.cau2: In the month of Māgha, when the sun enters Capricorn, everyone comes to Prayāga, the king of holy places.
Gods, demons, kinnaras (celestial musicians) and men in their ranks all bathe with reverence at the Triveṇī.
bal.44.cau3: They worship the lotus feet of Veṇīmādhava, and their bodies thrill with joy as they touch the undying banyan.
Bharadvāja's hermitage is most holy, supremely delightful and dear to the hearts of great sages.
bal.44.cau4: There the sages and seers who go to the king of holy places to bathe gather together.
They bathe at dawn with eagerness and tell one another the tales of Śrī Hari's virtues.
bal.44.do44: They expound the nature of Brahman, the rules of dharma and the distinctions among the principles of being,
and speak of devotion to the Lord, joined with knowledge and dispassion.
bal.45.cau1: So they bathe all through Māgha, and then all go back to their own hermitages.
Every year there is great joy; after bathing in the season of Makara the companies of sages depart.
bal.45.cau2: Once, after the whole season of Makara had been spent in bathing, all the great sages left for their hermitages.
Bharadvāja clasped the feet of the supremely discerning sage Yājñavalkya and kept him back.
bal.45.cau3: With reverence he washed his lotus feet and seated him on a most holy seat.
After worshipping him, the sage praised his fair fame and spoke in most holy and gentle words:
bal.45.cau4: My lord, I have one great doubt, and the whole truth of the Vedas lies in your hand.
I feel fear and shame in speaking of it, yet if I do not speak, great harm will come.
bal.45.do45: My lord, the saints state this rule, and the Vedas, Purāṇas and sages sing it too:
Pure discernment does not arise in the heart of one who keeps secrets from his guru.
bal.46.cau1: With this in mind I lay bare my delusion; my lord, be kind to your servant and take it away.
The saints, the Purāṇas and the Upaniṣads have sung of the boundless power of the name of Rāma.
bal.46.cau2: The imperishable Śambhu, the Lord Śiva, a treasury of knowledge and virtue, repeats it without ceasing.
The beings of the four kinds of birth in the world attain the supreme state when they die in Kāśī.
bal.46.cau3: That too, king of sages, is the glory of Rāma's name, which Śiva in his mercy teaches them.
My lord, I ask you: who is Rāma? Treasury of mercy, explain it to me.
bal.46.cau4: One Rāma is the son of the king of Avadh, whose deeds are known to all the world.
He suffered boundless grief in separation from his wife, and in his anger killed Rāvaṇa in battle.
bal.46.do46: My lord, is it this Rāma, or someone else, whose name Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura, repeats?
You are the abode of truth and know all; weigh it with discernment and tell me.
bal.47.cau1: My lord, tell me that story in full, so that this great delusion of mine may be removed.
Yājñavalkya smiled and said: The greatness of Śrī Rāma is known to you.
bal.47.cau2: You are a devotee of Śrī Rāma in thought, deed and word, and I have seen through your cleverness.
You want to hear the profound virtues of Śrī Rāma, and so you have asked as though you knew nothing at all.
bal.47.cau3: Dear one, listen with reverence and with your whole mind; I tell the lovely story of Śrī Rāma.
Great delusion is the huge buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura, and the story of Śrī Rāma is the fearsome goddess Kālikā.
bal.47.cau4: The story of Śrī Rāma is like the rays of the moon, which the saints drink in as the cakora birds do.
Bhavānī had just such a doubt, and Mahādeva then explained it to her at length.
bal.47.do47: Now, as far as my understanding reaches, I tell that dialogue of Umā and Śiva.
Hear, sage, when it took place and for what reason, and your sorrow will be gone.
bal.48.cau1: Once, in the Tretā age, Śiva went to the sage Agastya, who was born from a pitcher.
With him was Satī, Bhavānī, the mother of the world. Knowing him to be the Lord of all, the sage worshipped him.
bal.48.cau2: The great sage told the story of Śrī Rāma, and Śiva listened to it with delight.
Then the sage asked about lovely devotion to Hari, and Śiva, finding him a worthy listener, told him of it.
bal.48.cau3: Telling and hearing the tales of Śrī Rāma's virtues, Śiva, lord of the mountain, stayed there some days.
Then, taking leave of the sage, Śiva, the enemy of Tripura, set off for home with Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa.
bal.48.cau4: At that time Śrī Hari had come down as an avatāra in the line of Raghu, to remove the burden of the earth.
Giving up the kingdom at his father's word, the imperishable Lord was roaming the Daṇḍaka forest as one detached from the world.
bal.48.do48क: As he went, Śiva pondered in his heart how he might see the Lord.
The Lord has come down in a hidden form; if I go to him, everyone will know.
bal.48.so48ख: There was great turmoil in Śiva's heart, but Satī did not know its secret.
Tulasīdāsa says: he longed to see him; his mind was afraid, but his eyes were greedy for the sight.
bal.49.cau1: Rāvaṇa asked for his death at the hands of a man, and the Lord wants to make Brahmā's word come true.
If I do not go, I will be left with regret. Śiva kept thinking it over, but could find no way that would work.
bal.49.cau2: So the Lord Śiva fell prey to worry. At that very time Rāvaṇa went
and took the base Mārīca with him, and Mārīca at once became a false deer.
bal.49.cau3: The fool carried off Vaidehī by a trick; he did not know the Lord's power for what it was.
Having slain the deer, Śrī Hari came back with his brother, and seeing the hermitage empty, his eyes filled with tears.
bal.49.cau4: Like any man, Śrī Rāma is distraught at the separation; the two brothers wander through the forest searching.
In him who never knows union or parting, the pain of separation was plainly seen.
bal.49.do49: The deeds of Śrī Rāma are most wonderful; only the truly wise understand them.
Those of dull mind, in the grip of delusion, hold something else in their hearts.
bal.50.cau1: At that moment Śiva saw Śrī Rāma, and his heart was filled with a rare and great joy.
He gazed his fill on that ocean of beauty, but knowing the time was not right, he did not make himself known.
bal.50.cau2: Glory to him who is being, consciousness and bliss, who makes the world pure: saying this, Śiva, the destroyer of Kāma, went on.
Śiva, the abode of grace, went on his way with Satī, thrilling with joy again and again.
bal.50.cau3: Seeing Śiva in that state, Satī felt a great doubt arise in her heart, and she thought:
Śiva is revered by the world and is its Lord; before him gods, men and sages all bow their heads.
bal.50.cau4: Yet he has bowed to a king's son, calling him being, consciousness and bliss, the supreme abode,
and gazing on his beauty became so rapt that even now the love in his heart will not be held back.
bal.50.do50: Brahman, which is all-pervading, stainless, unborn, without parts, without desire and without distinction,
and which the Vedas do not know: can it take a body and become a man?
bal.51.cau1: Viṣṇu, who took a human body for the good of the gods, is all-knowing as Śiva is.
Would he, the abode of knowledge, the husband of Lakṣmī, the enemy of the asuras, search for a woman like one who does not know?
bal.51.cau2: Yet Śiva's word can never be false; everyone knows that Śiva knows all.
So a boundless doubt arose in her mind, and no light of understanding spread through her heart.
bal.51.cau3: Though Bhavānī said nothing openly, Śiva, who dwells within all, knew everything.
Śiva said: Listen, Satī; this is your nature as a woman. Such a doubt should never be kept in the heart.
bal.51.cau4: He whose story the sage Agastya sang, and of devotion to whom I spoke to the sage,
is Śrī Rāma, my chosen deity, whom steadfast sages ever serve.
bal.51.cha1: He on whom steadfast sages, yogīs and siddhas ever meditate with pure minds,
whose glory the Vedas, Purāṇas and Āgamas sing, saying neti (not this),
that same Śrī Rāma, the all-pervading Brahman, master of all the worlds and lord of māyā,
has come down for the sake of his devotees as the jewel of the Raghu line; he is ever free, bound by none.
bal.51.so51: Though Śiva told her many times, his teaching did not take hold in her heart.
Knowing in his heart the power of Hari's māyā, Śiva smiled and said:
bal.52.cau1: If your mind is so full of doubt, why do you not go and test him?
Until you come back to me, I will sit here in the shade of this banyan.
bal.52.cau2: Think with discernment and do whatever will clear away this great delusion and error.
With Śiva's leave Satī set out, wondering as she went: Well, what am I to do?
bal.52.cau3: Here Śiva reckoned in his mind that no good lay ahead for Dakṣa's daughter.
Her doubts do not go even when I tell her; fate is against her, and no good will come.
bal.52.cau4: Whatever Śrī Rāma has ordained, that alone will come to pass; who would argue and make it grow more branches?
With these words Śiva began to repeat the name of Hari, and Satī went to where the Lord, the abode of bliss, was.
bal.52.do52: Having thought it over again and again, Satī took on the form of Sītā
and went on ahead along the path by which the king of men was coming.
bal.53.cau1: Lakṣmaṇa saw the guise Umā had put on; he was astonished, and great bewilderment filled his heart.
Very grave, he could say nothing; steady of mind, he knew the Lord's power.
bal.53.cau2: The Lord of the gods, who sees all and dwells within all, knew Satī's deceit.
He is that all-knowing Lord Śrī Rāma, by remembering whom ignorance is dispelled.
bal.53.cau3: Even there Satī wanted to keep the truth hidden: see the power of a woman's nature.
Praising within himself the power of his own māyā, Śrī Rāma smiled and spoke in a gentle voice.
bal.53.cau4: The Lord joined his palms, bowed, and gave his own name together with his father's.
Then he said: Where is Śiva, whose banner bears the bull? Why are you wandering alone in the forest?
bal.53.do53: Hearing Śrī Rāma's gentle and deep words, Satī was overcome with embarrassment.
Afraid, she set off back to Śiva, with great anxiety in her heart.
bal.54.cau1: Satī thought: I did not heed what Śiva said, and laid my own ignorance on Śrī Rāma.
What answer will I give when I go back now? At this a terrible burning rose in her heart.
bal.54.cau2: Śrī Rāma knew that Satī was grieved, and revealed something of his power to her.
As she went along the way, Satī saw a marvel: ahead of her was Śrī Rāma, with Sītā and his brother.
bal.54.cau3: She turned to look behind her, and saw the Lord there as well, lovely in form, with his brother and Sītā.
Wherever she looked, there the Lord was seated, served by accomplished siddhas and great sages.
bal.54.cau4: She saw many Śivas, Brahmās and Viṣṇus, each of boundless might, one greater than the next.
She saw all the gods, in many forms, bowing at the Lord's feet and serving him.
bal.54.do54: She saw Satīs, Brahmāṇīs and Lakṣmīs without number and beyond compare,
each in a form to match whatever guise Brahmā and the other gods wore.
bal.55.cau1: As many Śrī Rāmas as she saw here and there, so many sets of all the gods did she see, with their consorts.
All the moving and unmoving beings in the world she saw as well, in their many kinds.
bal.55.cau2: Gods in many forms were worshipping the Lord, but she saw no second form of Śrī Rāma.
She saw Śrī Rāma with Sītā many times over, but not in many different guises.
bal.55.cau3: The same Śrī Rāma, the same Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā: seeing this, Satī was filled with fear.
Her heart trembled, she lost all awareness of her body, and she sat down on the path with her eyes shut.
bal.55.cau4: Then, opening her eyes, she looked, and Dakṣa's daughter could see nothing there.
Bowing her head again and again at Śrī Rāma's feet, she went to where Śiva, lord of the mountain, was.
bal.55.do55: When she came near, Śiva smiled and asked how she fared,
and said: How did you put him to the test? Tell me the whole truth.
bal.56.cau1: Satī had understood Śrī Rāma's power, and out of fear she hid the truth from Śiva.
She said: My lord, I put him to no test at all; I bowed to him just as you did.
bal.56.cau2: What you said cannot be false; I trust it completely in my heart.
Then Śiva looked in meditation and knew everything Satī had done.
bal.56.cau3: Then he bowed his head to Śrī Rāma's māyā, which had moved Satī to speak a lie.
Wise Śiva reflected in his heart that destiny, which is Hari's will, is mighty.
bal.56.cau4: Satī had taken the guise of Sītā, and at this a deep sorrow came over Śiva's heart.
He thought: If I now show love to Satī, the path of devotion will be lost and wrong will be done.
bal.56.do56: She is supremely pure, so she cannot be abandoned, and to love her would be a great sin.
Śiva says nothing openly, but there is deep anguish in his heart.
bal.57.cau1: Then Śaṅkara bowed his head at the Lord's feet, and as he remembered Śrī Rāma this came into his heart:
While Satī is in this body, there shall be no union between her and me. Śiva made this resolve in his mind.
bal.57.cau2: Having resolved thus, Śaṅkara, steady of mind, set off for his home, remembering Śrī Rāma.
As he went, a lovely voice sounded from the sky: Glory to Maheśa! You have held devotion firm, and held it well.
bal.57.cau3: Who else but you could make such a vow? You are Śrī Rāma's devotee, all-powerful, the Lord.
Hearing the voice from the sky, Satī grew anxious at heart, and with hesitation she asked Śiva:
bal.57.cau4: What vow have you made? Tell me, compassionate one, my Lord, home of truth, merciful to the lowly.
Though Satī asked in many ways, Śiva, the enemy of Tripura, did not tell her.
bal.57.do57क: Satī guessed in her heart that Śiva, who knows all, knew everything.
She thought: I, a woman dull and unknowing by nature, practised deceit on Śiva.
bal.57.so57ख: See how good is the way of love: water mixed in milk is sold as milk;
but then, once the sourness of deceit falls in, the two part and the flavour is gone.
bal.58.cau1: Understanding what she had done, Satī was troubled at heart; her boundless anxiety cannot be told.
She thought: Śiva, the ocean of mercy, is supremely unfathomable; he has not spoken my offence openly.
bal.58.cau2: Seeing Śaṅkara's manner, Bhavānī knew that her lord had forsaken her, and she was distressed at heart.
Knowing her own sin, she could say nothing; her heart burned fiercely, like a potter's kiln.
bal.58.cau3: Seeing Satī troubled, Śiva of the bull banner told her lovely stories to comfort her.
Telling many tales of old along the way, the Lord of the universe reached Kailāsa.
bal.58.cau4: There, mindful of his vow, Śiva sat beneath the banyan tree in the lotus posture.
Śaṅkara took up his own natural state, and an unbroken, boundless samādhi (deep meditative absorption) came upon him.
bal.58.do58: Satī then lived on Kailāsa, with great sorrow in her mind.
No one knew anything of the secret; her days passed, each one like an age.
bal.59.cau1: Each day a new and heavy grief weighed on Satī's heart: When shall I cross this ocean of sorrow?
I dishonoured Śrī Rāma, and then took my husband's word for false;
bal.59.cau2: the Creator has given me the fruit of that, and he did only what was right.
But now, O Creator, it does not become you to keep me alive, cut off from Śaṅkara.
bal.59.cau3: The remorse in her heart is beyond words. Wise Satī remembered Śrī Rāma within her mind:
If the Lord is called merciful to the lowly, and the Vedas sing his glory as the remover of distress,
bal.59.cau4: then with joined palms I pray: let this body of mine soon fall away.
If I love Śiva's feet, and this is truly my vow in mind, deed and word,
bal.59.do59: then hear me, all-seeing Lord, and quickly find the means
by which I may die without effort and be rid of this unbearable calamity.
bal.60.cau1: So the daughter of the Prajāpati grieved; her sorrow was heavy, cruel and beyond telling.
When eighty-seven thousand years had passed, Śiva the imperishable came out of samādhi.
bal.60.cau2: Śiva began to remember the name of Rāma, and Satī knew that the Lord of the world had awoken.
She went and bowed at Śiva's feet, and Śaṅkara gave her a seat facing him.
bal.60.cau3: He began to tell the delightful stories of Hari. At that time Dakṣa became a Prajāpati:
Brahmā considered and saw that he was fit in every way, and made Dakṣa chief of the Prajāpatis.
bal.60.cau4: When Dakṣa gained such great authority, great pride entered his heart.
No one has ever been born in this world who gained lordship and was not made proud by it.
bal.60.do60: Dakṣa summoned all the sages and began a great sacrifice.
He respectfully invited all the gods who receive a share of the sacrifice.
bal.61.cau1: Kinnaras, Nāgas, Siddhas, Gandharvas and all the gods set out with their wives.
All the gods except Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Maheśa went, their aerial cars made ready.
bal.61.cau2: Satī saw aerial cars, lovely and of many kinds, passing through the sky.
Celestial women sang so sweetly that, as their singing reached the ears of sages, the sages' meditation broke.
bal.61.cau3: Then she asked, and Śiva told her all of it. Hearing of her father's sacrifice, she was somewhat glad.
She thought: If Maheśa gives me leave, I will go there on this pretext and stay a few days.
bal.61.cau4: Being forsaken by her husband was a heavy grief in her heart, but mindful of her own offence she did not speak of it.
Satī spoke in charming words steeped in fear, hesitation and love:
bal.61.do61: There is a great festival at my father's house. If you permit it, my Lord,
then, O home of compassion, I would go with all respect to see it.
bal.62.cau1: Śiva said: You have spoken well, and it pleases my mind too; but it is not right that no invitation was sent.
Dakṣa has called all his daughters, but out of enmity towards me he has forgotten even you.
bal.62.cau2: In Brahmā's assembly he took offence at me, and for that he slights me even now.
Bhavānī, if you go uninvited, neither courtesy nor affection nor regard will remain.
bal.62.cau3: Though no doubt one should go even uninvited to the house of a friend, a master, a father or a teacher,
yet where someone bears hostility, going there brings no good.
