bal.62.cau4: Śiva counselled her in many ways, but, ruled by what was to be, no understanding came into her heart.
The Lord said: If you go without being invited, to my mind it is not a good thing.
bal.62.do62: Śiva tried every way of persuading her, but Dakṣa's daughter would not stay.
Then Śiva, the enemy of Tripura, sent his chief attendants with her and let her go.
bal.63.cau1: When Bhavānī came to her father's house, no one welcomed her, for fear of Dakṣa.
Only her mother met her warmly and with respect; her sisters met her with many smiles.
bal.63.cau2: Dakṣa did not so much as ask after her welfare; at the sight of Satī his whole body burned.
Then Satī went and looked at the sacrifice; nowhere could she see a share for Śiva.
bal.63.cau3: Then what Śaṅkara had said rose in her mind; seeing the insult to her lord, her heart burned.
The earlier sorrow had not gripped her heart as this great anguish did.
bal.63.cau4: Though the world holds many cruel sorrows, the hardest of all is dishonour among one's own kin.
Realising this, Satī grew very angry; her mother tried in many ways to calm her.
bal.63.do63: She could not bear the insult to Śiva, and her heart would not be calmed.
Then, forcefully rebuking the whole assembly, she spoke in anger:
bal.64.cau1: Hear me, members of this assembly and all you great sages: all who have spoken or listened to slander of Śaṅkara
shall at once receive its fruit, and my father too shall repent it fully.
bal.64.cau2: Where slander of the saints, of Śiva or of the Lord of Lakṣmī is heard, the rule is this:
if one has the power, cut out the slanderer's tongue; if not, shut one's ears and flee from there.
bal.64.cau3: Maheśa, the enemy of Tripura, is the soul of the world, its father, and the well-wisher of all.
My dull-witted father reviles him, and this body was born of Dakṣa's seed.
bal.64.cau4: For that reason I shall give up this body at once, holding in my heart the moon-crested Lord of the bull banner.
With these words she burned her body in the fire of yoga, and a cry of grief rose throughout the sacrifice.
bal.64.do64: Hearing of Satī's death, Śiva's attendants began to wreck the sacrifice.
Bhṛgu, lord of sages, saw it being laid waste and guarded it.
bal.65.cau1: When Śaṅkara received all the news, in his anger he sent Vīrabhadra.
He went and destroyed the sacrifice, and gave all the gods the fruit they had earned.
bal.65.cau2: Dakṣa met the fate the world knows well, the fate of anyone who turns away from Śiva.
This story is known to all the world, so I have told it briefly.
bal.65.cau3: As she died, Satī asked Śrī Hari for a boon: love for Śiva's feet, birth after birth.
For that reason she went to the house of Himālaya and was born, taking the body of Pārvatī.
bal.65.cau4: From the time Umā came to the mountain's house, every attainment and every kind of wealth filled the place.
Sages made fine hermitages here and there, and Himālaya gave them fitting places to dwell.
bal.65.do65: All the trees, fresh and of many kinds, were always in flower and fruit.
On that lovely mountain, mines of gems of many kinds came to light.
bal.66.cau1: All the rivers flow with holy water; birds, beasts and bees all live in happiness.
All creatures have given up their natural enmity, and on the mountain all love one another.
bal.66.cau2: With Girijā come to his house, the mountain shines as a devotee shines who has gained devotion to Śrī Rāma.
In his house there is fresh joy every day, and Brahmā and the other gods sing his glory.
bal.66.cau3: When Nārada heard all the news, he went to the mountain's home simply out of eager curiosity.
The king of mountains received him with great honour, washed his feet and gave him a fine seat.
bal.66.cau4: With his wife he bowed his head at the sage's feet, and had the whole house sprinkled with the water of his feet.
The mountain spoke at length of his own good fortune, then called his daughter and set her at the sage's feet.
bal.66.do66: He said: You know past, present and future; you know all things, and you can go everywhere.
O best of sages, consider in your heart and tell me my daughter's faults and virtues.
bal.67.cau1: The sage smiled and said in gentle words of deep meaning: Your daughter is a mine of every virtue.
She is beautiful, of fine character by her very nature, and wise; her names are Umā, Ambikā and Bhavānī.
bal.67.cau2: The maiden bears every auspicious mark; she will always be dear to her husband.
Her married happiness will stand unshaken for ever, and through her, her father and mother will win fame.
bal.67.cau3: She will be worshipped throughout the world; for one who serves her nothing will be out of reach.
Remembering her name, the women of the world will walk the sword's edge of faithfulness to their husbands.
bal.67.cau4: King of the mountains, your daughter bears good marks. Now hear the few faults there are as well:
without qualities, without honour, with no mother or father, indifferent, with every doubt gone,
bal.67.do67: a yogī with matted hair, desireless at heart, naked and of inauspicious dress:
such is the husband she will have; such is the line drawn on her hand.
bal.68.cau1: Hearing the sage's words and knowing in their hearts that they were true, the couple grieved, while Umā rejoiced.
Even Nārada did not perceive this difference: their state was one, but their understanding was not the same.
bal.68.cau2: All the companions, Girijā, the mountain king and Mainā were thrilled in body, their eyes filled with tears.
The divine sage's word cannot prove false; Umā kept that word treasured in her heart.
bal.68.cau3: Love for Śiva's lotus feet sprang up in her, but a doubt came into her mind that he would be hard to win.
Knowing the moment unfit, she hid her love, and went and sat once more in a companion's lap.
bal.68.cau4: The divine sage's word cannot prove false: so the couple and the wise companions were troubled.
Steadying his heart, the king of the mountains said: My lord, tell me, what remedy should be tried?
bal.68.do68: The lord of sages said: Listen, Himavān: what the Creator has written on the forehead
none can erase, whether god, dānava, man, nāga or sage.
bal.69.cau1: Even so, I will tell you one remedy; it may succeed if fate lends its help.
Umā will find just such a groom as I described to you; of that there is no doubt.
bal.69.cau2: All the faults of the groom that I have described, I judge to be in Śiva.
If the marriage is with Śaṅkara, everyone will call even the faults the equal of virtues.
bal.69.cau3: If Hari sleeps with a serpent for his bed, the wise lay no fault at all on him for it.
The sun and fire consume juices of every kind, yet no one calls them bad.
bal.69.cau4: All waters, the clean and the unclean, flow in the Gaṅgā, yet no one calls the Gaṅgā impure.
No fault clings to the mighty, my lord, any more than to the sun, to fire or to the Gaṅgā.
bal.69.do69: If dull-witted men, proud of their discernment, try to vie with them in this,
they lie in hell for a whole aeon. Can a living being be the equal of the Lord?
bal.70.cau1: Even when a liquor is made with Gaṅgā water, the saints, knowing it for liquor, never drink it.
Yet as that same liquor becomes pure once it joins the Gaṅgā, so is the difference between the Lord and one who is not the Lord.
bal.70.cau2: Śiva is by his very nature the almighty Lord; in this marriage there is good in every way.
Maheśa is hard to win by worship; yet, when hardship is borne, he is quickly pleased.
bal.70.cau3: If your daughter performs austerities, Śiva, the foe of Tripura, can erase even what is destined.
Though there are many grooms in the world, for her there is no other but Śiva.
bal.70.cau4: He grants boons, breaks the distress of those who bow to him, is an ocean of mercy and the delight of his servants' hearts.
Without worshipping Śiva, the fruit one longs for is not won even by practising yoga and japa millions of times.
bal.70.do70: With these words Nārada remembered Śrī Hari and gave Girijā his blessing.
This good will now surely come; give up your doubt, lord of the mountains.
bal.71.cau1: Saying this, the sage went to Brahmā's realm. Now hear what happened next.
Finding her husband alone, Mainā said: My lord, I did not understand the sage's words.
bal.71.cau2: If the house, the groom and the family are beyond compare, then give our daughter in a marriage worthy of her.
Otherwise the girl had better stay unmarried; husband, Umā is as dear to me as life.
bal.71.cau3: If no groom worthy of Girijā is found, everyone will say that mountains are dull by nature.
Weigh this, husband, and arrange the marriage so that no anguish burns in the heart afterwards.
bal.71.cau4: Saying this, she fell at his feet, laying her head on them. The lord of the mountains lovingly said:
Fire may break out in the moon, but Nārada's word cannot prove untrue.
bal.71.do71: Beloved, put away all your worry and remember the blessed Lord.
He who fashioned Pārvatī will himself bring about her good.
bal.72.cau1: Now, if you love your daughter, go and give her this counsel:
let her perform such austerities as will win her Maheśa; by no other means will the trouble end.
bal.72.cau2: Nārada's words hold a hidden meaning and are well founded; Śiva of the bull banner is beautiful and a treasury of every virtue.
Weigh this and give up your misgiving; Śaṅkara is spotless in every way.
bal.72.cau3: Hearing her husband's words, glad at heart, she rose at once and went to Girijā.
At the sight of Umā her eyes filled with tears, and lovingly she seated her in her lap.
bal.72.cau4: Again and again she clasps her to her bosom; her throat is choked and she can say nothing.
Bhavānī, the all-knowing mother of the world, spoke gentle words that gave her mother comfort:
bal.72.do72: Listen, mother: I had a dream, and I will tell it to you.
A handsome, fair-skinned, most excellent Brahmin gave me this counsel:
bal.73.cau1: Daughter of the mountain, hold what Nārada said to be true, and go and perform austerities.
This counsel has pleased your mother and father too. Austerity gives happiness and destroys sorrow and faults.
bal.73.cau2: By the power of austerity the Creator makes the universe; by the power of austerity Viṣṇu protects the whole world.
By the power of austerity Śiva brings destruction; by the power of austerity Śeṣa bears the weight of the earth.
bal.73.cau3: Bhavānī, all creation rests on austerity; knowing this in your heart, go and perform austerities.
Hearing these words the mother was amazed; she called the mountain king and told him the dream.
bal.73.cau4: After reasoning with her mother and father in many ways, Umā set out joyfully to perform austerities.
Her dear family, her father and her mother were distraught; no word would come to their lips.
bal.73.do73: Then the sage Vedaśirā came and explained things to them all.
Hearing of Pārvatī's greatness, they found comfort.
bal.74.cau1: Holding in her heart the feet of the lord of her life, Umā went to the forest and began her austerities.
Her body was too delicate for austerity, yet, remembering her lord's feet, she gave up every comfort.
bal.74.cau2: Each day new love for those feet sprang up in her; she forgot her body, and her mind was given to austerity.
For a thousand years she ate roots and fruit, and spent a hundred years living on greens.
bal.74.cau3: For some days her food was water and air, and for some days she kept a strict fast.
For three thousand years she ate only the leaves of the bel tree that fell dried to the ground.
bal.74.cau4: Then she gave up even the dry leaves, and so Umā came to be called Aparṇā (the leafless).
Seeing Umā's body wasted by austerity, the deep voice of Brahmā rang out from the sky:
bal.74.do74: Daughter of the king of the mountains, listen: your heart's wish is fulfilled.
Give up all this unbearable hardship; now Śiva, the foe of Tripura, will be yours.
bal.75.cau1: Bhavānī, there have been many steadfast sages and wise ones, but none has performed austerities like these.
Now hold this excellent word of Brahmā in your heart, knowing it ever true and always pure.
bal.75.cau2: As soon as your father comes to call you, give up your resolve and go home then and there.
When the seven sages come to you, know then that the word of Brahmā, lord of speech, has proved true.
bal.75.cau3: Hearing the words the Creator spoke from the sky, Girijā was thrilled in every limb and rejoiced.
I have sung the lovely story of Umā; now hear the delightful story of Śiva.
bal.75.cau4: Ever since Satī went and gave up her body, dispassion had filled Śiva's mind.
He ever repeats the name of Śrī Rāma, and here and there he listens to the many virtues of Śrī Rāma being told.
bal.75.do75: Śiva, all consciousness and bliss, the home of joy, free from delusion, pride and desire,
wanders the earth holding in his heart Śrī Hari, the delight of all the worlds.
bal.76.cau1: In one place he teaches the sages knowledge, in another he tells of Śrī Rāma's virtues.
Though he is free of desire, yet Śiva, the all-wise Lord, is grieved by the pain of separation from his devotee.
bal.76.cau2: In this way much time went by, and his love for Śrī Rāma's feet grew new every day.
Śrī Rāma saw Śaṅkara's discipline and love, and the unwavering line of devotion in his heart.
bal.76.cau3: Then Śrī Rāma, grateful and compassionate, appeared, a treasury of beauty and goodness, of vast splendour.
He praised Śaṅkara in many ways, saying: Who but you could have kept such a vow?
bal.76.cau4: Śrī Rāma reasoned with Śiva in many ways and told him of Pārvatī's birth.
The Lord, treasury of mercy, described in detail Girijā's most holy deeds.
bal.76.do76: Śrī Rāma said: Śiva, if you have love for me, now hear my request:
go and marry the daughter of the mountain; grant me this, since I ask it of you.
bal.77.cau1: Śiva said: Though such a thing is not fitting, yet the word of my Lord cannot be set aside.
To take your command on my head and carry it out, my Lord, is our highest dharma.
bal.77.cau2: The word of mother, father, guru and master should be carried out without deliberation, knowing it to be auspicious.
You are in every way my greatest well-wisher; my Lord, your command is on my head.
bal.77.cau3: Hearing Śaṅkara's words, framed in devotion, discernment and dharma, the Lord was pleased.
The Lord said: Hara, your vow has held. Now keep in your heart what I have told you.
bal.77.cau4: With these words the Lord vanished, and Śaṅkara kept that same form of his in his heart.
Just then the seven sages came to Śiva, and Lord Śiva spoke to them in very gracious words:
bal.77.do77: Go to Pārvatī and test her love;
then prompt the mountain king to have her sent home, and clear away the doubt.
bal.78.cau1: How did the sages find Gaurī there? Like austerity itself in bodily form.
The sages said: Listen, daughter of the mountain: for what reason are you performing such severe austerity?
bal.78.cau2: Whom do you worship, and what is it you want? Why not tell us the true secret?
Pārvatī said: My mind shrinks from saying it; you will laugh to hear my foolishness.
bal.78.cau3: My mind has grown obstinate and will not listen to counsel; it wants to raise a wall on water.
Taking what Nārada said as the truth, I want to fly without wings.
bal.78.cau4: See my folly, O sages: I want Śiva, always, as my husband.
bal.78.do78: Hearing these words the sages laughed and said: Your body is born of a mountain.
Tell us, who has ever heard Nārada's counsel and kept a settled home?
bal.79.cau1: He went and taught Dakṣa's sons, and they never came back to set eyes on home again.
He ruined Citraketu's household, and Hiraṇyakaśipu too came to the same pass.
bal.79.cau2: Whoever listens to Nārada's advice, man or woman, surely leaves home and turns beggar.
His mind is crafty though his body bears the marks of a good man; he wants to make everyone like himself.
bal.79.cau3: Trusting his words, you want a husband who is by nature indifferent to all,
without merit, without shame, poorly clad, a bearer of skulls, without family or home, naked and wreathed in serpents.
bal.79.cau4: Tell us, what happiness is there in winning such a husband? Led astray by that cheat, you have truly lost your way.
At the bidding of the elders Śiva married Satī, and then, neglecting her, he brought about her death.
bal.79.do79: Now Śiva sleeps at ease without a care, eating what he begs.
Can a wife ever stay in the home of those who are solitary by nature?
bal.80.cau1: Even now, take our advice; we have thought of a fine husband for you,
most handsome, pure, a giver of joy and gentle in nature, whose fame and divine play the Vedas sing,
bal.80.cau2: free from every flaw, a store of all virtues, the Lord of Lakṣmī who dwells in the city of Vaikuṇṭha.
Such a husband we will bring and unite with you. Hearing this, Bhavānī smiled and said:
bal.80.cau3: You spoke the truth: this body was born of a mountain. My obstinacy will not leave me, though my body may.
Gold too comes out of stone, yet even when it is burnt it does not give up its nature.
bal.80.cau4: I will not forsake Nārada's words; whether my home flourishes or falls to ruin, I am not afraid.
For one who has no faith in the words of the guru, happiness and success are not within easy reach even in a dream.
bal.80.do80: Mahādeva may be a house of faults and Viṣṇu the home of every virtue,
but when one's heart delights in someone, one's concern is with that one alone.
bal.81.cau1: Had you met me first, great sages, I would have heard your advice and received it with bowed head.
Now I have given my whole life away for Śiva; who is to weigh merits and faults?
bal.81.cau2: If your heart is set on it and you cannot rest without arranging a match,
then those fond of such pastimes need never be idle; the world has many grooms and maidens.
bal.81.cau3: For ten million births my resolve stands: I will wed Śiva or else stay unmarried.
I will not give up Nārada's teaching, even if Maheśa himself tells me to a hundred times.
bal.81.cau4: The Mother of the world said: I fall at your feet; go home now, it has grown late.
Seeing her love, the wise sages said: Glory, glory to you, Mother of the world, Bhavānī.
bal.81.do81: You are māyā and Śiva is the Lord; the two of you are the father and mother of the whole world.
Bowing their heads at her feet, the sages went away, thrilling with joy again and again.
bal.82.cau1: The sages went and sent Himavān, who pleaded with Girijā and brought her home.
Then the seven sages went to Śiva and told him all of Umā's story.
bal.82.cau2: Hearing of her love, Śiva was lost in it, and the seven sages went home rejoicing.
Then the wise Śiva steadied his mind and began to meditate on Śrī Rāma.
bal.82.cau3: At that time there arose a demon named Tāraka, mighty in arm, in glory, strength and splendour.
He conquered all the worlds and their guardians, and the gods were stripped of happiness and wealth.
bal.82.cau4: Ageless and deathless, he could not be defeated; the gods fought many kinds of battle and lost.
Then they went to Brahmā and cried out for help, and Brahmā saw all the gods in distress.
bal.82.do82: Brahmā explained it to them all: This demon will meet his death
when a son is born of Śiva's seed; he alone will conquer him in battle.
bal.83.cau1: Hear what I say and set about the means; it will come about, and God will help.
Satī, who gave up her body at Dakṣa's sacrifice, has been born again in the home of Himācala.
bal.83.cau2: She has performed austerity to win Śambhu as her husband, but Śiva has left everything and sits absorbed in samādhi.
Though it is a great dilemma, still hear one suggestion of mine.
bal.83.cau3: Send Kāma to Śiva, to go and stir unrest in Śaṅkara's mind.
Then we will go and bow our heads to Śiva and, by pressing him, have the marriage brought about.
bal.83.cau4: In this way the good of the gods may well be served. Everyone said the plan was excellent.
The gods praised him with great fervour, and Kāma, five-arrowed and fish-bannered, appeared.
bal.83.do83: The gods told him all their trouble. Hearing it, he thought it over,
and Kāma smiled and said: To set myself against Śiva bodes no good for me.
bal.84.cau1: Even so I will do your work, for the Veda calls service to others the highest dharma.
One who gives up his body for another's good is ever praised by the saints.
bal.84.cau2: So saying, he bowed his head to all and set off, his bow of flowers in hand, with his companions.
As he went, Kāma reflected in his heart: Opposing Śiva means certain death for me.
bal.84.cau3: Then he spread his influence abroad and made the whole world subject to himself.
When the fish-bannered god grew angry, in a moment all the bounds of the Veda were wiped away.
bal.84.cau4: Celibacy, vows, self-restraint of many kinds, fortitude, dharma, knowledge, realised knowledge,
good conduct, japa, yoga, dispassion: the whole army of Discernment fled in fear.
bal.84.cha1: Discernment fled with his allies; his mighty warriors turned back from the battlefield.
At that time they went and hid in the caves of the mountain of the holy scriptures.
The world was thrown into turmoil: O Creator, what is going to happen? Who will protect us?
Who has two heads, that the lord of Rati in his anger has taken up bow and arrow against him?
bal.84.do84: All the living things of the world, unmoving and moving, that bear the names of female and male,
abandoned each their own bounds and fell under the sway of Kāma.
bal.85.cau1: Every heart was filled with the longing of love; seeing the creepers, the branches of the trees bent towards them.
Rivers swelled and rushed to the ocean, and ponds and pools flowed together.
bal.85.cau2: Where such is told of the state of insentient things, who can tell what the sentient did?
Beasts and birds that roam the sky, the water and the land forgot the proper season and fell under the sway of desire.
bal.85.cau3: All the worlds were blind with desire and restless; the cakravāka birds no longer heeded night or day.
Gods, demons, men, kinnaras, serpents, pretas, piśācas, bhūtas and vetālas:
bal.85.cau4: their state I have not described at length, knowing them to be ever the slaves of desire.
Siddhas, the dispassionate, great sages and yogis: they too fell under the sway of desire and pined in separation.
bal.85.cha1: When even the lords of yogis and the ascetics fell under the sway of desire, who would speak of the lowly?
Those who had always seen the moving and unmoving world as full of Brahman now saw it full of women.
Women saw the world as full of men, and men saw it all as full of women.
For two daṇḍas (some forty-eight minutes), within the universe, this was the sport that Kāma wrought.
bal.85.so85: No one could hold firm; Kāma stole the hearts of all.
Only those whom Śrī Rāma kept safe escaped at that time.
bal.86.cau1: For two ghaṛīs this spectacle went on, until Kāma came near Śiva.
Seeing Śiva, Kāma was struck with dread, and the whole world returned to its former state.
bal.86.cau2: At once every creature was at ease again, like drunkards when their intoxication wears off.
Seeing Rudra, Kāma was afraid; Lord Śiva is unassailable and hard to reach.
bal.86.cau3: To turn back would bring shame, and nothing could be done; resolved on death, he devised a plan.
At once he brought forth lovely Spring, king of the seasons, and rows of young trees shone in full bloom.
bal.86.cau4: Forests, groves, stepwells, ponds and every quarter of the sky became surpassingly lovely.
Everywhere love seemed to overflow, and at the sight Kāma woke even in minds that were dead.
bal.86.cha1: Love wakes even in dead minds; the beauty of the forest is beyond telling.
The cool, fragrant, gentle breeze was truly a friend to the fire of love.
In the lakes many lotuses opened, and swarms of lovely bees hummed.
Swans, cuckoos and parrots called sweetly, and the apsarās sang and danced.
bal.86.do86: Having tried all his arts in countless ways, Kāma was defeated with all his army.
Śiva's unshakeable samādhi did not stir, and Kāma, who dwells in the heart, grew angry.
bal.87.cau1: Seeing a fine branch of a mango tree, Kāma climbed onto it, his mind full of anger.
He fitted his arrows to his bow of flowers and, taking aim in fierce anger, drew it back to his ear.
bal.87.cau2: He loosed his fierce arrows and they struck Śiva's heart. Then the samādhi broke and he awoke.
The Lord's mind was greatly disturbed; opening his eyes, he looked all around.
bal.87.cau3: He saw Kāma among the fragrant leaves of the mango, and his anger rose, and the three worlds trembled.
Then Śiva opened his third eye, and at his glance Kāma was burnt to ashes.
bal.87.cau4: A great cry of dismay rose in the world; the gods were afraid and the asuras rejoiced.
Those given to pleasure grieved, thinking of the joys of desire, and seekers and yogis were freed from their thorn.
bal.87.cha1: The yogis were freed from their thorn. When Rati heard what had become of her husband, she fainted.
Weeping, crying out in many ways and pleading piteously, she went to Śaṅkara.
With deep love she entreated him in many ways and stood before him with joined hands.
The Lord Śiva, quickly pleased and compassionate, looked on the helpless woman and spoke these true words:
bal.87.do87: Rati, from now on your lord's name will be Anaṅga, the bodiless.
Without a body he will pervade all. Now listen to the story of your meeting with him again.
bal.88.cau1: When Kṛṣṇa descends in the line of Yadu to take away the earth's great burden,
Kṛṣṇa's son will be your husband. My word never proves false.
bal.88.cau2: Hearing Śaṅkara's words, Rati went away. Now I will tell another part of the story in full.
The gods received all the news, and Brahmā and the others went to Vaikuṇṭha.
bal.88.cau3: All the gods, with Viṣṇu and Brahmā, went to where Śiva, the home of grace, was.
Each of them praised him in turn, and Śiva, who wears the moon as his crest, was pleased.
bal.88.cau4: Śiva, the ocean of mercy, whose banner bears the bull, said: Tell me, immortals, why have you come?
Brahmā said: Lord, you know every heart; even so, moved by devotion, I make my plea, my Master.
bal.88.do88: Śaṅkara, in the hearts of all the gods there is this great longing:
they wish, my Lord, to see your marriage with their own eyes.
bal.89.cau1: O you who humbled Kāma's pride, do something so that we may see this festival to our eyes' content.
O ocean of mercy, having burnt Kāma you granted Rati a boon; that was very well done.
bal.89.cau2: To punish and then show grace, my Lord, is the very nature of masters.
Pārvatī has performed boundless austerity; now accept her as your own.
bal.89.cau3: Hearing Brahmā's plea and weighing what the Lord Śrī Rāma had said, Śiva gladly answered: So be it.
Then the gods beat their kettledrums and, showering flowers, cried: Glory, glory to the lord of the gods!
bal.89.cau4: Knowing the moment had come, the seven sages arrived, and Brahmā at once sent them to the mountain king's home.
They went first to where Bhavānī was, and spoke sweet words steeped in guile:
bal.89.do89: Then you would not listen to us, holding to Nārada's counsel.
Now your vow has come to nothing: Maheśa has burnt Kāma.
bal.90.cau1: Hearing this, Bhavānī smiled and said: Wise sages, rich in realised knowledge, you have spoken aptly.
By your reckoning Kāma has been burnt only now, so until now Śiva must have been subject to passion.
bal.90.cau2: To my mind Śiva has always been a yogi, unborn, faultless, free of desire and untouched by pleasure.
If I have served Śiva knowing him to be so, with love, in deed, mind and word,
bal.90.cau3: then hear, lords among sages: the Lord, the treasury of grace, will make my vow come true.
Your saying that Śiva has burnt Kāma is itself a great failure of your discernment.
bal.90.cau4: Dear sirs, it is the very nature of fire that frost never goes near it;
if it came near, it would surely perish. So it is with Kāma and Maheśa.
bal.90.do90: The sages were glad at heart to hear her words and to see her love and faith.
They bowed their heads to Bhavānī, set out and went to the mountain king.
bal.91.cau1: They told the king of the mountains all that had happened. Hearing that Kāma had been burnt, he was much grieved.
Then they told him of the boon given to Rati, and hearing it Himavān was greatly pleased.
bal.91.cau2: Reflecting in his heart on Śiva's greatness, he respectfully sent for eminent sages.
Having them weigh the good day, the good constellation and the good hour, he soon had the wedding time fixed by Vedic rule.
bal.91.cau3: The mountain king gave that very letter of the wedding time to the seven sages and, clasping their feet, made his request.
They went and gave the letter to Brahmā; as he read it, his heart could not contain its love.
bal.91.cau4: Brahmā read out the wedding time to all, and all the sages and the whole assembly of the gods rejoiced.
Flowers rained from the sky, music played, and auspicious pitchers were set out in all ten directions.
bal.91.do91: All the gods began to deck out their mounts and aerial cars of every kind.
Blessed, auspicious omens appear, and the apsarās sing.
bal.92.cau1: Śambhu's gaṇas adorn Śiva. They make a crown of his matted hair and set a wedding crest of serpents on it.
He wore serpents for earrings and bracelets; ash is on his body, and a lion's skin serves for his garment.
bal.92.cau2: The moon on his brow, lovely Gaṅgā on his head, three eyes, and a serpent for his sacred thread;
poison in his throat, and on his breast a garland of human skulls: his dress is inauspicious, yet he is the home of all that is auspicious, and compassionate.
bal.92.cau3: A trident and a ḍamaru drum shine in his hands. Śiva set out riding his bull as the music played.
Seeing Śiva, the wives of the gods smile and say: There is no bride in the world fit for this bridegroom.
bal.92.cau4: Viṣṇu, Brahmā and the hosts of gods, each riding his own mount, went along in the wedding procession.
The company of the gods was matchless in every way, yet the procession did not suit the bridegroom.
bal.92.do92: Then Viṣṇu summoned all the guardians of the quarters and, smiling, spoke thus:
All of you go separately, each with his own following.
bal.93.cau1: Brothers, this procession does not match the bridegroom; will you go to another's city and make yourselves a laughing-stock?
Hearing Viṣṇu's words, the gods smiled and drew apart, each with his own host.
bal.93.cau2: Maheśa smiles to himself: Hari never gives up his teasing.
Hearing these most dear words of his dear one, he sent Bhṛṅgī to summon all his gaṇas.
bal.93.cau3: Hearing Śiva's command they all came and bowed their heads at their Lord's lotus feet.
Mounts of every sort, garb of every sort: Śiva laughed to see his own company.
bal.93.cau4: One has no face and another many faces; one has neither feet nor hands, another many feet and arms.
One has many eyes, another none; one is sturdy and well fed, another very thin.
bal.93.cha1: One is lean, another very fat; one is in a pure state, another in an impure.
They wear fearsome ornaments, carry skulls in their hands, and all have bodies smeared with fresh blood.
With the faces of donkeys, dogs, swine and jackals, the gaṇas wear countless guises: who could count them?
Pretas and piśācas of many kinds and bands of yoginīs are there, beyond describing.
bal.93.so93: The spirits are all wild and carefree; they dance and sing songs.
They look utterly strange, and they talk in the oddest ways.
bal.94.cau1: As the bridegroom, so the procession turned out; all along the way there is sport of every kind.
Here, the mountain king put up a pavilion so wondrous that it cannot be described.
bal.94.cau2: All the mountains there are in the world, small and great, more than any account could finish,
and every forest, ocean, river and lake: Himavān sent an invitation to them all.
bal.94.cau3: Able to take any form they wished, they took on handsome bodies and set out with their companies and their fair women.
All of them went to the mountain king's home and sang auspicious songs with affection.
bal.94.cau4: The mountain king had already had many houses made ready, and all took their lodging in them as befitted each.
Seeing the city's lovely splendour, even Brahmā's craft seems slight.
bal.94.cha1: Truly, seeing the city's splendour, the Creator's craft seemed slight.
Forests, gardens, wells, ponds and rivers are all lovely: who could describe them?
Auspicious arches, pennants and banners in great number grace every house.
The women and men there are handsome and clever; at the sight of their beauty even sages' minds are charmed.
bal.94.do94: Can the city where the Mother of the world was born be described?
There prosperity, accomplishment, wealth and happiness grow ever new each day.
bal.95.cau1: When the city heard that the procession had come near, it was all astir, and its splendour grew.
The welcoming party put on their finery, decked out mounts of many kinds, and went out with respect to receive it.
bal.95.cau2: They were glad at heart to see the army of the gods, and seeing Hari they were overjoyed.
But when they began to look at Śiva's company, all their mounts took fright and bolted.
bal.95.cau3: The grown-ups kept their nerve and stayed there, but the children all ran for their lives.
When they reach home and their fathers and mothers ask, they speak with their bodies trembling in fear:
bal.95.cau4: What can we say? It cannot be put into words. Is it the army of Yama, or a wedding procession?
The bridegroom is mad, and rides a bull; serpents, skulls and ash are his ornaments.
bal.95.cha1: Ash is on his body, serpents and skulls are his ornaments; he is naked, matted-haired and terrifying;
with him are ghosts, pretas, piśācas, yoginīs and demons with fearsome faces.
Whoever stays alive after seeing the procession must truly have great merit;
he alone will see Umā's wedding. So the boys said in house after house.
bal.95.do95: Understanding that it was all Maheśa's company, the mothers and fathers smile.
They reassured the children in many ways: Do not be afraid; there is nothing to fear.
bal.96.cau1: The welcoming party brought the procession in and gave everyone fine lodgings.
Mainā made ready the auspicious ārati, and the women with her sing joyful songs of blessing.
bal.96.cau2: A golden platter shines in her fair hands, and she went joyfully to perform the welcoming rite for Śiva.
When they saw Rudra's fearsome garb, the women's hearts were seized with great fear.
bal.96.cau3: In great terror they fled and went into the house, and Maheśa went to where the lodgings were.
Mainā's heart was filled with deep grief, and she called the mountain king's daughter to her.
bal.96.cau4: With great tenderness Mainā seated her in her lap, and her eyes, like blue lotuses, filled with tears.
She said: The Creator who gave you such beauty: how could that dullard make your bridegroom a madman?
bal.96.cha1: How could the Creator who gave you beauty make your bridegroom a madman?
The fruit that ought to grow on the tree of wishes is being forced onto a babul.
With you I will throw myself from a mountain, burn in fire or fall into the sea.
Let the home be lost, let the world speak ill of me, but while I live I will not hold this wedding.
bal.96.do96: Seeing the mountain king's queen in sorrow, all the women were distressed.
Mindful of her love for her daughter, Mainā laments, weeping and crying out:
bal.97.cau1: What harm had I ever done Nārada, that he has laid waste my settled home?
He it was who gave Umā such counsel that she performed austerity for a mad bridegroom.
bal.97.cau2: Truly he knows neither attachment nor affection; he is detached, with no wealth, no home, no wife.
He brings ruin on other people's homes and knows neither shame nor fear. What does a woman who has never borne a child know of the pain of childbirth?
bal.97.cau3: Seeing her mother distraught, Bhavānī spoke gentle words full of discernment:
Think of it in this way, Mother, and do not grieve: what the Creator has fashioned cannot be turned aside.
bal.97.cau4: If a mad husband is written in my fate, why should anyone be blamed?
Can the lines the Creator has written be erased by you? Mother, do not take the blame upon yourself for nothing.
bal.97.cha1: Do not take the blame upon yourself, Mother; give up lamenting, this is not the time for it.
Whatever sorrow or joy is written on my forehead, I shall meet with it wherever I go.
Hearing Umā's humble and gentle words, all the women grieved,
and blaming the Creator in many ways, they shed tears from their eyes.
bal.97.do97: At that moment, together with Nārada and the seven sages,
Himavān, the snowy mountain, heard the news and came home at once.
bal.98.cau1: Then Nārada calmed everyone and told them the story of what had gone before.
He said: Mainā, listen to my words, for they are true: your daughter Bhavānī is the Mother of the world.
bal.98.cau2: She is unborn, without beginning, the imperishable Śakti, ever dwelling as one half of Śiva's body.
She brings about the creation, preservation and dissolution of the world, and by her own will takes on a body in play.
bal.98.cau3: First she was born in the house of Dakṣa, named Satī, and was given a beautiful form.
There too Satī was wedded to Śaṅkara; the story is famous throughout the world.
bal.98.cau4: Once, as she was coming back with Śiva, she saw Śrī Rāma, the sun to the lotus of the Raghu line.
Delusion came over her; she did not do as Śiva told her, and, misled, she took on the guise of Sītā.
bal.98.cha1: Because Satī took on the guise of Sītā, Śaṅkara forsook her for that offence.
Then, parted from Śiva, she went to her father's sacrifice and was consumed in the fire of yoga.
Now, born in your house, she has performed severe austerity for her own husband.
Knowing this, give up your doubts: Girijā is forever the beloved of Śaṅkara.
bal.98.do98: Then, hearing Nārada's words, everyone's sorrow was gone,
and in a moment the news spread through the whole city, from house to house.
bal.99.cau1: Then Mainā and Himavān rejoiced and bowed again and again at Pārvatī's feet.
Women and men, children, the young and the old: all the people of the city were overjoyed.
bal.99.cau2: Auspicious songs began to be sung in the city, and everyone set out many golden pitchers.
A feast of many kinds was prepared, following such practice as the science of cookery lays down.
bal.99.cau3: Can that feast be described, in the house where Mother Bhavānī dwells?
All the bridegroom's party, Viṣṇu, Brahmā and the gods of every kind, were invited with respect.
bal.99.cau4: The diners sat down in many rows, and skilled cooks began to serve.
Knowing that the gods were dining, the women in their groups began to sing gālīs, the teasing songs of a wedding, in soft voices.
bal.99.cha1: The lovely women sing their teasing songs in sweet voices and make playful jibes.
The gods take a very long time over their meal, delighting to hear the banter.
The joy that swelled while they dined could not be told by ten million mouths.
When they had rinsed their mouths, betel was given, and each went to the lodging where he was staying.
bal.99.do99: Then the sages came and told Himavān the auspicious hour for the wedding,
and seeing that it was time for the marriage, the gods were sent for.
bal.100.cau1: All the gods were invited with respect, and each was given a fitting seat.
The altar was prepared according to the rule of the Veda, and the women sang lovely auspicious songs.
bal.100.cau2: There was a throne, most divine and lovely, made by Brahmā, beyond all describing.
Śiva sat on it, bowing his head to the Brahmins and remembering in his heart his own Lord, Śrī Rāma.
bal.100.cau3: Then the great sages had Umā sent for; her friends adorned her and brought her.
Seeing her beauty, all the gods were spellbound; is there a poet in the world who could describe such loveliness?
bal.100.cau4: Knowing her to be the Mother of the world and Śiva's consort, the gods bowed to her in their hearts.
Bhavānī is the very limit of beauty; ten million mouths could not describe it.
bal.100.cha1: Not even with ten million mouths can the great beauty of the Mother of the world be described.
The Vedas, Śeṣa and Sarasvatī shrink from telling it; what then of Tulasī, dull of mind?
Mother Bhavānī, the mine of beauty, went into the pavilion, to the centre where Śiva was.
For shyness she cannot look at her lord's lotus feet, yet her mind, like a bee, is there.
bal.100.do100: At the sages' bidding Śiva and Bhavānī worshipped Gaṇeśa.
Let no one who hears this have doubts; let him know in his heart that the gods are without beginning.
bal.101.cau1: The great sages had every rite of marriage performed just as the Veda sings of it.
The king of the mountains, taking kuśa grass and his daughter's hand, gave her to Śiva, knowing her to be Bhavānī.
bal.101.cau2: When Maheśa took her hand in marriage, all the lords of the gods rejoiced at heart.
The best of the sages chanted Vedic mantras, and the gods cried: Glory, glory, glory to Śaṅkara!
bal.101.cau3: Instruments of many kinds played, and flowers rained from the sky in many ways.
The marriage of Śiva and Girijā was done, and the whole universe was filled with joy.
bal.101.cau4: Maidservants and menservants, horses, chariots, elephants, cows, clothes, gems and goods of every kind,
grain and vessels of gold, loaded in carts, were given as dowry beyond all describing.
bal.101.cha1: When he had given dowry of many kinds, the snowy mountain joined his palms and said:
Śaṅkara, you whose every wish is fulfilled, what can I give you? And he stayed clasping his lotus feet.
Then Śiva, the ocean of mercy, set his father-in-law at ease in every way.
Then Mainā clasped his lotus feet, her heart brimming with love.
bal.101.do101: Mainā said: My Lord, Umā is as dear to me as life; make her a maid of your house,
and forgive every offence. Now be gracious and grant me this boon.
bal.102.cau1: Śiva reassured his mother-in-law in many ways; she bowed her head at his feet and went into the house.
Then the mother called Umā to her, took her on her lap and gave her good counsel:
bal.102.cau2: Always worship Śaṅkara's feet. This is a wife's dharma: her husband is her god, and there is no other.
Even as she spoke, tears filled her eyes, and she clasped her daughter to her heart once more.
bal.102.cau3: She said: Why did the Creator make woman in the world? One who depends on another has no happiness even in a dream.
The mother was overcome with love, but, seeing that it was no time for grief, she steadied herself.
bal.102.cau4: Again and again the mother embraces her and falls, clasping her feet; that supreme love is beyond all telling.
Bhavānī met and embraced all the women, and then went and clung once more to her mother's breast.
bal.102.cha1: After embracing her mother once more she set off, and everyone gave her fitting blessings.
She kept turning back to look at her mother; then her friends took her to Śiva.
Having satisfied all who had come asking for gifts, Śaṅkara set off for home with Umā.
All the immortals rejoiced and rained down flowers, and fine drums sounded in the sky.
bal.102.do102: Then Himavān, out of great affection, went along with them to see them on their way.
Śiva, whose banner bears the bull, comforted him in many ways and bade him farewell.
bal.103.cau1: The king of the mountains came home at once and called together all the mountains and lakes.
With respect, gifts, courtesy and great honour, Himavān gave each of them leave to go.
bal.103.cau2: As soon as Śiva reached Kailāsa, all the gods went back each to his own world.
Śiva and Bhavānī are the father and mother of the world, so I do not describe their love in detail.
bal.103.cau3: Enjoying pleasures of many kinds, they lived on Kailāsa with their attendants, the gaṇas.
The love-play of Śiva and Girijā was ever new, and in this way a long time went by.
bal.103.cau4: Then the six-faced son was born, who slew the demon Tāraka in battle.
The birth of Ṣaṇmukha is well known in the Āgamas, the Vedas and the Purāṇas; the whole world knows of it.
bal.103.cha1: The world knows the birth of Ṣaṇmukha, his deeds, his glory and his great valour.
That is why I have told the story of the son of Śiva, whose banner bears the bull, only in brief.
The men and women who tell or sing of this marriage of Umā and Śiva
will ever find happiness in auspicious undertakings and the festivities of marriage.
bal.103.do103: The deeds of Girijā's beloved are an ocean whose farther shore not even the Vedas can reach;
how then can Tulasīdāsa, so dull of mind and unlettered, describe them?
bal.104.cau1: Hearing Śiva's story, so rich in feeling and so lovely, the sage Bharadvāja was filled with joy.
His longing for the story grew greatly; tears filled his eyes and the hair on his body stood on end.
bal.104.cau2: Overcome with love, he could not bring a word to his lips; seeing his state the wise sage Yājñavalkya rejoiced.
He said: Ah, lord of sages, blessed is your birth: the lord of Gaurī is as dear to you as life.
bal.104.cau3: Those who have no love for Śiva's lotus feet never please Śrī Rāma, not even in a dream.
Guileless love for the feet of Śiva, Lord of the universe: this is the mark of a devotee of Śrī Rāma.
bal.104.cau4: Who is so true to the vow of devotion to Śrī Rāma as Śiva, who forsook a wife such as Satī though there was no sin in her?
By his vow he showed what devotion to Śrī Rāma is. Who else, brother, is as dear to Śrī Rāma as Śiva?
bal.104.do104: By telling Śiva's story first, I have come to know your heart.
You are a pure servant of Śrī Rāma, free of every fault.
bal.105.cau1: I have learnt your virtues and your nature; now listen as I tell the play of Śrī Rāma.
Listen, sage: the joy in my mind today at meeting you cannot be put into words.
bal.105.cau2: The story of Śrī Rāma is utterly boundless, lord of sages; a thousand million lords of serpents could not tell it.
Yet, remembering the Lord who holds the bow in his hand, the master of speech, I tell it at length as I have heard it.
bal.105.cau3: Sarasvatī is like a wooden puppet, and the Lord Śrī Rāma, the inner controller, is the one who holds its strings.
When he shows grace to a poet, knowing him for his own, he makes Speech dance in the courtyard of that poet's heart.
bal.105.cau4: I bow to that same compassionate Śrī Rāma and tell the clear tale of his virtues.
Most delightful is Kailāsa, the best of mountains, where Śiva and Umā always dwell.
bal.105.do105: Siddhas, ascetics, yogis, gods, kinnaras and hosts of sages:
all these who have done good live there and serve Śiva, the root of bliss.
bal.106.cau1: Those who turn their faces from Hari and Hara and do not love dharma never go there, even in a dream.
On that mountain stands a vast banyan tree, ever new and lovely at all times.
bal.106.cau2: A breeze of the three kinds, cool, gentle and fragrant, blows there, and its shade is very cool; the Vedas sing of it as the tree where Śiva rests.
Once the Lord Śiva went beneath it, and at the sight of the tree his heart was filled with joy.
bal.106.cau3: With his own hand the compassionate Śiva spread a lion's skin and sat there at ease.
His body is fair as the kunda flower, the moon and the conch; his arms are long, and he wears the bark garment of a sage.
bal.106.cau4: His feet are like fresh red lotuses; the radiance of his nails dispels the darkness in his devotees' hearts.
Serpents and ashes are the ornaments of Śiva, the foe of Tripura; his face outshines the beauty of the autumn moon.
bal.106.do106: On his head are a crown of matted locks and the Gaṅgā; his eyes are large as lotuses.
Blue of throat, a treasury of loveliness, he has the crescent moon shining on his brow.
bal.107.cau1: Seated there, Śiva, the foe of Kāma, looked as though the sentiment of peace (śānta rasa) had itself taken a body.
Knowing it to be a good moment, Pārvatī, Mother Bhavānī, went to Śiva.
bal.107.cau2: Knowing her to be his beloved, Śiva welcomed her with great honour and gave her a seat at his left side.
She sat down beside Śiva, rejoicing, and the story of her former birth came to her mind.
bal.107.cau3: Sensing greater affection for her in her husband's heart, Umā smiled and spoke in loving words.
The daughter of the mountain wished to ask about the story that brings good to all the worlds.
bal.107.cau4: Pārvatī said: Lord of the universe, my Lord, foe of Tripura, your greatness is known in all three worlds.
Moving and unmoving beings, nāgas, men and gods all serve your lotus feet.
bal.107.do107: Lord, you are almighty and all-knowing, Śiva the auspicious, the home of every art and virtue,
a treasury of yoga, knowledge and dispassion; to those who bow to you, your name is a wish-granting tree.
bal.108.cau1: Abode of joy, if you are pleased with me and truly know me as your own servant,
then, Lord, tell me Śrī Rāma's story in its many ways and take away my ignorance.
bal.108.cau2: Should one whose home is beneath the wish-granting tree suffer the pain that poverty brings?
You who wear the moon, weigh this in your heart, my Lord, and take away the heavy confusion of my mind.
bal.108.cau3: Lord, the sages who speak of the highest truth call Śrī Rāma Brahman without beginning,
and Śeṣa, Sarasvatī, the Vedas and the Purāṇas all sing his virtues.
bal.108.cau4: And you too, foe of Kāma, repeat Rāma, Rāma with reverence day and night.
Is this Rāma the same who is the son of the king of Avadh, or someone else, unborn, beyond attributes, whose ways no one can perceive?
bal.108.do108: If he is a king's son, how can he be Brahman, he whose mind was distraught at his separation from his wife?
Seeing his acts and hearing his greatness, my mind is utterly bewildered.
bal.109.cau1: If there is someone else, free of desire, all-pervading and almighty, explain him to me, my Lord.
Knowing me to be ignorant, do not hold anger in your heart; do whatever will end my delusion.
bal.109.cau2: In the forest I saw Śrī Rāma's lordship, but, overcome with fear, I did not tell you.
Even so, my impure mind did not come to understand, and I have reaped the fruit of that in full.
bal.109.cau3: Even now some doubt remains in my mind; be gracious, I beg you with joined palms.
Lord, at that time you taught me in many ways; keep that in mind, my Lord, and do not be angry.
bal.109.cau4: The delusion I had then is not in me now; my mind has a longing for Śrī Rāma's story.
Tell the holy tale of Śrī Rāma's virtues, Lord of the gods, adorned with the king of serpents.
bal.109.do109: I bow to your feet with my head on the ground, and with joined palms I entreat you:
draw out the essence of the Vedas' teaching and describe the spotless glory of Śrī Rāma.
bal.110.cau1: Though a woman is not held entitled to this, I am your servant in mind, deed and word.
The saints do not keep back even a hidden truth where they find a seeker in distress who is fit to receive it.
bal.110.cau2: King of the gods, in deep distress I ask: be merciful and tell me Śrī Rāma's story.
First consider and tell me the reason why Brahman without attributes took on a form with attributes.
bal.110.cau3: Then, Lord, tell of Śrī Rāma's incarnation, and then of his noble childhood deeds.
Tell how he married Jānakī, and for what fault he gave up the kingdom.
bal.110.cau4: Tell, my Lord, of the boundless deeds he did while living in the forest, and how he killed Rāvaṇa.
Tell all the many deeds he did when seated on the throne, Śaṅkara, whose nature is bliss.
bal.110.do110: Then, home of compassion, tell of the wonder Śrī Rāma worked:
how the jewel of the Raghu line went to his own abode together with his people.
bal.111.cau1: Then, Lord, explain in full that truth in whose realisation the wise sages are absorbed.
Then describe devotion, knowledge, realised knowledge and dispassion, each with its divisions.
bal.111.cau2: And tell me, my Lord of utterly pure discernment, the many other mysteries of Śrī Rāma.
Lord, whatever I may not have asked, that too, merciful one, do not keep hidden.
bal.111.cau3: The Vedas proclaim you the guru of the three worlds; what can other, lowly beings know?
Umā's questions, lovely by nature and free of guile, pleased Śiva's heart when he heard them.
bal.111.cau4: All of Śrī Rāma's deeds rose in Śiva's heart; he thrilled with love, and his eyes filled with tears.
The form of Śrī Rāma came into his heart, and he knew supreme bliss, a joy beyond measure.
bal.111.do111: For two daṇḍas (some forty-eight minutes) he stayed absorbed in the joy of meditation; then he drew his mind outward,
and Maheśa joyfully began to tell the story of Śrī Rāma.
bal.112.cau1: Śiva said: Without knowing him, even the false seems true, as a rope seems a snake until it is recognised;
on knowing him, the world is lost from sight, as the illusion of a dream goes when one wakes.
bal.112.cau2: I bow to that same Śrī Rāma in his form as a child, by repeating whose name every attainment comes easily.
May he, the home of blessing and remover of ill, who plays in Daśaratha's courtyard, melt with mercy.
bal.112.cau3: Having bowed to Śrī Rāma, Śiva, the foe of Tripura, spoke with joy words like nectar:
Blessed, blessed are you, daughter of the mountain king; there is no benefactor equal to you.
bal.112.cau4: You have asked for the story of Śrī Rāma, a Gaṅgā that makes all the worlds pure.
You love the feet of Śrī Rāma, and you have asked your questions for the good of the world.
bal.112.do112: Pārvatī, by Śrī Rāma's grace, not even in a dream does your mind hold
any grief, delusion, doubt or error, as I see it.
bal.113.cau1: Yet you raised that very doubt, so that the telling and hearing of the story may do good to all.
Those who have not heard the story of Hari with their ears have ear-holes like the holes of snakes.
bal.113.cau2: Eyes that have never looked upon saints are no more than the eyes on a peacock's feathers.
Those heads that do not bow at the feet of Hari and the guru are like bitter gourds.
bal.113.cau3: Those beings who have not brought devotion to Hari into their hearts are like corpses though alive.
A tongue that does not sing Śrī Rāma's virtues is no better than a frog's.
bal.113.cau4: Hard as the thunderbolt and unfeeling is the breast that does not rejoice to hear of Hari's deeds.
Girijā, listen to Śrī Rāma's līlā, which works the good of the gods and bewilders the demons.
bal.113.do113: Śrī Rāma's story is like the wish-granting cow of the gods: served, it gives every joy;
and the gatherings of the good are all the worlds of the gods. Knowing this, who would not hear it?
bal.114.cau1: Śrī Rāma's story is a lovely clap of the hands that sends the birds of doubt flying.
Śrī Rāma's story is the axe that fells the tree of the Kali age; daughter of the mountain king, hear it with reverence.
bal.114.cau2: Śrī Rāma's lovely names, virtues and deeds, his births and acts, are countless, and the Vedas have sung them.
As the Lord Śrī Rāma is endless, so his story, fame and virtues are manifold.
bal.114.cau3: Still, as I have heard it and as far as my understanding goes, I will tell it, seeing your great love.
Umā, your question is lovely by nature, gives joy and has the approval of the saints, and it pleased me.
bal.114.cau4: But one thing did not please me, Bhavānī, though you said it under the sway of delusion:
what you said, that the one whom the Vedas sing and on whom the sages fix their meditation is some other Rāma.
bal.114.do114: Base men say and hear such things, those whom the ghoul of delusion has seized,
hypocrites turned away from Hari's feet, who know neither false nor true.
bal.115.cau1: The ignorant, the unskilled, the blind and the luckless, on the mirror of whose minds the scum of sense-pleasures has settled;
the lustful, the deceitful and the deeply crooked, who have never seen an assembly of saints even in a dream:
bal.115.cau2: such are the ones who speak words the Vedas do not approve, who can see neither gain nor loss.
With a soiled mirror and without eyes, how can those wretched ones see Śrī Rāma's form?
bal.115.cau3: Those who have no discernment of the Lord without attributes or with them babble many words of their own invention.
Under the sway of Hari's māyā they wander lost in the world; there is nothing they cannot say.
bal.115.cau4: The crazed, the possessed and the drunk do not speak considered words.
As for those who have drunk the wine of great delusion, pay no heed to what they say.
bal.115.so115: Weigh this in your heart, give up doubt, and worship Śrī Rāma's feet.
Daughter of the mountain king, hear my words: to the darkness of error they are the rays of the sun.
bal.116.cau1: Between the Lord with attributes and the Lord without them there is no difference at all: so sing the sages, the Purāṇas, the wise and the Vedas.
He who is without attributes, formless, beyond perception and unborn takes on attributes, won over by the love of his devotees.
bal.116.cau2: How is he who is free of attributes the same as the one who has them? Just as water, ice and hail are not separate things.
His name is a sun to the darkness of error: how can delusion be spoken of in connection with him?
bal.116.cau3: Śrī Rāma is the sun of being, consciousness and bliss; there is not the least trace of the night of delusion in him.
The Lord is by his very nature light itself; so in him there is no dawn of realised knowledge either.
bal.116.cau4: Joy and grief, knowledge and ignorance, the sense of I and pride: these belong to the individual soul.
Śrī Rāma, as the whole world knows, is the all-pervading Brahman, supreme bliss, the Supreme Lord, the Ancient One.
bal.116.do116: He who is the renowned Puruṣa, the treasury of light, the manifest one, the lord of all things high and low,
he is the jewel of Raghu's line, my master. So saying, Śiva bowed his head.
bal.117.cau1: The ignorant do not see their own error, and these dull-witted creatures lay delusion on the Lord,
just as people of poor judgement see a veil of cloud across the sky and say that the sun is hidden.
bal.117.cau2: One who looks with a finger pressed against his eye sees, to his mind, two moons.
Umā, such delusion about Śrī Rāma is like darkness, smoke and dust appearing in the sky.
bal.117.cau3: The objects of sense, the senses, the gods of the senses and the individual soul: each of these is made conscious by the next.
The one who is the supreme light of them all is Śrī Rāma, the beginningless lord of Avadh.
bal.117.cau4: The world is what is lit, and Śrī Rāma is what lights it; he is the master of māyā, the home of knowledge and of every virtue.
Through his reality, inert māyā, aided by delusion, appears as though it were real.
bal.117.do117: As silver appears in a shell, and water in the rays of the sun,
though it is false in all three times, still no one can dispel that illusion.
bal.118.cau1: In just this way the world rests on Hari; though it is unreal, it still gives pain.
If someone cuts off one's head in a dream, the pain does not go away until one wakes.
bal.118.cau2: Girijā, he by whose grace such error is wiped away is the compassionate Śrī Rāma.
No one has found his beginning or his end; reasoning with their understanding, the Vedas have sung of him thus:
bal.118.cau3: Without feet he walks, without ears he hears, without hands he does works of many kinds.
Without a mouth he enjoys every taste, and without speech he speaks: he is the great yogī.
bal.118.cau4: Without a body he touches, without eyes he sees, without a nose he takes in every scent.
So in every way his doings are beyond this world, and his greatness cannot be described.
bal.118.do118: He whom the Vedas and the wise sing in this way, on whom the sages meditate,
is the son of Daśaratha, the Lord of Kosala, the Lord himself, come for the good of his devotees.
bal.119.cau1: When I see a creature dying in Kāśī, by the power of his name I set it free from sorrow;
he is my Lord, Śrī Rāma, master of all that moves and does not move, who dwells within every heart.
bal.119.cau2: Even when people utter his name helplessly, the sins they have committed over many births are burnt away;
and those who remember him with reverence cross the ocean of worldly existence as one crosses a cow's hoof-print.
bal.119.cau3: Bhavānī, Śrī Rāma is that Supreme Self; the words of error you spoke about him are most improper.
When such doubt enters the heart, knowledge, dispassion and every virtue depart.
bal.119.cau4: When she heard Śiva's words, which shatter error, all that her false reasoning had built gave way.
Love and faith for the feet of Śrī Rāma took hold of her, and her dreadful disbelief came to an end.
bal.119.do119: Clasping again and again the lotus feet of her lord Śiva and joining her lotus hands,
Girijā spoke words of beauty, as though steeped in the nectar of love:
bal.120.cau1: On hearing your words, which are like the rays of the moon, the fierce autumn heat of delusion has passed.
In your compassion you have taken away all my doubt, and I have come to understand the true nature of Śrī Rāma.
bal.120.cau2: My lord, by your grace my sorrow is now gone; by the favour of my Lord's feet I am at peace.
Now, knowing me for your own handmaid, though I am by nature a dull and unknowing woman,
bal.120.cau3: tell me what I asked at first, if you are pleased with me, my Lord.
Śrī Rāma is Brahman, pure consciousness, imperishable, apart from all and dwelling in the city of every heart;
bal.120.cau4: why then, my lord, did he take a human body? Explain it to me, Vṛṣaketu, lord of the bull banner.
When he heard Umā's deeply humble words and saw her pure love for Śrī Rāma's story,
bal.120.do120क: Then Śaṅkara, the foe of Kāma, wise by nature, rejoiced in his heart,
and praising Umā in many ways, the treasury of grace then spoke:
bal.120.so120ख: Listen, Bhavānī, to the auspicious story, the spotless Rāmacaritamānasa,
which Bhuśuṇḍi told at length and Garuḍa, king of the birds, heard.
bal.120.so120ग: How that noble dialogue came about I shall tell later.
Now hear the story of Śrī Rāma's incarnation, supremely beautiful and free of all stain.
bal.120.so120घ: Hari's virtues, names, stories and forms are boundless, countless and beyond measure.
I tell them as far as my own understanding goes; Umā, listen with reverence.
bal.121.cau1: Listen, Girijā: the lovely deeds of Hari are many and bright, and the Vedas and scriptures have sung them.
The cause from which Hari's incarnation comes cannot be stated as being exactly this and thus.
bal.121.cau2: Śrī Rāma lies beyond the reach of intellect, mind and speech: this is our view; listen, wise one.
Yet whatever the saints, sages, Vedas and Purāṇas say, each reasoning by their own understanding,
bal.121.cau3: in the same way, fair-faced one, I tell you the cause as I myself understand it.
Whenever dharma declines, and vile and arrogant asuras grow strong,
bal.121.cau4: and commit wrongs beyond describing, and Brahmins, cows, the gods and the earth are in distress,
then the Lord, the treasury of grace, takes bodies of many kinds and relieves the suffering of the good.
bal.121.do121: He slays the asuras and restores the gods, he keeps the bounds set by his own Vedas,
and spreads his bright glory through the world: this is the cause of Śrī Rāma's birth.
bal.122.cau1: By singing that same glory his devotees cross worldly existence; the ocean of mercy takes a body for the good of his own.
The causes of Śrī Rāma's birth are many, and each is more wondrous than the one before.
bal.122.cau2: I shall tell in detail of one or two of his births; listen attentively, wise Bhavānī.
Hari has two dear door-keepers, Jaya and Vijaya, known to all.
bal.122.cau3: Through a Brahmin's curse the two brothers took the bodies of asuras of darkness:
Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, famed throughout the world, who broke the pride of Indra, lord of the gods.
bal.122.cau4: They were renowned heroes, victorious in battle. Taking the body of a boar, the Lord struck down one of them;
then, becoming the man-lion, he slew the other and spread far and wide the fame of his devotee Prahlāda.
bal.122.do122: Those same two went on to become demons, great heroes and mighty:
Kumbhakarṇa and Rāvaṇa, fine warriors who conquered the gods, as the world knows.
bal.123.cau1: Slain by the Lord, they were still not set free, for by the Brahmin's word they were to have three births.
Once, for their good, the Lord who loves his devotees took a body.
bal.123.cau2: Kaśyapa and Aditi were then his father and mother, who became renowned as Daśaratha and Kausalyā.
In one kalpa he came down in this way and did holy deeds in the world.
bal.123.cau3: In one kalpa, seeing the gods in distress, all of them beaten in battle by Jalandhara,
Śiva fought him in a battle without end, but the mighty dānava would not die though struck.
bal.123.cau4: The wife of that king of the asuras was supremely chaste; by her power even Śiva, the foe of Tripura, could not conquer him.
bal.123.do123: By a trick the Lord broke her vow and did the work of the gods.
When she learnt the secret, she grew angry and laid a curse on him.
bal.124.cau1: Hari, the treasury of play, the compassionate Lord, accepted her curse as binding.
There Jalandhara became Rāvaṇa, and Śrī Rāma slew him in battle and gave him the supreme state.
bal.124.cau2: This was the cause of one birth, for which Śrī Rāma took a human body.
Listen, sage: the story of the Lord in each incarnation has been told by poets in many ways.
bal.124.cau3: Once Nārada laid a curse, and for that the incarnation came about in one kalpa.
Girijā was astonished to hear this, and said: Nārada is a devotee of Viṣṇu, and wise besides.
bal.124.cau4: For what reason did the sage lay the curse? What wrong had the lord of Ramā done?
Tell me this story, Purāri; delusion in the mind of a sage is a great wonder.
bal.124.do124क: Then Maheśa smiled and said: No one is wise, and no one a fool;
as Śrī Rāma makes anyone at any time, so that one becomes in that very moment.
bal.124.so124ख: I tell the story of Śrī Rāma's virtues; Bharadvāja, listen with reverence.
Tulasīdāsa, cast off pride and arrogance and worship Śrī Rāma, who breaks the round of worldly existence.
bal.125.cau1: In the Himālaya there was a cave of great holiness, and near it flowed the lovely Gaṅgā.
The hermitage was supremely pure and lovely; when Nārada, the divine sage, saw it, it delighted his heart.
bal.125.cau2: Gazing on the mountains, the river and the stretches of forest, he was filled with love for the feet of the lord of Ramā.
As he remembered Hari, the curse lost its hold, and his mind, pure by nature, passed into samādhi.
bal.125.cau3: Seeing the sage in this state, Indra, lord of the gods, grew afraid. He called Kāma and showed him honour,
and said: Go with your companions on my behalf. Kāma, whose banner bears a fish, set out rejoicing at heart.
bal.125.cau4: The fear in Indra's mind was this: the divine sage wants to live in my city.
Those in the world who are lustful and greedy fear everyone, like the crafty crow.
bal.125.do125: As a foolish dog with a dry bone runs off on seeing a lion,
the dull creature thinking it might snatch the bone away, just so Indra felt no shame.
bal.126.cau1: When Kāma went to that hermitage, he created spring by his own māyā.
Trees of every kind burst into many-coloured bloom; cuckoos sang and bees hummed.
bal.126.cau2: A pleasant threefold breeze began to blow, cool, gentle and fragrant, fanning the fire of desire.
Rambhā and the other young celestial nymphs, skilled in all the arts of Kāma,
bal.126.cau3: sang with many rippling melodic runs and played in many ways with balls in their hands.
Seeing these helpers, Kāma was glad, and then he worked wiles of many kinds.
bal.126.cau4: But no art of Kāma touched the sage at all, and the sinful god of love grew afraid for himself.
Can anyone encroach on the bounds of one whose mighty guardian is the Lord of Lakṣmī?
bal.126.do126: Then, admitting defeat in his heart, Kāma, terrified, with his helpers,
went and clasped the sage's feet, speaking most piteous words.
bal.127.cau1: No anger at all arose in Nārada's mind; with kind words he set Kāma at ease.
Then Kāma bowed his head at the sage's feet and, given leave, went away with his helpers.
bal.127.cau2: Going to Indra's assembly, he told everything: the sage's gentleness and his own doings.
All who heard it were amazed; they praised the sage and bowed their heads to Śrī Hari.
bal.127.cau3: Then Nārada went to Śiva, with the pride in his mind that he had conquered Kāma.
He told Śaṅkara what Kāma had done, and Maheśa, knowing him very dear, gave him counsel.
bal.127.cau4: Śiva said: O sage, I entreat you again and again: as you have told this story to me,
never tell it so to Śrī Hari; even if the subject comes up, keep it hidden even then.
bal.127.do127: Śiva gave counsel for his good, but it did not please Nārada.
Bharadvāja, hear this marvel: the will of Śrī Hari is mighty.
bal.128.cau1: Whatever Śrī Rāma wishes to do, that alone comes to pass; there is no one who can make it otherwise.
Śiva's words did not please the sage's mind, and he went away to the world of Brahmā.
bal.128.cau2: Once the chief of sages, skilled in song, with a fine vīṇā in his hand and singing the virtues of Śrī Hari,
went to the Ocean of Milk, where dwells Śrīnivāsa, the crown of the Vedas.
bal.128.cau3: The Lord, Lakṣmī's abode, rose in delight and met him, and sat down on a seat with the seer.
The Lord of all that moves and does not move said with a smile: O sage, after many days you have shown this kindness.
bal.128.cau4: Though Śiva had forbidden it beforehand, Nārada told all that Kāma had done.
Mighty beyond measure is Śrī Rāma's māyā: who has been born in the world whom it does not delude?
bal.128.do128: With a stern face but in gentle words the blessed Lord said:
Remembering you wipes away delusion, desire, pride and arrogance.
bal.129.cau1: Listen, O sage: delusion arises in the mind of one who has no knowledge or dispassion in his heart.
You are devoted to the vow of celibacy and steady of mind; can the god of love trouble you?
bal.129.cau2: Nārada said with pride: Lord, it is all your grace.
The ocean of compassion reflected in his mind and saw that a great tree of pride had sprouted in Nārada's heart.
bal.129.cau3: He thought: I will soon root it out and throw it away; my vow is to do good to my servants.
I will surely devise the means that brings the sage his good and is a sport for me as well.
bal.129.cau4: Then Nārada bowed his head at Śrī Hari's feet and went his way, the pride swelling in his heart.
Then the Lord of Śrī urged on his māyā; hear the hard things it did.
bal.129.do129: On his way it built a city a hundred yojanas wide,
fashioned in many ways, finer even than Vaikuṇṭha, the city of Śrīnivāsa.
bal.130.cau1: In the city lived men and women so fair that they seemed to be many Kāmas and Ratis in bodily form.
In that city lived a king named Śīlanidhi, with countless horses, elephants and hosts of troops.
bal.130.cau2: His wealth and pleasures equalled those of a hundred Indras; he was the home of beauty, splendour, strength and statecraft.
His daughter was Viśvamohinī, at the sight of whose beauty even Lakṣmī would be enchanted.
bal.130.cau3: She was the Lord's māyā itself, a mine of every virtue; how could her beauty be described?
That princess was holding her svayaṃvara (the choosing of a husband), and countless kings had come there.
bal.130.cau4: Full of curiosity, the sage went into that city and asked the townspeople about everything.
Having heard all that was afoot, he came to the palace, and the king worshipped the sage and gave him a seat.
bal.130.do130: The king brought the princess and showed her to Nārada, saying:
My lord, consider in your heart and tell me all her merits and faults.
bal.131.cau1: At the sight of her beauty the sage forgot his dispassion and kept gazing at her a long while.
Seeing the marks on her, he lost himself; there was joy in his heart, but he did not reveal the marks openly.
bal.131.cau2: The marks showed that whoever weds her will become immortal, and no one will conquer him on the field of battle.
All that moves and does not move will serve the one whom Śīlanidhi's daughter chooses.
bal.131.cau3: Weighing all the marks, he kept them in his heart, and made up a few things to tell the king.
Telling the king that his daughter bore auspicious marks, Nārada left, with a worry in his mind.
bal.131.cau4: He thought: Let me go and, after thinking it over, make the effort by which this maiden would choose me.
Neither japa nor austerity can do anything at this hour. O Creator, by what means can I win the girl?
bal.131.do131: What this occasion needs is the highest splendour and great beauty of form,
so that the princess, seeing it, is charmed and then puts the victory garland on me.
bal.132.cau1: Let me ask Śrī Hari for beauty; but, oh, going to him will take a great while.
No one wishes me well as Śrī Hari does; may he be my helper at this hour.
bal.132.cau2: At that time he prayed in many ways, and the playful, compassionate Lord appeared.
Seeing the Lord, the sage's eyes were soothed, and he rejoiced in his heart that the work would be done.
bal.132.cau3: In great distress he told the whole story and said: Be gracious and be my helper.
Lord, give me your own form; in no other way can I win her.
bal.132.cau4: My Lord, do quickly whatever will bring my good; I am your servant.
Seeing the vast power of his own māyā, the Lord, merciful to the lowly, laughed inwardly and said:
bal.132.do132: Listen, Nārada: whatever way will bring your highest good,
that is what I will do, and nothing else; my word is never false.
bal.133.cau1: A patient tormented by illness asks for harmful food, and the physician does not give it; listen, O sage and yogī.
In the same way I have resolved on your good. Saying this, the Lord vanished.
bal.133.cau2: Overpowered by māyā, the sage was bewildered and did not grasp the hidden sense of Śrī Hari's words.
The king of seers went at once to the place where the ground for the svayaṃvara had been laid out.
bal.133.cau3: The kings, finely adorned, sat on their own seats, each with his company.
The sage rejoiced in his mind: My beauty is great; passing me by, she will not choose another even by mistake.
bal.133.cau4: For the sage's good, the treasury of mercy had given him an ugliness beyond description.
Yet no one could see this play; taking him for Nārada, all bowed their heads to him.
bal.133.do133: Two of Rudra's gaṇas (attendants) were there, and they knew the whole secret.
In the guise of Brahmins they went about watching everything; they too were great lovers of fun.
bal.134.cau1: In the gathering where the sage had gone and sat, his pride in his beauty swelling in his heart,
there sat Maheśa's two gaṇas too; in their Brahmin guise no one could see what they were about.
bal.134.cau2: They kept making jibes for Nārada to hear: Śrī Hari has given him fine beauty indeed!
The princess will be charmed by his looks and, taking him for Hari (the Lord, and also a monkey), will choose him above all.
bal.134.cau3: The sage was deluded, his mind in another's hands, and Śiva's gaṇas laughed with great delight.
Though the sage heard their strange words, he could not make sense of them, his reason steeped in delusion.
bal.134.cau4: No one saw this special play; only the princess saw that form of his:
a monkey's face and a dreadful body; at the sight of it, anger rose in her heart.
bal.134.do134: Then the princess moved forward with her companions, like a royal swan.
She goes round looking at all the kings, the victory garland in her lotus hands.
bal.135.cau1: The side where Nārada sat, all puffed up, she did not look towards even by mistake.
Again and again the sage strains upward and grows restless; seeing his state, Śiva's gaṇas smile.
bal.135.cau2: The compassionate Lord, taking a king's form, went there, and the princess joyfully put the victory garland on him.
The Lord, Lakṣmī's abode, carried off the bride, and the whole gathering of kings was left disappointed.
bal.135.cau3: The sage was in great distress, his reason ruined by delusion, as though a jewel tied in a knot had slipped out and fallen.
Then Śiva's gaṇas said with a smile: Go and look at your face in a mirror.
bal.135.cau4: Saying this, the two fled in great fear. The sage looked into water and saw his face.
Seeing his guise, his anger rose high, and he laid a very harsh curse on them:
bal.135.do135: You are deceitful and sinful, both of you: go and become demons.
You laughed at me; take the fruit of it. Now laugh at a sage again!
bal.136.cau1: Then he looked in the water and found his own form again; even so, there was no contentment in his heart.
His lips quivering and anger in his mind, he set off at once to the Lord of Lakṣmī.
bal.136.cau2: He thought: I shall either curse him or go and die; he has made me a laughing-stock in the world.
Midway on the road he met the Lord, the foe of the demons, and with him were Lakṣmī and that very princess.
bal.136.cau3: The Lord of the gods spoke sweet words: Sage, where are you going like one distraught?
On hearing these words a great anger rose in him; in the grip of māyā, his mind had lost its awareness.
bal.136.cau4: Nārada said: You cannot bear to see another's wealth; you are full of envy and deceit.
When the ocean was churned you drove Rudra mad, and by urging the gods on you made him drink the poison.
bal.136.do136: You gave the wine to the demons and the poison to Śaṅkara, and kept Lakṣmī and the lovely gem for yourself.
You are crooked and serve your own ends; your dealings are always deceitful.
bal.137.cau1: You are utterly free, with no one over your head; whatever pleases your mind, that you do.
You make the good bad and the bad good, and hold neither dismay nor joy in your heart.
bal.137.cau2: Cheating everyone time after time, you have grown used to it; your mind is quite without fear and always in high spirits.
Good and evil deeds do not bind you; till now no one has brought you to account.
bal.137.cau3: Now you have sent your gift to the right house (one that will return it); you will reap the fruit of your own doing.
The body in which you deceived me, that very body you shall take: this is my curse.
bal.137.cau4: You gave me the likeness of a monkey; so monkeys will be your helpers.
You have done me great harm; you will suffer in separation from your wife.
bal.137.do137: Accepting the curse on his head, the Lord rejoiced in his heart and pleaded with him at length,
and the treasury of mercy drew back the full force of his māyā.
bal.138.cau1: When Śrī Hari had sent his māyā far away, neither Lakṣmī nor the princess was there.
Then the sage, in great fear, clasped Śrī Hari's feet: Protect me, you who take away the distress of those who bow to you.
bal.138.cau2: O compassionate Lord, let my curse be false. The Lord, kind to the lowly, said: It was my own will.
The sage said: I have spoken many harsh words; how will my sins be wiped away?
bal.138.cau3: The Lord said: Go and repeat the hundred names of Śaṅkara, and your heart will at once find peace.
No one is as dear to me as Śiva; never let go of this faith, even by mistake.
bal.138.cau4: Sage, one to whom Śiva, the foe of Tripura, does not show grace does not attain devotion to me.
Holding this in your heart, go and roam the earth; māyā will not come near you now.
bal.138.do138: Having consoled the sage in many ways, the Lord then vanished,
and Nārada set off for Satyaloka, singing the praises of Śrī Rāma.
bal.139.cau1: Śiva's gaṇas saw the sage going along the road, his delusion gone and his mind full of joy.
In great fear they came to Nārada, clasped his feet and spoke in distress:
