bal.139.cau2: King of sages, we are not Brahmins but Śiva's gaṇas; we committed a great offence and have reaped its fruit.
Compassionate one, show us grace in this curse. Nārada, kind to the lowly, said:
bal.139.cau3: Go, both of you, and become demons; may you have great splendour, glory and strength.
When by the strength of your arms you have conquered the world, then Viṣṇu will take a human body.
bal.139.cau4: Your death will come in battle at Śrī Hari's hands; you will be set free and not return to worldly existence.
The two bowed their heads at the sage's feet and went away, and in due time they became demons.
bal.139.do139: In one kalpa, for this reason, the Lord took incarnation as a man;
he is Śrī Hari, who delights the gods, brings joy to the good and destroys the burden of the earth.
bal.140.cau1: In this way Śrī Hari's births and deeds are many, beautiful, joy-giving and wonderful.
In every kalpa the Lord comes down to earth and performs lovely deeds of many kinds.
bal.140.cau2: Each time, great sages have sung his story, composing supremely holy works.
They have told of various incomparable episodes; hearing them, the wise are not surprised.
bal.140.cau3: Śrī Hari is endless, and endless is his story; all the saints tell it and hear it in many ways.
The charming deeds of Śrī Rāmacandra could not be sung to the end even in ten million kalpas.
bal.140.cau4: Bhavānī, I have told this episode because Śrī Hari's māyā deludes even wise sages.
The Lord is playful and does good to those who bow to him; he is easily reached by service and takes away every sorrow.
bal.140.so140: Among gods, men and sages there is no one whom mighty māyā does not delude.
Reflecting on this in the mind, one should worship the Lord of the great Māyā.
bal.141.cau1: Hear another cause, daughter of the mountain; I tell its wonderful story in full:
the cause for which the unborn Brahman, without attributes or form, became king of Kosala's city.
bal.141.cau2: The Lord you saw wandering in the forest with his brother, in the garb of a hermit,
whose deeds, Bhavānī, so bewildered you when you were in Satī's body,
bal.141.cau3: even now its shadow has not left you: hear his deeds, which cure the disease of delusion.
All the play he performed in that incarnation I shall tell, as far as my understanding goes.
bal.141.cau4: Bharadvāja, hearing Śaṅkara's words, Umā smiled, shy and full of love.
Then Śiva, whose banner bears the bull, began to describe the cause for which that incarnation came about.
bal.141.do141: That I tell you in full, lord of sages; listen with your whole mind.
The story of Śrī Rāma takes away the impurities of the Kali age; it brings blessings and is lovely.
bal.142.cau1: Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā, from whom the incomparable human race came forth:
the couple's practice of dharma was excellent, and even today the Vedas sing of the path they set.
bal.142.cau2: King Uttānapāda was his son, and his son was Dhruva, the devotee of Hari.
His younger son was named Priyavrata, whom the Vedas and Purāṇas praise.
bal.142.cau3: Then there was Devahūti, his daughter, the beloved wife of the sage Kardama,
who bore in her womb the primal God, the Lord kind to the lowly, the compassionate Kapila,
bal.142.cau4: the Lord who openly set forth the Sāṅkhya śāstra and is skilled in the analysis of the principles of being.
That Manu ruled for a long time and kept the Lord's command in every way.
bal.142.so142: Dispassion from the objects of the senses does not come while one lives at home, and the fourth stage of life had arrived.
Great sorrow filled his heart that his life had passed without devotion to Hari.
bal.143.cau1: Then he pressed the kingdom on his son and set out for the forest with his wife.
Naimiṣa is renowned, the best of tīrthas, most holy, granting attainment to those who strive.
bal.143.cau2: Communities of sages and siddhas live there, and there King Manu went with a glad heart.
Going along the way, the steadfast pair shone as if knowledge and devotion had taken bodies.
bal.143.cau3: They reached the bank of the Dhenumatī (the Gomatī) and bathed joyfully in its clear water.
Siddhas and wise sages came to meet him, knowing him for a royal sage who bore the weight of dharma.
bal.143.cau4: Wherever there were lovely tīrthas, the sages respectfully took them to every one.
Their bodies lean, dressed in hermits' clothes, they hear the Purāṇas every day in the company of the good.
bal.143.do143: And they repeat the twelve-syllable mantra with love;
the minds of the couple were deeply fixed on the lotus feet of Vāsudeva.
bal.144.cau1: They live on greens, fruits and roots, and remember Brahman, who is being, consciousness and bliss.
Then they began austerities for Śrī Hari, giving up roots and fruits and living on water alone.
bal.144.cau2: In their hearts there is a constant longing to see with their eyes that supreme Lord
who is without attributes, undivided, endless and without beginning, on whom those who speak of the highest truth meditate;
bal.144.cau3: whom the Veda describes as 'not this, not this'; who is bliss in himself, free of all limiting conditions, beyond compare;
from a part of whom many Śivas, Brahmās and Viṣṇus come into being.
bal.144.cau4: Even such a Lord is ruled by his servant, and for his devotee takes a body for his play.
They think: if this word spoken by the Vedas is true, our longing will be fulfilled.
bal.144.do144: In this way six thousand years went by, with water as their food;
then for seven thousand years they lived on air alone.
bal.145.cau1: For ten thousand years they gave up even that, and both stood on one foot.
Seeing their boundless austerity, Brahmā, Hari and Hara came to Manu many times.
bal.145.cau2: They tempted them in many ways, urging them to ask a boon; but the two were supremely steadfast, and for all the gods' attempts to move them, they would not be moved.
Their bodies had wasted away to mere bone, but in their minds they felt not even a little pain.
bal.145.cau3: The all-knowing Lord knew the ascetic king and queen to be his own servants, with no refuge but him.
A voice spoke from the sky: Ask, ask a boon. It was supremely deep and steeped in the nectar of grace.
bal.145.cau4: When that lovely voice, which could bring the dead to life, passed through the openings of their ears into their hearts,
their bodies grew hale, full and fair, as though they had just come from home.
bal.145.do145: Hearing words like nectar to the ears, their bodies thrilled and bloomed with joy.
Manu prostrated himself and spoke, his heart unable to hold its love.
bal.146.cau1: Listen, you who are a wish-fulfilling tree and a wish-granting cow to your servants, and the dust of whose feet Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva revere.
You are easily reached through service and give every joy; you protect those who bow to you and are the Lord of all that moves and does not move.
bal.146.cau2: Friend of the helpless, if you have love for us, be pleased and grant us this boon:
the form that dwells in Śiva's mind, the form for which sages strive,
bal.146.cau3: the swan of the Mānasa lake of Bhuśuṇḍi's mind, which the Vedas praise as both with attributes and without —
let us see that form to our eyes' fill. Be gracious, you who free those who bow to you from their distress.
bal.146.cau4: The couple's words, gentle, humble and steeped in the sweetness of love, were most dear to the Lord.
The Lord who loves his devotees, the treasury of grace, in whom the whole universe dwells, the Blessed Lord, appeared before them.
bal.146.do146: He is dark like the blue lotus, the sapphire and the blue rain-cloud.
Seeing the beauty of his body, hundreds of millions upon millions of Kāmadevas are put to shame.
bal.147.cau1: His face, like the autumn moon, is the very limit of beauty; his cheeks and chin are lovely, and his neck is like a conch.
His lips are red, his teeth and nose are beautiful, and his smile puts to shame the moon's whole mass of rays.
bal.147.cau2: His eyes, like fresh lotuses, are lovely to see, and his glance is graceful and dear to the heart.
His eyebrows rob Kāma's bow of its beauty, and the tilaka on the expanse of his forehead is radiant.
bal.147.cau3: His earrings are shaped like makaras, a crown gleams on his head, and his curling locks look like a swarm of bees.
On his chest are the Śrīvatsa mark, a lovely garland of forest flowers, a jewelled pendant, necklaces and ornaments of gems.
bal.147.cau4: His neck is like a lion's, his sacred thread is lovely, and the ornaments on his arms are beautiful too.
His mighty arms are shapely like an elephant's trunk; a quiver is at his waist, and arrow and bow are in his hands.
bal.147.do147: His yellow robe puts lightning to shame, and on his belly are three fine folds.
His navel is so charming that it seems to snatch away the beauty of the Yamunā's whirlpools.
bal.148.cau1: His lotus feet are beyond description; in them dwell the bees of the sages' minds.
At his left side shines the primal Śakti, ever in accord with him, the treasury of beauty and the root of the world —
bal.148.cau2: she from a portion of whom countless Lakṣmīs, Umās and Brahmāṇīs arise, mines of every virtue,
and by the play of whose eyebrow the world comes into being: she is Sītā, at Śrī Rāma's left.
bal.148.cau3: Beholding the form of Hari, an ocean of beauty, they stayed gazing without a blink, their eyelids held still.
They look with reverence on that peerless form, and still Manu and Śatarūpā cannot have their fill of it.
bal.148.cau4: Overcome with joy, they forgot the state of their bodies and, clasping his feet with their hands, fell flat like staffs.
With his own lotus hands the Lord touched their heads, and he, the very mass of compassion, raised them at once.
bal.148.do148: Then the treasury of grace said: Knowing that I am well pleased,
and taking me for a great giver, ask for whatever boon your heart desires.
bal.149.cau1: Hearing the Lord's words, Manu joined his palms, gathered his composure and spoke in gentle words:
My Lord, with the sight of your lotus feet every desire of ours is now fulfilled.
bal.149.cau2: There is one great longing in my heart; it is both easy and hard, and it cannot be put into words.
For you, my master, it is very easy to grant; it seems hard to me because of my own littleness.
bal.149.cau3: As a poor man who has found the wish-fulfilling tree of the gods hesitates to ask it for great wealth,
because he does not know its power, so doubt rises in my heart.
bal.149.cau4: You know it, knower of all hearts; fulfil my wish, my master.
The Lord said: Put aside your hesitation, king, and ask of me; there is nothing of mine that cannot be given to you.
bal.149.do149: Manu said: Crown of all givers, treasury of grace, my Lord, I tell you what is truly in my heart:
I want a son like you. What is there to hide from the Lord?
bal.150.cau1: Seeing his love and hearing his priceless words, the ocean of compassion said: So be it.
Where could I go to look for one like myself? King, I myself will come and be your son.
bal.150.cau2: Seeing Śatarūpā with her palms joined, the Lord said: Goddess, ask for whatever boon you wish.
Śatarūpā said: My Lord, the boon the wise king has asked for, compassionate one, has pleased me greatly.
bal.150.cau3: But, my Lord, it is great boldness, even though, friend of your devotees, it pleases you.
You are the father of Brahmā and the rest, the Lord of the world, Brahman, dwelling within every heart.
bal.150.cau4: When I consider this, doubt rises in my mind; yet what the Lord has said is the final word.
My Lord, those who are your own devotees: the joy they find and the state they reach,
bal.150.do150: that same joy, that same state, that same devotion, that same love for your feet,
that same discernment and that same way of life, my Lord, graciously grant us.
bal.151.cau1: Hearing her gentle, deep, lovely and finely wrought words, the ocean of mercy spoke gently:
Whatever wish is in your mind, I have granted it all; have no doubt of it.
bal.151.cau2: Mother, by my grace the discernment you have, which is not of this world, will never fade.
Bowing to his feet, Manu spoke again: My Lord, I have one more request.
bal.151.cau3: Let my love for your feet be love for you as my son, and let anyone call me a great fool if they will.
As a snake cannot live without its gem, or a fish without water, so let my life depend on you.
bal.151.cau4: Having asked for such a boon, Manu stayed clasping the Lord's feet, and the ocean of compassion said: So be it.
Now do as I command: go and live in the capital of Indra, king of the gods.
bal.151.so151: There, dear one, you will enjoy abundant pleasures, and when some time has passed
you will be king of Avadh; then I will be your son.
bal.152.cau1: Taking on a human form shaped by my own will, I will appear in your home.
Taking a body along with my portions, dear one, I will perform deeds that bring joy to devotees,
bal.152.cau2: and fortunate people who hear them with reverence will cross the ocean of worldly existence, giving up attachment and pride.
The primal Śakti, who brought the world into being, this māyā of mine, will also take birth.
bal.152.cau3: I will fulfil your longing; my vow is true, true, true.
Saying this again and again, the Lord, the treasury of grace, vanished from sight.
bal.152.cau4: Holding in their hearts the Lord who is gracious to his devotees, the couple lived for some time in that hermitage.
When the time came, they left their bodies without effort and went to dwell in Amarāvatī.
bal.152.do152: This most holy history Śiva, whose banner bears the bull, told to Umā.
Bharadvāja, listen now to a further cause of the birth of Śrī Rāma.
bal.153.cau1: Listen, sage, to the holy and ancient story that Śiva told to Girijā.
There was a land called Kekaya, famed throughout the world, and King Satyaketu lived there.
bal.153.cau2: He bore the yoke of dharma, was a treasury of sound policy, and was full of splendour, glory, good character and strength.
Two heroic sons were born to him, homes of every virtue and greatly steadfast in battle.
bal.153.cau3: The elder son, heir to the kingdom, was named Pratāpabhānu.
The other son was named Arimardana; the strength of his arms was matchless, and in battle he stood unmoved.
bal.153.cau4: Between the two brothers there was the closest harmony, a love free of every fault and guile.
The king gave the kingdom to his elder son and himself left for the forest, for the sake of Hari.
bal.153.do153: When Pratāpabhānu became king, his rule was proclaimed throughout the land.
He cared for his subjects well, by the rule of the Vedas, and nowhere was there a trace of sin.
bal.154.cau1: The king had a wise minister devoted to his good, Dharmaruci by name, the equal of Śukra.
His minister was wise, his brother a mighty hero, and he himself a mass of glory, steadfast in battle.
bal.154.cau2: He had with him a boundless fourfold army, countless fine warriors, every one of them a fighter in battle.
At the sight of his army the king rejoiced, and the kettledrums thundered.
bal.154.cau3: He marshalled his army for conquest and, fixing an auspicious day, set out to the beat of drums.
Battles broke out in many places, and he conquered every king by force.
bal.154.cau4: By the strength of his arms he brought the seven continents under his sway, and took tribute from each king and let him go.
At that time the whole circle of the earth had a single ruler, Pratāpabhānu.
bal.154.do154: Having brought the world under his own sway by the might of his arms, the king entered his city.
He pursued wealth, dharma, pleasure and the other joys, each at its proper time.
bal.155.cau1: Drawing strength from King Pratāpabhānu, the lovely earth became a wish-granting cow.
His subjects were free of all sorrow and happy, and the men and women were righteous and beautiful.
bal.155.cau2: The minister Dharmaruci loved Hari's feet, and for the king's good he always taught him sound policy.
The king ever served his guru, the gods, the saints, the ancestors and the Brahmins, all of them.
bal.155.cau3: All the duties of a king that the Vedas set out, he carried out with reverence and took joy in them.
Every day he gave gifts of many kinds, and he listened to the excellent śāstras, the Vedas and the Purāṇas.
bal.155.cau4: He had many stepwells, wells and ponds made, flower gardens and beautiful orchards,
and at every place of pilgrimage he built lovely homes for Brahmins and temples to the gods, wonderfully wrought.
bal.155.do155: Of all the sacrifices the Purāṇas and the Vedas describe, every single one
the king performed a thousand times over, with love.
bal.156.cau1: In his heart there was no seeking after any fruit; the king was discerning and supremely wise.
Whatever dharma the wise king did, in deed, in mind and in speech, he offered it all to Vāsudeva.
bal.156.cau2: Once the king mounted a fine horse and, with his whole hunting party made ready,
went into the deep forest of the Vindhya hills, where he killed many pure deer.
bal.156.cau3: Roaming the forest, the king saw a wild boar, as if Rāhu had seized the moon and hidden in the forest.
The moon is too large to fit inside his mouth, and, as if in anger, he will not spit it out either.
bal.156.cau4: So the beauty of the boar's fearsome tusks has been told; its body too was huge and very stout.
Hearing the sound of the horse, it grunted and looked about, startled, with its ears pricked up.
bal.156.do156: Seeing that huge boar, like the peak of a blue mountain,
the king touched his horse with the whip and sped towards it, crying out that now it had no escape.
bal.157.cau1: Seeing the horse coming with a great noise, the boar ran off at the speed of the wind.
At once the king fitted an arrow; at the sight of the arrow the boar pressed itself flat to the ground.
bal.157.cau2: Taking aim again and again, the king loosed his arrows, but by trickery the boar kept its body safe.
Now in sight, now hidden, the beast ran on, and the king, in the grip of anger, followed hard behind it.
bal.157.cau3: The boar went far off into a thick, deep forest, where neither elephant nor horse could make its way.
The king was all alone and the forest full of hardship, yet the king would not leave the beast's track.
bal.157.cau4: Seeing how very steadfast the king was, the boar fled into a deep mountain cave.
Seeing that it could not be reached, the king was full of regret; turning back, he lost his way in that great forest.
bal.157.do157: Worn out with fatigue, hungry and thirsty, the king, with his horse,
searched in distress for a river or a lake, and without water he grew faint.
bal.158.cau1: As he roamed the forest he came upon a hermitage; there, in the false guise of a sage, lived a king
whose country this king had taken from him, and who had left his army on the battlefield and fled.
bal.158.cau2: Knowing the time to be Pratāpabhānu's, and judging it very much against himself,
he did not go home, for great shame filled his mind, nor did that proud king come to terms with Pratāpabhānu.
bal.158.cau3: Holding down the anger in his heart, that king dwelt in the forest as a pauper would, in an ascetic's garb.
King Pratāpabhānu went up to him, and he knew him at once for Pratāpabhānu.
bal.158.cau4: Being thirsty, the king did not recognise him; seeing his fair garb, he took him for a great sage.
He got down from his horse and bowed, but, being very shrewd, he did not tell his own name.
bal.158.do158: Seeing the king thirsty, he showed him a lake.
Gladly the king bathed and drank there, and his horse with him.
bal.159.cau1: All his weariness left him and the king was at ease. The ascetic took him to his own hermitage.
Knowing that the sun had set, he gave him a seat; then the ascetic spoke in a gentle voice:
bal.159.cau2: Who are you? Why do you roam the forest alone, a handsome young man, careless of your life?
You bear the marks of an emperor; seeing them, great pity rises in me.
bal.159.cau3: The king said: Hear me, lord of sages. I am the minister of a king named Pratāpabhānu.
I strayed from the path while roaming on the hunt, and by great good fortune have come here and seen your feet.
bal.159.cau4: The sight of you is rare for us; I take it that some good is about to come.
The sage said: Dear one, it has grown dark, and your city is seventy yojanas away.
bal.159.do159क: Listen, wise one: the night is fearful, the forest deep, and there is no path to be seen.
Knowing this, stay here tonight, and go when the day breaks.
bal.159.do159ख: Tulasīdāsa says: As destiny is, so is the help one finds.
Either it comes to a person of itself, or it takes that person to where it is.
bal.160.cau1: Saying, Very well, my lord, and taking the command upon his head, the king tied his horse to a tree and sat down.
The king praised him in many ways, bowed at his feet and counted himself fortunate.
bal.160.cau2: Then he spoke in gentle, pleasing words: My lord, thinking of you as a father, I make bold to ask:
lord of sages, knowing me as your son and servant, tell me your name, my lord, and tell it in full.
bal.160.cau3: The king did not know him, but he knew the king; the king was kind of heart, and he was cunning in deceit.
An enemy, a kṣatriya besides, and a king besides, he meant to gain his ends by guile and by force.
bal.160.cau4: Brooding on the joys of royalty, that enemy was in pain; his breast smouldered like the fire in a potter's kiln.
Hearing with his own ears the king's guileless words, he called his enmity to mind and rejoiced at heart.
bal.160.do160: Steeping his words in deceit, he spoke softly and with cunning:
My name now is Beggar; I am without wealth and without a home.
bal.161.cau1: The king said: Those who, like you, are treasuries of realised knowledge, their pride melted away,
always keep their true selves hidden; able in every way, they go about in a lowly guise.
bal.161.cau2: That is why the saints and the Vedas proclaim aloud that those who own nothing at all are dear to Śrī Hari.
Over one like you, penniless, a beggar, homeless, even Brahmā and Śiva are left in doubt.
bal.161.cau3: Whoever you are, whatever you are, I bow at your feet; be gracious to me now, master.
Seeing the king's natural love, and the special trust he placed in him,
bal.161.cau4: and when he had made the king wholly his own, he spoke with a show of yet greater affection:
Listen, king, I tell you in all sincerity: much time has passed while I have lived here.
bal.161.do161क: Till now no one has met me, and I make myself known to no one;
for the world's esteem is like a fire that burns up the forest of austerity.
bal.161.so161ख: Tulasīdāsa says: Seeing a fair guise, not fools alone but clever men too are deceived.
Look at the beautiful peacock: its voice is like nectar, and its food is snakes.
bal.162.cau1: The ascetic said: That is why I live hidden in the world; apart from Śrī Hari I have no purpose whatever.
The Lord knows all, without anything being made known to him; say, what attainment comes of pleasing the world?
bal.162.cau2: You are pure and right-minded, and very dear to me, and you have love and faith in me.
Now, dear one, if I hide anything from you, a grievous fault will fall upon me.
bal.162.cau3: The more the ascetic spoke of detachment, the more the king's trust grew.
When he saw the king was under his sway in deed, mind and speech, the ascetic, meditating as a heron does, said:
bal.162.cau4: Brother, my name is Ekatanu. At this the king bowed his head once more and said:
Knowing me as your very own servant, explain to me the meaning of the name.
bal.162.do162: The ascetic said: When the first creation came into being, I was born then.
My name is Ekatanu, One Body, because I never took another body after that.
bal.163.cau1: Son, do not wonder at it in your mind: nothing is beyond the reach of austerity.
By the power of austerity the Creator makes the world; by the power of austerity Viṣṇu became its protector.
bal.163.cau2: By the power of austerity Śiva brings about destruction; there is nothing in the world austerity cannot reach.
At these words a deep affection rose in the king; and the ascetic set about telling ancient tales.
bal.163.cau3: He told many histories of karma and dharma, and set out the nature of dispassion and discernment.
He told at length the tales of creation, preservation and dissolution, with wonders beyond measure.
bal.163.cau4: Hearing this, the king fell under the ascetic's sway, and then he began to tell his own name.
The ascetic said: King, I know you; you practised a deception, and I liked it.
bal.163.so163: Listen, king: such is the rule of policy, that kings do not tell their names just anywhere.
Considering that shrewdness of yours, I have come to love you greatly.
bal.164.cau1: Your name is Pratāpabhānu, and King Satyaketu was your father.
By my guru's grace I know everything, king, but I do not speak of it, knowing it would harm me.
bal.164.cau2: Dear one, seeing your natural uprightness, your love and trust and your skill in policy,
fondness for you has sprung up in my mind, and since you ask, I tell you my own story.
bal.164.cau3: Now I am pleased, have no doubt of it; ask, king, for whatever your heart desires.
The king was glad at these fair words; he took hold of his feet and pleaded with him in many ways:
bal.164.cau4: Sage, ocean of mercy, by the sight of you the four fruits of life are in the palm of my hand.
Yet, seeing my lord pleased, let me ask a boon hard to win and be free from sorrow.
bal.164.do164: May my body know neither old age nor death nor pain; may no one defeat me in battle;
and may I rule the earth alone, without an enemy, for a hundred kalpas.
bal.165.cau1: The ascetic said: King, may it be so. One thing, though, is hard; listen to that as well.
Even Death will bow its head at your feet, king, leaving aside only the race of Brahmins.
bal.165.cau2: By the power of austerity the Brahmins are ever mighty; against their wrath there is no protector.
If you bring the Brahmins under your sway, king, then Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśa will be under your sway.
bal.165.cau3: Force does not prevail against the race of Brahmins; I tell you the truth with both arms raised.
Listen, king: but for a Brahmin's curse, you will not perish at any time.
bal.165.cau4: The king rejoiced to hear his words, and said: My lord, now I shall not perish.
By your grace, Lord, treasury of mercy, all will be well with me at all times.
bal.165.do165: Saying, So be it, the crooked false sage spoke again:
If you tell anyone of our meeting and of your losing your way, then the blame will not be mine.
bal.166.cau1: That is why I forbid you, O king: telling this story would do you the greatest harm.
The moment this tale falls on a sixth ear, you will be destroyed; my word is true.
bal.166.cau2: Listen, Pratāpabhānu: if this comes out, or through a Brahmin's curse, you will be destroyed;
by no other means will you die, even if Hari and Hara grow angry at heart.
bal.166.cau3: Clasping his feet, the king said: It is true, my lord. Tell me, who can shield anyone from the anger of a Brahmin or a guru?
If the Creator is angry, the guru shields; but against the guru's enmity there is no protector in the world.
bal.166.cau4: If I do not go by your word, let me be destroyed; I have no care for that.
One fear alone frightens my mind, my lord: a Brahmin's curse is terrible indeed.
bal.166.do166: By what means can Brahmins come under my sway? Be gracious and tell me that too.
O compassionate to the lowly, apart from you I see no well-wisher of mine.
bal.167.cau1: The false sage said: Listen, O king: there are many means in the world, but they are hard to carry out, and even then they may or may not succeed.
There is one very easy means, but in it lies one difficulty.
bal.167.cau2: That device, O king, is in my hands, but I cannot go to your city.
From the day I was born until today, I have not gone to anyone's house or village.
bal.167.cau3: If I do not go, harm comes to you; a dilemma has arisen today.
Hearing this, the king spoke gently: My lord, the Vedas set forth this principle:
bal.167.cau4: The great show love to the small: the mountains always bear blades of grass on their heads;
foam floats on the crown of the unfathomable ocean, and the earth continually holds dust on its head.
bal.167.do167: Saying this, the king clasped his feet: Master, be gracious.
For my sake, my lord, bear this trouble; you are good and compassionate to the lowly.
bal.168.cau1: Knowing the king to be in his power, the ascetic, skilled in deceit, said:
Listen, O king, I tell you truly: nothing in the world is hard for me to obtain.
bal.168.cau2: I will surely do your work; you are my devotee in mind, body and speech.
The power of yoga, of skilful means, of austerity and of mantras bears fruit only when it is kept hidden.
bal.168.cau3: If I cook the meal, O king, and you serve it, and no one knows who I am,
then whoever eats that food will, every one of them, do as you command.
bal.168.cau4: And whoever dines in their houses, listen, O king, he too will come under your sway.
Go, O king, and set this plan in motion; take a vow for a full year.
bal.168.do168: Every day invite a hundred thousand fresh Brahmins with their families;
and for as long as your vow lasts, I will prepare the feast each day.
bal.169.cau1: In this way, O king, with very little trouble all the Brahmins will come under your sway.
The Brahmins will perform fire offerings, sacrifices and worship, and through these the gods too will easily come under your sway.
bal.169.cau2: I tell you one more sign to know me by: I will never come in this guise.
By my māyā, O king, I will spirit away your family priest and bring him here.
bal.169.cau3: By the power of my austerities I will make him like myself and keep him here for a full year;
and I, listen, O king, will take his guise and accomplish your work in every way.
bal.169.cau4: Much of the night has passed; now go to sleep. On the third day, O king, you and I will meet.
By the power of my austerities I will carry you home, horse and all, while you sleep.
bal.169.do169: I will come wearing that guise; know me then,
when I call you aside alone and tell you the whole story.
bal.170.cau1: Obeying his bidding, the king lay down to sleep, and the master of deceit went and sat on his seat.
The weary king fell into a deep sleep; but how could the other sleep, so great was his anxiety?
bal.170.cau2: There came the demon Kālaketu, who had turned himself into a boar and misled the king.
He was the ascetic king's closest friend, and knew a great many deceits.
bal.170.cau3: He had a hundred sons and ten brothers, very wicked, unconquerable and a torment to the gods.
The king had earlier slain them all in battle, when he saw the distress of the Brahmins, the saints and the gods.
bal.170.cau4: Remembering the old enmity, that wicked one met the ascetic king and they took counsel together,
and devised the very plan by which their enemy would be destroyed. Under the sway of destiny, the king knew nothing of it.
bal.170.do170: A powerful enemy, even if alone, should never be counted as small:
Rāhu, with only his head left, still torments the sun and the moon.
bal.171.cau1: Seeing his friend, the ascetic king rose with joy to greet him and was glad.
He told his friend the whole story, and the demon, delighted, said:
bal.171.cau2: Listen, O king: now I have the enemy in hand, since you have done as I counselled.
Put away your worry and sleep; the Creator has cured the disease without medicine.
bal.171.cau3: I will sweep the enemy away, root and all, with his whole line, and come to meet you on the fourth day.
After reassuring the ascetic king at length, that great deceiver, exceedingly wrathful, went on his way.
bal.171.cau4: He brought Pratāpabhānu, together with his horse, home in a moment.
He laid the king to sleep beside the queen and tied the horse up properly in the stable.
bal.171.do171: Next he bore off the king's family priest,
and took him away and kept him in a mountain cave, having bewildered his mind with māyā.
bal.172.cau1: Taking on the priest's form himself, he went and lay down on the priest's fine bed.
The king woke before daybreak and, seeing his own palace, was filled with wonder.
bal.172.cau2: Inwardly reckoning the sage's greatness, he rose quietly so that the queen would not know,
mounted that same horse and went to the forest; no man or woman of the city knew of it.
bal.172.cau3: When two watches had passed, the king returned; there was rejoicing in every house and festive music played.
When the king saw the priest, he gazed at him in wonder, remembering that very task.
bal.172.cau4: The three days passed for the king like an age; his mind stayed fixed on the false sage's feet.
Knowing the time had come, the priest came and explained the whole plan to the king.
bal.172.do172: Recognising his guru, the king rejoiced; under delusion he had no sense left.
At once he invited a hundred thousand of the best Brahmins, each with his family.
bal.173.cau1: The priest prepared the feast, of the six tastes and the four kinds, as the Vedas describe;
he made a meal of māyā, with dishes so many that no one could count them.
bal.173.cau2: He cooked the meat of many kinds of animals, and into it the wicked one mixed the flesh of Brahmins.
All the Brahmins were called to the meal; their feet were washed and they were seated with honour.
bal.173.cau3: Just as the king began to serve, at that very moment a voice spoke from the sky:
Brahmins, rise, each of you, and go home; there is great harm here, do not eat this food.
bal.173.cau4: Brahmin flesh has been cooked in the meal. Believing it, all the Brahmins rose.
The king was distraught, his reason lost in delusion; under the sway of destiny, no word came to his lips.
bal.173.do173: Then the Brahmins spoke in anger, without giving it any thought:
Go, foolish king, and become a demon, you and your family.
bal.174.cau1: Base kṣatriya, you invited the Brahmins in order to destroy them, together with their whole company.
God has preserved our dharma; you will perish, you and your family.
bal.174.cau2: Within a year may you be destroyed; not one of your line will be left to offer water to the dead.
At the curse the king was deeply distraught with terror. Then once again a noble voice came from the sky:
bal.174.cau3: Brahmins, you did not weigh your curse before you gave it; the king has done no wrong.
All the Brahmins were astonished to hear the voice from the sky. The king went to the place where the food was kept.
bal.174.cau4: There was neither food nor the Brahmin cook. The king turned back, his mind full of boundless worry.
He told the Brahmins all that had happened and, terrified and overwhelmed, fell to the ground.
bal.174.do174: The Brahmins said: O king, what is destined cannot be wiped out, though the fault is not yours.
Nothing that is done can make it otherwise: a Brahmin's curse is terrible indeed.
bal.175.cau1: Saying this, all the Brahmins departed. The people of the city came to hear the news.
They grieve and lay the blame on fate, which, while fashioning a swan, made a crow.
bal.175.cau2: Having brought the priest back to his house, the demon sent word to the ascetic.
That wicked one sent letters far and wide, and all the kings, each with his army arrayed, came rushing.
bal.175.cau3: They beat their war drums and laid siege to the city; every day there was fighting of many kinds.
All the warriors fell fighting after valiant deeds, and the king too fell to the ground with his brother.
bal.175.cau4: Not one of Satyaketu's line survived; how could a Brahmin's curse prove false?
All the kings, having conquered the enemy and settled the city, went home to their own cities with victory and fame.
bal.175.do175: Listen, Bharadvāja: when the Creator turns against someone,
for him dust becomes like Mount Meru, his father becomes Yama, and a rope becomes like a snake.
bal.176.cau1: Listen, O sage: in time that same king, with all his company, became a demon.
He had ten heads and twenty mighty arms; Rāvaṇa was his name, a fierce and powerful hero.
bal.176.cau2: The king's younger brother, Arimardana by name, became Kumbhakarṇa, a storehouse of strength.
The king's minister, whose name was Dharmaruci, became Rāvaṇa's younger half-brother.
bal.176.cau3: Vibhīṣaṇa was his name, whom the whole world knows, a devotee of Viṣṇu and a treasury of realised knowledge.
Those who had been the king's sons and servants became many dreadful demons.
bal.176.cau4: They were wicked, of many kinds, able to take any form at will, crooked, terrible and void of discernment;
merciless, violent, every one of them sinful, tormentors of the world beyond all telling.
bal.176.do176: Though they were born in the holy, spotless and peerless line of Pulastya,
yet, by the curse of the Brahmins, all of them became sin incarnate.
bal.177.cau1: The three brothers performed austerities of many kinds, so severe that they cannot be described.
Seeing their austerity, Brahmā came near and said: Ask a boon, my son; I am pleased.
bal.177.cau2: Making supplication and clasping his feet, Rāvaṇa said: Listen, Lord of the world:
may we die at no one's hand save those of two races, monkeys and men.
bal.177.cau3: So be it; you have performed great austerity: this was the boon that Brahmā and I (Śiva) together granted him.
Then the lord Brahmā went to Kumbhakarṇa, and on seeing him he was astonished at heart.
bal.177.cau4: Brahmā thought: If this wicked one eats every day, the whole world will be laid waste.
So, prompting Sarasvatī, he turned Kumbhakarṇa's mind, and Kumbhakarṇa asked for six months' sleep.
bal.177.do177: Then he went to Vibhīṣaṇa and said: My son, ask for a boon.
Vibhīṣaṇa asked for pure love of the Lord's lotus feet.
bal.178.cau1: Having granted them their boons Brahmā departed, and they came home delighted.
Maya had a daughter named Mandodarī, supremely beautiful, a jewel among women.
bal.178.cau2: Maya brought that very daughter and gave her to Rāvaṇa, knowing that he would become lord of the demons.
Rāvaṇa rejoiced at gaining a good wife, and then he went and had both his brothers married.
bal.178.cau3: In the midst of the ocean stood a mountain, Trikūṭa, made by Brahmā, very vast and hard to reach.
That same mountain the demon Maya adorned anew with countless jewelled mansions wrought of gold.
bal.178.cau4: Like Bhogāvatī, where the serpent race dwells, and like Amarāvatī, the home of Indra,
yet lovelier than they and exceedingly formidable, it is famed in the world by the name of Laṅkā.
bal.178.do178क: The ocean, exceedingly deep, runs round it on all four sides as its moat;
its strong rampart of gold is studded with jewels; its workmanship is beyond description.
bal.178.do178ख: In whatever kalpa, whoever becomes lord of the demons, impelled by Śrī Hari,
he, a hero, glorious and of matchless might, dwells there with his host.
bal.179.cau1: Mighty demon warriors used to live there; the gods slew them all in battle.
Now there dwell, sent by Indra, millions of guards of Kubera, lord of the yakṣas.
bal.179.cau2: Rāvaṇa somehow came to hear of this; he arrayed his army, went and laid siege to the fort.
Seeing his formidable warriors and great host, the yakṣas fled for their lives.
bal.179.cau3: Then Rāvaṇa went round and viewed the whole city; his cares left him and his joy was great.
Judging it beautiful and by its very nature hard to reach, Rāvaṇa made his capital there.
bal.179.cau4: He allotted houses to each as each deserved, and made all the demons happy.
Once he marched against Kubera, won the aerial car Puṣpaka and brought it away.
bal.179.do179: Then, in mere sport, he went and lifted up Kailāsa,
and went away greatly pleased, as though he had weighed the strength of his arms.
bal.180.cau1: Happiness, wealth, sons, army, allies, victory, glory, strength, intellect and greatness —
all these grew ever anew, as greed grows with every gain.
bal.180.cau2: His brother was Kumbhakarṇa, of such surpassing might that no match for him was ever born in the world.
He would drink and sleep for six months, and when he woke the three worlds were in terror.
bal.180.cau3: Had he eaten every day, the whole world would soon have been ruined.
His steadfastness in battle is beyond telling; and there were countless mighty heroes like him.
bal.180.cau4: Meghanāda was Rāvaṇa's eldest son, counted first among the warriors of the world.
No one could stand before him in battle; in the city of the gods there was ever a rout.
bal.180.do180: such was the host of great warriors, each one of whom could conquer the world.
bal.181.cau1: All of them could take any form at will and knew every kind of māyā; not even in dreams had they dharma or mercy.
Once Rāvaṇa sat in his assembly and looked upon his countless family:
bal.181.cau2: hosts of sons, his people, kinsmen and grandsons — who could count the demon race to its end?
Seeing his army, Rāvaṇa, proud by nature, spoke words steeped in anger and arrogance:
bal.181.cau3: Listen, all you hosts of demons: the hordes of gods are our enemies.
They do not fight face to face; seeing a strong foe, they run away.
bal.181.cau4: There is one way by which they die; I shall explain it, so hear it now.
Brahmin-feasts, sacrifices, fire offerings and śrāddha rites — go, all of you, and obstruct them all.
bal.181.do181: Weak with hunger and drained of strength, the gods will easily come over to me.
Then I shall either slay them, or let them go once I have thoroughly made them my own.
bal.182.cau1: Then he summoned Meghanāda, instructed him, and stirred up his strength and his enmity:
Those gods who are steadfast and mighty in battle, who take pride in fighting,
bal.182.cau2: conquer them in battle and bring them back bound. The son rose and accepted his father's command.
In this way he gave his orders to all, and himself set out with a mace in his hand.
bal.182.cau3: As Rāvaṇa walks, the earth quakes; at his roar the wives of the gods miscarry.
Hearing that Rāvaṇa was coming in wrath, the gods made for the caves of Mount Meru.
bal.182.cau4: Rāvaṇa found all the lovely realms of the guardians of the quarters deserted.
Again and again he roared a mighty lion's roar, challenging the gods and hurling abuse at them.
bal.182.cau5: Drunk with the frenzy of war he roamed the world, seeking a match, but found none anywhere.
The Sun, the Moon, the Wind, Varuṇa, Kubera, Agni, Kāla, Yama and all who held authority,
bal.182.cau6: kinnaras, siddhas, men, gods and nāgas — he relentlessly went after them all.
Wherever in Brahmā's creation there were embodied beings, men and women, all were subject to Rāvaṇa.
bal.182.cau7: All, in fear, did his bidding, and came daily to bow humbly at his feet.
bal.182.do182क: By the might of his arms he had brought the world under his sway and left no one free.
Rāvaṇa, the jewel of overlords, ruled by his own counsel alone.
bal.182.do182ख: Daughters of gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, men, kinnaras and nāgas —
many lovely and noble women — these he won by the strength of his own arms and made his wives.
bal.183.cau1: Whatever Rāvaṇa told Indrajit, Indrajit had, as it were, done all of it already.
Now hear what those did whom he had commanded first.
bal.183.cau2: The hosts of demons, terrible to behold, all sinful, tormentors of the gods —
those hordes of asuras wrought havoc and, by māyā, took on many forms.
bal.183.cau3: Whatever would tear dharma up by the roots, all that they did, against the Vedas.
In every land where they found cows and Brahmins, they set fire to its cities, villages and towns.
bal.183.cau4: Good conduct was nowhere to be found; no one honoured the gods, the Brahmins or the guru.
There was no devotion to Śrī Hari, no sacrifice, austerity or knowledge; not even in dreams were the Vedas and Purāṇas heard.
bal.183.cha1: Japa, yoga, dispassion, austerity, the shares of sacrifice — if Rāvaṇa so much as heard of them,
he would rise and rush there himself; he let nothing remain, but seized and destroyed it all.
So corrupt did the world's conduct become that dharma was not heard of by any ear.
Whoever recited the Vedas and Purāṇas, him he harried in many ways and drove from the land.
bal.183.so183: There is no describing the terrible wrongs that the demons committed.
They loved violence exceedingly: what limit could there be to their sins?
bal.184.cau1: The wicked multiplied: thieves, gamblers, and those who lusted after others' wealth and others' wives.
They honoured neither mother, father nor gods, and made holy men serve them.
bal.184.cau2: Bhavānī, all beings whose conduct is such, know them to be demons.
Seeing dharma in such extreme decline, Earth, deeply afraid, was in anguish.
bal.184.cau3: Earth thought: Mountains, rivers and oceans are no burden to me as heavy as a single one who harms others.
She saw all dharma turned upside down, yet, afraid of Rāvaṇa, she could not speak.
bal.184.cau4: Having thought it over in her heart, she took the form of a cow and went where all the gods and sages were.
Weeping, she told them her anguish, but no one could do anything.
bal.184.cha1: The gods, sages and gandharvas all went together to the world of Brahmā;
and with them, in a cow's form, went poor Earth, utterly distraught with fear and grief.
Brahmā understood it all and reflected in his mind: nothing here is in my power.
He said: The Imperishable One whose handmaid you are is your helper, and ours as well.
bal.184.so184: Brahmā said: Earth, hold your mind steady and remember the feet of Śrī Hari.
The Lord knows the pain of his servants; he will shatter this dreadful calamity.
bal.185.cau1: All the gods sat and deliberated: where could the Lord be found, so that they might make their appeal to him?
One said they should go to the city of Vaikuṇṭha; another said that the Lord dwells in the ocean of milk.
bal.185.cau2: In whatever heart there is devotion and love, of whatever kind, there the Lord always appears in that same way.
Girijā, I too was in that assembly, and when the moment came I said a word.
bal.185.cau3: Śrī Hari pervades all, present everywhere alike; I know that he becomes manifest through love.
In any place or time, in the directions or the spaces between them, tell me: where is the place where the Lord is not?
bal.185.cau4: He fills all that moves and all that does not move, yet is apart from all, free of attachment; through love the Lord appears, as fire does.
My words found favour in every mind, and Brahmā praised them, saying: Well said, well said.
bal.185.do185: Hearing this, Brahmā rejoiced at heart; his body thrilled and tears flowed from his eyes.
Steady of mind and fully attentive, he joined his palms and began to offer praise.
bal.186.cha1: Glory, glory to you, O Lord of the gods, giver of joy to your servants, protector of those who bow to you, O Bhagavān!
Benefactor of cows and Brahmins, glory to you, foe of the demons, beloved husband of Lakṣmī, the Ocean's daughter!
Protector of the gods and of Earth, wondrous are your deeds; their secret no one knows.
He who is compassionate by nature, kind to the lowly: may he be gracious to us.
bal.186.cha2: Glory, glory to you, the Imperishable, dweller in every heart, all-pervading, supreme bliss!
Unknowable, beyond the senses, holy in your deeds, untouched by māyā, Mukunda!
For whose sake hosts of sages, dispassionate and free of delusion, yet full of deep love,
meditate night and day and sing his many virtues — glory to him, Saccidānanda!
bal.186.cha3: He who brought forth creation and made it threefold, with no second as companion or helper —
may that destroyer of sin take thought for us, who know neither devotion nor worship.
He who breaks the fear of worldly existence, delights the minds of sages and destroys hosts of calamities —
in mind, word and deed, leaving aside the habit of cleverness, all the hosts of gods have come to him for refuge.
bal.186.cha4: He whom Sarasvatī, the Vedas, Śeṣa and all the seers — not one of them — have known;
he to whom, as the Vedas proclaim, the lowly are dear — may that Śrī Bhagavān melt with mercy.
O Mount Mandara that churns the ocean of worldly existence, beautiful in every way, temple of virtues, mass of joy:
sages, siddhas and all the gods, utterly stricken with fear, bow, O Lord, at your lotus feet.
bal.186.do186: Knowing the gods and Earth to be afraid, and hearing their words filled with love,
a deep voice spoke from the sky, taking away grief and doubt.
bal.187.cau1: Do not be afraid, sages, siddhas and king of the gods; for your sake I will put on a human form.
With my portions I will descend as a man in the noble line of the Sun.
bal.187.cau2: Kaśyapa and Aditi performed great austerities, and long ago I gave them a boon.
They have appeared in Kosalapurī as Daśaratha and Kausalyā, a royal pair among men.
bal.187.cau3: I will go and be born in their house as the four brothers, the ornaments of the line of Raghu.
I will make every word of Nārada come true; I will descend together with my supreme Śakti.
bal.187.cau4: I will take away all the burden of the earth. Hosts of gods, be free of fear.
Hearing with their own ears this divine voice in the sky, the gods turned back at once, their hearts at peace.
bal.187.cau5: Then Brahmā reassured Earth; her fear left her, and confidence came into her heart.
bal.187.do187: Brahmā went back to his own world, having given the gods this instruction:
Take on the bodies of monkeys, each of you, go to the earth and serve the feet of Śrī Hari.
bal.188.cau1: All the gods went each to his own abode, and they and Earth found rest of mind.
Glad at the command Brahmā had given, the gods carried it out without delay.
bal.188.cau2: On earth they took the bodies of forest dwellers, with matchless strength and might.
All were heroes, with mountains, trees and claws for weapons; steady of mind, they watched for the coming of Śrī Hari.
bal.188.cau3: They filled the mountains and forests everywhere, and lived there, each forming his own fine troop.
All this lovely story I have told; now hear what I left aside in between.
bal.188.cau4: In Avadhapurī there reigned a king, the jewel of Raghu's line, named Daśaratha, known in the Vedas.
He upheld dharma, was a treasury of virtues and was wise; in his heart was devotion to the Lord who bears the Śārṅga bow, and his mind was set on him.
bal.188.do188: Kausalyā and his other beloved queens were all of pure conduct,
devoted to their husband, firm in love, and humble at the lotus feet of Śrī Hari.
bal.189.cau1: Once the king grieved in his heart: I have no son.
At once the king went to his guru's house, fell at his feet and made earnest entreaty.
bal.189.cau2: He told his guru all his sorrow and joy, and Vasiṣṭha consoled him in many ways, saying:
Take heart: four sons will be born to you, famed in the three worlds, who take away the fear of devotees.
bal.189.cau3: Vasiṣṭha sent for the sage Śṛṅgī and had him perform an auspicious sacrifice for the gift of sons.
As the sage offered the oblations with devotion, Agni appeared, holding the charu in his hands.
bal.189.cau4: Agni said: All that Vasiṣṭha had in mind, the whole of your purpose, is fulfilled.
O king, go and share out this oblation, making portions as is fitting for each.
bal.189.do189: Then, having explained everything to the whole assembly, Agni vanished.
The king was immersed in supreme bliss; his heart could not contain his joy.
bal.190.cau1: Then the king called his beloved queens, and Kausalyā and the others came there.
Half of it he gave to Kausalyā, and the other half he made into two parts.
bal.190.cau2: One of these the king gave to Kaikeyī; what was left was again made into two parts.
Placing these in the hands of Kausalyā and Kaikeyī, and so gladdening their hearts, he gave them to Sumitrā.
bal.190.cau3: In this way all the queens conceived; they rejoiced at heart and were full of happiness.
From the day Śrī Hari came into the womb, joy and prosperity spread through all the worlds.
bal.190.cau4: In the palace all the queens shine, mines of beauty, gentleness and radiance.
Some time passed in happiness, and the moment came at which the Lord was to appear.
bal.190.do190: The yoga, the rising sign, the planets, the weekday and the lunar day all became favourable.
All that moves and all that does not move were filled with joy: the birth of Śrī Rāma is the root of happiness.
bal.191.cau1: It was the ninth lunar day of the holy month of Madhu (Caitra), in the bright fortnight, at the hour of Abhijit, dear to Śrī Hari.
It was midday, neither too cold nor too hot: a holy time, bringing rest to the world.
bal.191.cau2: A cool, gentle, fragrant breeze was blowing; the gods were glad, and the hearts of the saints eager.
The forests were in flower, the mountains glittered with gems, and every river poured forth streams of nectar.
bal.191.cau3: When Brahmā knew that the moment had come, all the gods set out, their aerial cars made ready.
The clear sky was crowded with hosts of gods, and troops of gandharvas sang his praises.
bal.191.cau4: They shower flowers by the handful; kettledrums boomed out across the sky.
Nāgas, sages and gods sing praises and bring their offerings of service in many ways.
bal.191.do191: The hosts of gods, having offered their prayers, returned each to his own abode.
The Lord, the dwelling of the world and the rest of all the worlds, became manifest.
bal.192.cha1: The compassionate Lord, kind to the lowly, the benefactor of Kausalyā, became manifest.
The mother was filled with joy as she thought on his wondrous form, which captivates the minds of sages.
A delight to the eyes, his body dark as a rain cloud, he held his own weapons in his four arms.
He wore ornaments and a garland of forest flowers, his eyes were large, and the slayer of Khara was an ocean of beauty.
bal.192.cha2: Joining her two palms, she said: O Infinite One, how am I to praise you?
You are beyond māyā, the guṇas and knowledge, and without measure: so the Vedas and Purāṇas declare.
The ocean of compassion and joy, the home of every virtue, of whom the Śrutis and the saints sing —
that Lord of Śrī, who loves his devotees, has become manifest for my good.
bal.192.cha3: Hosts of universes fashioned by māyā lie in each of your pores: so the Vedas say.
And you dwelt in my womb: hearing a thing so laughable, even the steadiest mind cannot stay firm.
When this knowledge had dawned in her, the Lord smiled; he wishes to perform his acts in many ways.
He told a pleasing story and made his mother understand, in such a way that she would love him as her son.
bal.192.cha4: Then the mother spoke again, her understanding changed: Dear child, give up this form,
and play the play of a child, so endearing; this joy is supreme and beyond compare.
Hearing her words, the all-knowing Lord of the gods became a baby and began to cry.
Those who sing this story attain the abode of Śrī Hari and do not fall into the well of worldly existence.
bal.192.do192: For the good of Brahmins, cows, gods and saints the Lord took birth as a man,
in a body made by his own will; he is beyond māyā, the guṇas and the senses.
bal.193.cau1: Hearing the baby's cry, a sound most dear, all the queens came in haste.
Joyful maids ran here and there, and all the people of the city were lost in delight.
bal.193.cau2: When Daśaratha heard with his own ears that a son was born, it was as though he were merged in the bliss of Brahman.
His heart full of supreme love and his body thrilling, he steadies his mind and tries to rise.
bal.193.cau3: He thinks: The Lord whose very name, when heard, brings blessing has come to my house.
His heart brimming with supreme bliss, the king called for his people and said: Let the music play.
bal.193.cau4: A summons went to the guru Vasiṣṭha, and he came with the Brahmins to the king's door.
They went in and saw the peerless child, a treasure of beauty, whose virtues could never be told to the end.
bal.193.do193: After performing the Nāndīmukha śrāddha, the king carried out all the birth rites,
and gave the Brahmins gold, cows, clothes and jewels.
bal.194.cau1: The city was covered with flags, banners and arches; how it was adorned cannot be told.
Flowers rain down from the sky, and all the people are lost in the bliss of Brahman.
bal.194.cau2: The women gathered in groups and set out; just as they were, in their everyday adornment, they rose and ran.
With golden pitchers and platters filled with auspicious things, they enter the king's gate, singing.
bal.194.cau3: They wave the lamps, make their offerings over the child, and again and again fall at his feet.
Māgadhas, sūtas, bards and singers sing the holy virtues of Śrī Rāma.
bal.194.cau4: Everyone gave away all they had, and those who received it did not keep it either.
In the middle of every lane there was a mire of musk, sandal and saffron.
bal.194.do194: In every house auspicious festive music is playing: the very root of beauty has appeared.
Everywhere the crowds of the city, women and men alike, are full of joy.
bal.195.cau1: Kaikeyī and Sumitrā, the two of them, also gave birth to beautiful sons.
That joy, that splendour, that hour and that gathering not even Sarasvatī or Śeṣa, king of serpents, can put into words.
bal.195.cau2: The city of Ayodhyā looks as though Night had come to meet the Lord;
but on seeing the sun she shrank, as it were, in her heart, and yet, thinking it over, she became the evening twilight.
bal.195.cau3: The dense smoke of aloe-wood incense is as it were the darkness, and the abīr flying in the air is as it were the red glow of dusk.
The clusters of gems on the palaces are as it were the stars, and the finial vase on the king's palace is that noble moon.
bal.195.cau4: The very gentle sound of Vedic chanting in the palaces is as it were the chirping of birds, in keeping with the hour.
Seeing this wonder, the sun forgot himself; a month went by, and he never knew it was passing.
bal.195.do195: A single day lasted a month, and no one knows the secret of it.
The sun stood still with his chariot; how then could night fall?
bal.196.cau1: No one came to know this secret; the sun went on his way singing praises.
Having seen the great festival, the gods, sages and nāgas went home, telling of their own good fortune.
bal.196.cau2: I will tell you one more secret of my own; listen, Girijā, for your mind is very steadfast.
The two of us, Kākabhuśuṇḍi and I, were together in human form, and no one recognised us.
bal.196.cau3: Swelling with supreme bliss, love and joy, we wandered the streets, lost in delight and forgetful of ourselves.
But only he knows this blessed story on whom the grace of Śrī Rāma rests.
bal.196.cau4: On that occasion, whoever came and in whatever way, the king gave each whatever pleased his heart.
The king gave away elephants, chariots, horses, gold, cows, diamonds and garments of many kinds.
bal.196.do196: Every heart was satisfied, and everywhere people gave their blessing:
May all the sons live long, the lords of Tulasīdāsa.
bal.197.cau1: Some days passed in this way; day and night went by unnoticed.
The king saw that it was time for the naming ceremony and sent for the wise sage.
bal.197.cau2: After worshipping the sage, the king spoke thus: Give them the names, O sage, that you have thought out and settled on.
The sage said: Their names are many and beyond compare, O king; still, I will tell them as my understanding allows.
bal.197.cau3: He who is an ocean of bliss and a store of joy, a single drop of whom brings comfort to the three worlds,
that abode of joy bears the name Rāma, giver of rest to all the worlds.
bal.197.cau4: He who sustains and nourishes the universe shall be named Bharata.
He whose remembrance destroys the enemy bears the name Śatrughna, which the Vedas have made known.
bal.197.do197: He who is the abode of auspicious marks, dear to Śrī Rāma and the support of the whole world,
to him Guru Vasiṣṭha gave the noble name Lakṣmaṇa.
bal.198.cau1: The guru gave these names after reflecting in his heart, and said: O king, your four sons are the essence of the Vedas.
He who is the wealth of sages, the all-in-all of his devotees and the very life of Śiva took delight in the joys of childhood play.
bal.198.cau2: From childhood Lakṣmaṇa knew Śrī Rāma as his own well-wisher and lord, and gave his heart to his feet.
Between the two brothers Bharata and Śatrughna there was a great love, such as that of a master and his servant.
bal.198.cau3: The two lovely pairs are each one dark and one fair; the mothers gaze on their beauty, breaking a straw against the evil eye.
All four are abodes of good conduct, beauty and virtue, and yet Śrī Rāma, the ocean of joy, surpasses them.
bal.198.cau4: The moon of grace is shining in his heart, and its rays show in his charming smile.
Sometimes in her lap, sometimes in the fine cradle, his mother caresses him, calling him her dear little one.
bal.198.do198: The all-pervading Brahman, stainless, without attributes and beyond all play,
that unborn one, won over by love and devotion, lies in Kausalyā's lap.
bal.199.cau1: His dark body has the beauty of countless Kāmadevas, like the blue lotus and the deep rain-cloud.
The light of the nails on his rosy lotus feet is as if pearls had settled on the petals of a lotus.
bal.199.cau2: On his feet shine the lines of the thunderbolt, the banner and the goad; the sound of his anklets enchants even the minds of sages.
Round his waist is a girdle of little bells, on his belly three folds; how deep his navel is, only one who has seen it knows.
bal.199.cau3: His long arms are decked with many ornaments, and on his breast a lion's-claw amulet is exceedingly lovely.
On his chest is the beauty of the jewelled necklace and its pendant, and the sight of the Brahmin's footprint captivates the mind.
bal.199.cau4: His neck is like a conch and his chin most lovely; the beauty of countless Kāmadevas spreads over his face.
His little teeth are two and two, and his lips are red; who could describe his nose and the tilaka?
bal.199.cau5: His ears are lovely and his cheeks most beautiful, and his sweet lisping words are very dear.
His birth-hair is smooth and curly, and his mother has dressed it in many ways.
bal.199.cau6: A little yellow frock has been put on him, and his crawling on knees and hands delights me.
Neither the Vedas nor Śeṣa can describe that form; only he knows it who has seen it, even in a dream.
bal.199.do199: He who is a mass of joy, beyond delusion, beyond knowledge, speech and the senses,
won over by the supreme love of his mother and father, plays the pure games of a child.
bal.200.cau1: Thus Śrī Rāma, father and mother of the world, brings joy to the people of Kosalapura.
Bhavānī, those who have set their love on the feet of Śrī Rāma: this is plainly their state.
bal.200.cau2: Turned away from Śrī Rāma, though one strive in a million ways, who can loosen the bonds of worldly existence?
Māyā, who holds all beings, moving and unmoving, in her power, herself stands in fear of the Lord.
bal.200.cau3: The Lord makes her dance at the play of his eyebrows; tell me, leaving such a Lord, whom should one worship?
To one who gives up cleverness in thought, deed and word and worships him, Śrī Rāma will show his grace.
bal.200.cau4: Thus the Lord played as a child and gave joy to all the people of the city.
Sometimes his mother takes him in her lap and rocks him; sometimes she lays him in the cradle and swings him.
bal.200.do200: Lost in love, Kausalyā does not notice the nights and days go by.
Overcome by love for her son, the mother sings of his childhood ways.
bal.201.cau1: Once the mother bathed him, adorned him and laid him in the cradle.
Then, to worship the Lord, the chosen deity of her line, she bathed.
bal.201.cau2: Having worshipped, she offered the food-offering and went herself to where the meal was being cooked.
Then the mother came back there, and on coming she saw her son eating.
bal.201.cau3: Frightened, the mother went to the child, and there she saw the child asleep once more.
Coming back again, she saw that same son there; her heart trembled and her mind could find no calm.
bal.201.cau4: She saw two children, one here and one there, and wondered: Is my mind deceived, or is there some other cause?
Seeing his mother distraught, Śrī Rāma laughed; the Lord gave a sweet smile.
bal.201.do201: He showed his mother his own wondrous, undivided form,
in every hair of which hung millions upon millions of universes.
bal.202.cau1: Countless suns, moons, Śivas and Brahmās, many mountains, rivers, oceans, earths and forests;
time, karma, the guṇas, knowledge and nature: these too she saw, such as no one had ever heard of.
bal.202.cau2: She saw Māyā, mighty in every way, standing in great fear with folded hands.
She saw the soul that Māyā makes dance, and she saw devotion, which sets it free.
bal.202.cau3: Her body thrilled, no words came to her lips, and closing her eyes she bowed her head at his feet.
Seeing his mother lost in wonder, Śrī Rāma, the slayer of Khara, became a child again.
bal.202.cau4: She could not even utter his praise; she was afraid, thinking: I took the father of the world for my son.
Śrī Hari reassured his mother in many ways: Listen, mother, do not speak of this anywhere.
bal.202.do202: Again and again, with folded hands, Kausalyā prays:
Lord, may your māyā never again take hold of me.
bal.203.cau1: Śrī Hari played many childhood games and gave great joy to his servants.
After some time all the brothers grew bigger, a joy to all their household.
bal.203.cau2: The guru came and performed the tonsure ceremony, and the Brahmins once more received rich gifts.
The four tender princes go about playing countless games of supreme charm.
bal.203.cau3: He who lies beyond the reach of thought, deed and word, that very Lord roams about King Daśaratha's courtyard.
When the king, sitting at his meal, calls him, he will not come away from his playmates.
bal.203.cau4: When Kausalyā goes to call him, the Lord toddles away on his little feet.
He whom the Vedas call neti, not this, and whose end even Śiva did not find, is chased by his mother, determined to catch him.
bal.203.cau5: He came in, his body grey with dust, and the king, smiling, sat him on his lap.
bal.203.do203: Even at his meal his mind is restless, and the moment he finds a chance, this way or that,
he runs off crowing with delight, his face smeared with curd and rice.
bal.204.cau1: These childhood deeds, so simple and so lovely, have been sung by Sarasvatī, Śeṣa, Śiva and the Vedas.
Those whose hearts are not drawn in love to them have been left deprived by the Creator.
bal.204.cau2: When all the brothers had grown to boyhood, the guru and their parents gave them the sacred thread.
Śrī Rāma went to the guru's house to study, and in a short time all learning came to him.
bal.204.cau3: That Śrī Hari, whose natural breath is the four Vedas, should study: this is a great marvel.
Accomplished in learning, humility, virtue and good conduct, they play all the games of kings.
bal.204.cau4: Bow and arrows look splendid in their hands; at the sight of their form all things moving and unmoving are enchanted.
In whatever streets the brothers roam, all the men and women stand still, spellbound.
bal.204.do204: To the people of Kosalapura, men and women, old and young,
all of them, the compassionate Śrī Rāma is dearer than life itself.
bal.205.cau1: Śrī Rāma calls his brothers and friends to go with him, and goes every day to the forest to hunt.
He kills only the beasts he knows in his heart to be pure, and each day brings them to show the king.
bal.205.cau2: The beasts struck down by Śrī Rāma's arrows left their bodies and went to the world of the gods.
He eats with his younger brothers and his friends, and does as his mother and father command.
bal.205.cau3: Whatever way the people of the city may be made happy, the treasury of mercy does just that.
He listens with attention to the Vedas and Purāṇas, and then himself explains them to his younger brothers.
bal.205.cau4: Rising at dawn, Śrī Rāma bows his head to his mother, his father and his guru.
Asking their leave, he does the work of the city, and the king rejoices at heart to see his ways.
bal.205.do205: He who pervades all, who is without parts, without desire, unborn and beyond the guṇas, who has neither name nor form,
performs for the sake of his devotees deeds of many kinds beyond compare.
bal.206.cau1: All these deeds I have sung and told; now listen with attention to the story that follows.
Viśvāmitra, the wise and great sage, made his dwelling in the forest, knowing it for a holy hermitage.
bal.206.cau2: There the sage practised japa, sacrifice and yoga, but he lived in great fear of Mārīca and Subāhu.
The moment the demons saw a sacrifice they rushed at it and wrought havoc, and the sage suffered.
bal.206.cau3: Anxiety took hold of the mind of Gādhi's son: these sinful demons will not die but by Śrī Hari.
Then the great sage reflected in his mind: the Lord has come down to take away the burden of the earth.
bal.206.cau4: On this very pretext let me go and see his feet, and with my entreaty bring back the two brothers.
The Lord who is the home of knowledge, dispassion and every virtue I shall see to my eyes' fill.
bal.206.do206: Cherishing many kinds of hopes as he went, he was not long on the way;
having bathed in the waters of the Sarayū, he came to the gate of the king's court.
bal.207.cau1: When the king heard of the sage's coming, he went to meet him, taking a company of Brahmins with him.
Prostrating himself, he honoured the sage, led him in and gave him his own seat.
bal.207.cau2: He washed his feet and worshipped him with great devotion, and said: Today there is no one as blessed as I.
He had many kinds of food served to him, and the great sage felt great joy in his heart.
bal.207.cau3: Then the king laid his four sons at the sage's feet; seeing Śrī Rāma, the sage forgot his own body.
Gazing at the beauty of his face he was lost in it, as a cakora is held by the full moon.
bal.207.cau4: Then the king, glad at heart, said: O sage, never before have you shown me such grace.
For what reason have you come? Tell me, and I shall lose no time in doing it.
bal.207.cau5: The sage said: Hosts of demons torment me; I have come to you, O king, with a request.
Give me Śrī Rāma with his younger brother; once the demons are slain I shall be under protection.
bal.207.do207: Give them, O king, with a glad heart; cast off attachment and ignorance.
For you, my lord, there will be dharma and fair fame, and for them the highest good.
bal.208.cau1: Hearing these most unwelcome words, the king's heart trembled and the light of his face faded.
He said: O Brahmin, in my old age I have had four sons; you have not weighed your words.
bal.208.cau2: Ask for land, cows, wealth and treasure; today I will eagerly give you everything I own.
Nothing is dearer than body and life; even those, O sage, I would give in a moment.
bal.208.cau3: Every one of my sons is as dear to me as life; but, my lord, I cannot bring myself to give Rāma.
Where are the demons, so dreadful and pitiless, and where my lovely sons, still only boys!
bal.208.cau4: Hearing the king's words, steeped in the sweetness of love, the wise sage was glad at heart.
Then Vasiṣṭha reasoned with the king in many ways, and the king's doubt was put to rest.
bal.208.cau5: With great affection the king called his two sons, held them to his heart and gave them much counsel.
He said: My lord, these two sons are my very life; O sage, you are their father, and no one else.
bal.208.do208क: Blessing his sons in many ways, the king gave them into the seer's care.
The Lord went to his mother's palace, bowed his head at her feet and set out.
bal.208.so208ख: The two heroes, lions among men, set out joyfully to take away the sage's fear,
oceans of mercy, steadfast of mind, the cause of the cause of the whole universe.
bal.209.cau1: Śrī Rāma's eyes are tinged with red, his chest broad and his arms mighty; his body is dark like the blue lotus and the tamāla tree.
At his waist are a yellow cloth and a fine quiver, girded tight; in his two hands a lovely bow and arrows.
bal.209.cau2: In the two lovely brothers, one dark and one fair, Viśvāmitra had found a great treasure.
He thought: I know now that the Lord is the god who cherishes Brahmins; for my sake the Lord has left even his father.
bal.209.cau3: As they went on their way the sage pointed out Tāṛakā; Tāṛakā heard and rushed at them in fury.
With a single arrow Śrī Rāma took her life, and, knowing her wretchedness, gave her his own abode.
bal.209.cau4: Then the seer knew in his heart that this was his own Lord, and to him, the treasury of all learning, he gave the lore
by which neither hunger nor thirst is felt, and the body shines with matchless strength and radiance.
bal.209.do209: Having given over all the weapons to the Lord, the sage brought him to his own hermitage,
and, knowing him for his true friend, with devotion gave him bulbs, roots and fruit to eat.
bal.210.cau1: In the morning Śrī Rāma said to the sage: Go and perform your sacrifice without fear.
All the sages began the fire offerings, and he himself stood guard over the sacrifice.
bal.210.cau2: Hearing of it, the wrathful demon Mārīca, enemy of the sages, rushed out with his helpers.
Śrī Rāma struck him with an arrow that had no head, and he went a hundred yojanas, to the far side of the ocean.
bal.210.cau3: Then with a fire arrow he slew Subāhu, and his younger brother destroyed the demon army.
The Lord who slew the demons and freed the Brahmins from fear is praised by all the gods and sages.
bal.210.cau4: Śrī Rāma stayed on there some days more, showing his kindness to the Brahmins.
Out of devotion the Brahmins told him many stories from the Purāṇas, though the Lord knew them all.
bal.210.cau5: Then the sage said respectfully, making it clear: Lord, come and see a spectacle.
Hearing of the bow sacrifice, Śrī Rāma set out joyfully with the great sage.
bal.210.cau6: On the way he saw a hermitage where there was no bird, no beast, no living creature of any kind.
Seeing a stone there, the Lord asked the sage, and the sage told him the whole story in full.
bal.210.do210: The sage said: Gautama's wife, under a curse, has taken a body of stone and patiently
longs for the dust of your lotus feet; O hero of the Raghus, show her your grace.
bal.211.cha1: As the holy feet that end all sorrow touched her, Ahalyā, austerity embodied, truly appeared.
Seeing Śrī Rāma, who brings joy to his devotees, she stood before him with joined palms.
Overcome with great love, her body thrilling, she could bring no words to her lips.
Most fortunate, she clung to his feet, and streams of tears flowed from both her eyes.
bal.211.cha2: Then she steadied her mind and knew the Lord, and through Śrī Rāma's grace she gained devotion.
In words most pure she began her hymn: Glory to you, O Lord of the Raghus, known through knowledge.
I am an impure woman, and you, Lord, purify the world; you are the enemy of Rāvaṇa and bring joy to your devotees.
O lotus-eyed one, who frees from the fear of worldly existence, protect me, protect me: I have come to you for refuge.
bal.211.cha3: The curse the sage laid on me has done me great good; I count it the highest favour,
for by it I have seen to my eyes' fill Śrī Hari, who frees from worldly existence; this alone Śaṅkara knows to be gain.
Lord, this is my prayer: I am simple of mind; my Lord, I ask no other boon.
Only let the bee of my mind drink, in love, the nectar of the pollen of your lotus feet.
bal.211.cha4: The feet from which came forth the most holy river of the gods, whom Śiva bore on his head,
those same lotus feet, which Brahmā worships, the compassionate Śrī Hari has placed on my head.
So, falling again and again at Śrī Hari's feet, the wife of Gautama took her leave.
Having gained the boon her heart most longed for, she went, full of joy, to her husband's world.
bal.211.do211: Such is the Lord, Śrī Hari, friend of the lowly, merciful without cause.
Wretched Tulasīdāsa, cast off deceit and worldly entanglement, and worship him.
bal.212.cau1: Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa went on with the sage and came to where the Gaṅgā flows, purifier of the world.
The son of Gādhi told them the whole story of how the river of the gods came down to the earth.
bal.212.cau2: Then the Lord bathed with the seers, and the Brahmins received gifts of many kinds.
Then, with the company of sages, he went on joyfully, and soon drew near the city of Videha.
bal.212.cau3: Śrī Rāma, seeing the charm of the city, was especially delighted, and his younger brother with him.
There are many stepwells, wells, streams and ponds, with water like nectar and steps of jewels.
bal.212.cau4: Lovely bees, drunk with nectar, hum, and birds of many colours sing sweetly.
Lotuses of every hue are in bloom, and the threefold breeze, cool, gentle and fragrant, gives delight at all times.
bal.212.do212: Flower gardens, orchards and groves, the home of a great many birds,
in flower, in fruit and in fresh leaf, grace the city on every side.
bal.213.cau1: The city's beauty is beyond describing; wherever the mind goes, there it is enchanted.
There are fine markets and wondrous canopies, studded with jewels, as though the Creator had adorned them with his own hands.
bal.213.cau2: Wealthy merchants of the best kind, like Kubera, the lord of riches, sit with goods of every sort.
The fine crossroads and pleasant lanes are always kept sprinkled with fragrance.
bal.213.cau3: Everyone's house is full of blessing, as though Kāmadeva, the lord of Rati, had painted them.
The men and women of the city are fair, pure and saintly, devoted to dharma, wise and full of virtue.
bal.213.cau4: Where Janaka's utterly matchless dwelling stands, the gods stop short in wonder at the sight of its splendour.
The mind is astonished at the sight of its walls, as though they had held within them the beauty of all the worlds.
bal.213.do213: There are white mansions, hung with curtains of jewels and gold, finely wrought in many ways.
The lovely palace where Sītā lives: how can its beauty be told?
bal.214.cau1: All the gateways are beautiful, with doors as strong as the thunderbolt, and kings, actors, Māgadhas and bards crowd about them.
Spacious stables for horses and elephants have been built, thronged at all times with horses, elephants and chariots.
bal.214.cau2: There are many heroes, ministers and commanders, and the houses of all of them are like royal palaces.
Outside the city, by lakes and rivers, many kings have pitched their camps here and there.
bal.214.cau3: Seeing a peerless mango grove there, comfortable in every respect and lovely in every way,
Viśvāmitra said: My heart is content with this place; let us stay here, O wise hero of the Raghus.
bal.214.cau4: Very well, my lord, said Śrī Rāma, the abode of grace, and he halted there with the company of sages.
Word reached Janaka, lord of Mithilā, that the great sage Viśvāmitra had arrived.
bal.214.do214: Taking with him his pure-hearted ministers, many warriors, eminent Brahmins, his guru and his kinsmen,
the king set out in this way, full of joy, to meet the chief of sages.
bal.215.cau1: He bowed, laying his head at the sage's feet, and the lord of sages gladly gave him his blessing.
Then he reverently saluted all the Brahmins, and the king rejoiced, knowing how great his good fortune was.
bal.215.cau2: Asking after his welfare again and again, Viśvāmitra had the king sit down.
At that moment the two brothers arrived; they had gone to see the flower garden.
bal.215.cau3: One dark, one fair, tender and in the bloom of youth, they delight the eyes and steal the heart of the whole world.
When Śrī Rāma came, everyone rose; Viśvāmitra seated the brothers beside him.
