bal.215.cau4: All were happy to see the two brothers; tears filled their eyes and their bodies thrilled.
Seeing that sweet, captivating form, Janaka, king of Videha, became more than ever videha, unaware of his body.
bal.215.do215: Knowing his mind to be immersed in love, the king summoned his discernment and steadied himself,
and bowing his head at the sage's feet he spoke in a deep voice choked with feeling:
bal.216.cau1: Tell me, my lord, are these two beautiful boys the pride of a family of sages, or upholders of a royal line?
Or has the Brahman whom the Vedas hymn as neti, not this, come here in two forms?
bal.216.cau2: My mind, by nature dispassion itself, stands spellbound like the cakora before the moon.
So I ask you sincerely, my lord: tell me, master, and hide nothing.
bal.216.cau3: Gazing on them with deep love, my mind has given up, in spite of itself, the bliss of Brahman.
The sage smiled and said: King, you have spoken well; your words cannot be untrue.
bal.216.cau4: They are dear to all beings, as many as there are. Hearing these words, Śrī Rāma smiles inwardly.
The sage went on: These jewels of Raghu's line are the sons of Daśaratha; the king sent them for my good.
bal.216.do216: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the two noble brothers, are abodes of beauty, goodness and strength.
The whole world is witness that they guarded the sacrifice, conquering the demons in battle.
bal.217.cau1: The king said: O sage, now that I have seen your feet, I cannot tell how great the power of my merit is.
These two beautiful brothers, one dark and one fair, give joy even to Joy itself.
bal.217.cau2: Their love for each other is holy, beyond words, lovely and dear to the heart.
Janaka, king of Videha, says in delight: Listen, my lord: it is a natural love, like that between Brahman and the soul.
bal.217.cau3: Again and again the king gazes at the Lord; his body thrills and his heart swells with joy.
Then, praising the sage and bowing his head at his feet, the king led them into the city.
bal.217.cau4: There was a beautiful mansion, pleasant at all times; there the king took them and gave them lodging.
After worship and every kind of service, the king took his leave and went home.
bal.217.do217: Śrī Rāma took his meal with the sages and rested,
and then the Lord sat with his brother; a full watch of the day still remained.
bal.218.cau1: In Lakṣmaṇa's heart there is a special longing to go and see Janakapura.
But in awe of the Lord, and shy before the sage as well, he does not say it openly, and smiles within himself.
bal.218.cau2: Śrī Rāma understood his younger brother's state of mind, and his love for his devotees welled up in his heart.
Most humbly, diffidently and with a smile, he spoke, having received his guru's leave:
bal.218.cau3: My lord, Lakṣmaṇa wishes to see the city, but out of diffidence and fear of you, master, he does not say so openly.
If you give me leave, I will show him the city and bring him back at once.
bal.218.cau4: Hearing this, the lord of sages spoke lovingly: Rāma, how could you not keep to what is proper?
Dear one, you are the guardian of the bounds of dharma, and, ruled by love, you give joy to your servants.
bal.218.do218: Go, both of you brothers, treasures of joy, see the city and come back.
Show your beautiful faces and make the eyes of all fruitful.
bal.219.cau1: Bowing at the sage's lotus feet, the two brothers, who delight the eyes of the world, set out.
Seeing their great beauty, crowds of boys went along with them, their eyes and hearts entranced.
bal.219.cau2: They wear yellow garments, quivers bound at the waist with sashes, and lovely bows and arrows shine in their hands.
Streaks of fine sandal paste suit the colour of their bodies; dark and fair, they are an enchanting pair.
bal.219.cau3: They have necks like a lion's and long arms; on their chests hang most beautiful necklaces of elephant pearls.
Their lovely eyes are like red lotuses, and their moon-like faces free one from the three afflictions.
bal.219.cau4: Golden flowers adorn their ears; at a glance they seem to steal the heart away.
Their glances are lovely, their brows finely arched, and the line of the tilak is as if a seal had been set upon beauty.
bal.219.do219: On their handsome heads are pretty four-cornered caps, and their hair is dark and curling.
From toe-nail to crown the two brothers are beautiful, every grace in its fitting place.
bal.220.cau1: The townspeople heard the news that the princes had come to see the city.
Leaving their homes and all their work, they ran, as if paupers had set out to plunder a treasure.
bal.220.cau2: Gazing on the two brothers, beautiful by nature, they rejoice, their eyes rewarded.
Young women, pressed to the windows of their houses, gaze lovingly on Śrī Rāma's beauty.
bal.220.cau3: They say to one another lovingly: Friend, these two have outshone the beauty of millions of Kāmadevas.
Among gods, men, demons, nāgas and sages, such beauty is heard of nowhere.
bal.220.cau4: Viṣṇu has four arms, Brahmā four faces, and Śiva, the foe of Tripura, a fearsome guise and five faces.
There is no other god, friend, with whom this beauty could be compared.
bal.220.do220: In the bloom of youth, abodes of exquisite beauty, one dark and one fair, they are homes of joy.
On each and every limb of theirs, hundreds of millions of Kāmadevas might be offered up.
bal.221.cau1: Tell me, friend, what embodied being is there who would not be enchanted on seeing this form?
One of them said lovingly, in a gentle voice: Listen, wise one, to what I have heard.
bal.221.cau2: These two are the sons of Daśaratha, a lovely pair like young swans.
They are the guardians of the sage Viśvāmitra's sacrifice, who slew the demons on the field of battle.
bal.221.cau3: The one with the dark body and lovely lotus eyes, who humbled the pride of Mārīca and Subāhu,
is Kausalyā's son, a mine of joy; his name is Rāma, and he holds bow and arrows in his hands.
bal.221.cau4: The fair youth, finely dressed, with bow and arrows in hand, behind Śrī Rāma,
is named Lakṣmaṇa, Śrī Rāma's younger brother; and listen, friend, his mother is Sumitrā.
bal.221.do221: Having done the Brahmin's work, and set free the sage's wife on the way, the two brothers
have come to see the bow-sacrifice. Hearing this, all the women rejoiced.
bal.222.cau1: Seeing Śrī Rāma's beauty, one of them says: This is the bridegroom fit for Jānakī.
Friend, if the king sees him, he will set aside his vow and insist on the marriage.
bal.222.cau2: Another says: The king has recognised them, and has received them with honour along with the sage.
But, friend, the king will not give up his vow; under the sway of fate he clings obstinately to folly.
bal.222.cau3: Another says: If the Creator is good, and he is said to give everyone their due reward,
then Jānakī will win this very bridegroom; there is no doubt of it, friend.
bal.222.cau4: If by fate such a union comes about, then everyone will have their life's wish fulfilled.
Friend, our longing is great for this reason: by this tie they would come here now and then.
bal.222.do222: Otherwise, listen, friend, the sight of them is far beyond our reach.
Such a meeting comes about only when there is abundant merit earned in the past.
bal.223.cau1: Another said: Friend, you have spoken well; this marriage would be of great good to all.
Someone says: Śaṅkara's bow is hard, and this dark youth is tender of body.
bal.223.cau2: It is all a dilemma, wise one. Hearing this, another says in a gentle voice:
Friend, some people say this of them: their power is great, though they look small.
bal.223.cau3: Ahalyā, who had sinned greatly, was saved by the touch of the dust of his lotus feet;
will he stop short of breaking Śiva's bow? Do not give up this faith even by mistake.
bal.223.cau4: Brahmā, who fashioned Sītā and adorned her, has after much thought fashioned this dark bridegroom.
Hearing her words, all were delighted, and say in gentle voices: May it be so.
bal.223.do223: In their hearts they rejoice, and throngs of fair-faced, lovely-eyed women shower flowers.
Wherever the two brothers go, there is supreme bliss.
bal.224.cau1: The two brothers went to the eastern side of the city, where the ground had been prepared for the bow-sacrifice.
A vast and lovely paved floor had been laid there, and a spotless, beautiful platform set up and adorned on it.
bal.224.cau2: On all four sides great golden stands had been built, where the kings would sit.
Behind them, close by and all around, a ring of other stands made a splendid sight.
bal.224.cau3: This ring was a little higher and lovely in every way, where the people of the city would come and sit.
Near them stood large and lovely white mansions, decked in many colours,
bal.224.cau4: where all the women would sit and watch, each in the place befitting her family.
The boys of the city, speaking gentle words again and again, respectfully show the Lord all that has been made.
bal.224.do224: On this pretext all the boys, moved by love, touch their charming forms;
seeing the two brothers again and again, they thrill all over, and great joy fills their hearts.
bal.225.cau1: Śrī Rāma saw that all the boys were held by love, and he praised the places with affection.
Each boy calls them over to whatever he likes, and the two brothers go along with affection.
bal.225.cau2: Śrī Rāma shows his younger brother all that has been made, speaking soft, sweet and charming words.
He at whose command māyā creates hosts of worlds in a fraction of the twinkling of an eye,
bal.225.cau3: that same Lord, compassionate to the lowly, gazes in wonder at the arena of the bow-sacrifice for the sake of devotion.
Having seen the sights, they set out for the guru, aware that they were late and fearful at heart.
bal.225.cau4: He whose terror makes Fear itself afraid is showing the power of worship.
Speaking soft, sweet and pleasing words, they sent the boys away against their will.
bal.225.do225: Fearful and loving, deeply humble and shy, the two brothers
bowed their heads at the guru's lotus feet and sat down when he bade them.
bal.226.cau1: As night came on the sage gave the command, and all performed the evening worship.
Then, as ancient stories and histories were told, two watches of the lovely night went by.
bal.226.cau2: Then the great sage went and lay down, and the two brothers began to press his feet —
they for whose lotus feet the dispassionate practise many kinds of japa and yoga,
bal.226.cau3: those same two brothers, as though won over by love, lovingly massage the guru's lotus feet.
Only when the sage had bidden him again and again did Śrī Rāma go and lie down.
bal.226.cau4: Lakṣmaṇa presses the Lord's feet, holding them to his heart, and finds supreme joy, with reverent fear and love.
Again and again the Lord said: Sleep, dear brother. Then he lay down, holding those lotus feet in his heart.
bal.226.do226: When the night was over, Lakṣmaṇa rose, hearing the crow of the cock.
The wise Śrī Rāma, Lord of the world, had woken even before the guru.
bal.227.cau1: They finished all their morning cleansing, went and bathed, completed the daily rites and bowed their heads to the sage.
Seeing that it was time, and with the guru's leave, the two brothers set out to gather flowers.
bal.227.cau2: They went and saw the king's fine garden, where spring, enchanted, had stayed on.
Many kinds of charming trees grew there, with fine canopies of creepers of every colour.
bal.227.cau3: Their fresh leaves, fruits and flowers were lovely; with their riches they put the trees of the gods to shame.
Cātakas, cuckoos, parrots and cakoras — the birds sang, and graceful peacocks danced.
bal.227.cau4: In the middle of the garden a lovely lake shone, with wondrously made steps of gems.
Its water was clear, with lotuses of many colours; water birds called and bees hummed.
bal.227.do227: Seeing the garden and the lake, the Lord rejoiced, and his brother with him.
This garden, which gives joy to Śrī Rāma, is supremely delightful.
bal.228.cau1: Looking all around and asking the gardeners, they began with glad hearts to pick leaves and flowers.
Just then Sītā came there; her mother had sent her to worship Girijā.
bal.228.cau2: With her came all her friends, lovely and wise, singing songs in charming voices.
Near the lake stood Girijā's temple, beautiful beyond words; the mind was enchanted at the sight of it.
bal.228.cau3: Having bathed in the lake with her friends, Sītā went with a glad heart to Gaurī's temple.
She worshipped with deep love and asked for a fine bridegroom worthy of her.
bal.228.cau4: One friend had left Sītā's side and gone to see the flower garden.
There she saw the two brothers, and came back to Sītā overcome by love.
bal.228.do228: The friends saw her state: her body thrilled and her eyes were full of tears.
All of them asked in gentle words: Tell us the reason for your joy.
bal.229.cau1: She said: Two princes have come to see the garden, in the bloom of youth and lovely in every way.
One dark, one fair — how can I describe them? Speech has no eyes, and the eyes have no speech.
bal.229.cau2: Hearing this all the wise friends rejoiced, sensing the great longing in Sītā's heart.
One of them said: Friend, these are the very princes who, we heard, came yesterday with the sage,
bal.229.cau3: who have cast the spell of their beauty and won over the men and women of the city.
Everywhere people are describing their beauty; they should certainly be seen, for they are well worth seeing.
bal.229.cau4: Her words greatly delighted Sītā, and her eyes grew impatient to see them.
She set out, with that dear friend going ahead; no one perceives her love of old.
bal.229.do229: Remembering Nārada's words, Sītā felt a holy love rise within her.
Startled, she looks in every direction, like a frightened young doe.
bal.230.cau1: Hearing the sound of bracelets, girdle-bells and anklets, Śrī Rāma, pondering in his heart, says to Lakṣmaṇa:
It is as though Kāmadeva has sounded his drum, resolved to conquer the world.
bal.230.cau2: So saying, he turned and looked that way: Sītā's face became the moon, and his eyes the cakora birds.
His lovely eyes grew still, as if Janaka's forebear Nimi, who dwells in the eyelids of all beings, had shyly left the lids.
bal.230.cau3: Seeing Sītā's beauty he felt joy; he praised it in his heart, but no words came.
It was as if Brahmā had put all his skill into shaping her and shown it openly to the world.
bal.230.cau4: She makes beauty itself more beautiful, like a lamp's flame burning in a house of loveliness.
The poets have made every simile stale with use: to whom shall I compare the daughter of Videha?
bal.230.do230: Having described Sītā's beauty in his heart and considered his own state,
the Lord, pure of mind, spoke to his younger brother words that suited the moment:
bal.231.cau1: Dear brother, this is that daughter of Janaka for whose sake the bow-sacrifice is being held.
Her friends have brought her to worship Gaurī; she moves about the garden, filling it with light.
bal.231.cau2: Seeing her unearthly beauty, my mind, pure by nature, is stirred.
The Creator knows the whole reason for it; but listen, brother: my auspicious limbs are throbbing.
bal.231.cau3: It is the natural way of the Raghus that their minds never set foot on a wrong path.
I have complete faith in my mind, which has never looked at another man's wife even in a dream.
bal.231.cau4: Those whose backs no enemy sees in battle, whose heart and glance no other man's wife can win,
and from whom those who ask never hear a no — such excellent men are few in the world.
bal.231.do231: While he talks with his younger brother, his mind, captivated by Sītā's beauty,
drinks like a bee the nectar of the beauty of her lotus face.
bal.232.cau1: Sītā looks all around, startled, her mind anxious: where have the young princes gone?
Wherever the fawn-eyed one turns her gaze, it is as though a row of white lotuses rains down there.
bal.232.cau2: Then her friends showed her, behind a screen of creepers, the lovely youths, one dark and one fair.
Seeing their beauty her eyes were filled with longing, and rejoiced as if they had recognised their own treasure.
bal.232.cau3: Her eyes grew still as they beheld Śrī Rāma's beauty; even the eyelids ceased to blink.
In the fullness of love her body forgot itself, like a cakora hen gazing at the autumn moon.
bal.232.cau4: Bringing Śrī Rāma into her heart by the path of her eyes, the wise one closed the doors of her eyelids.
When her friends saw Sītā overcome by love, they were abashed at heart and could say nothing.
bal.232.do232: At that moment the two brothers came out from the bower of creepers,
like two spotless moons emerging as they part a veil of cloud.
bal.233.cau1: The two handsome heroes are the very limit of beauty, their bodies glowing like blue and yellow lotuses.
Peacock feathers look fine on their heads, with clusters of flower buds set here and there among them.
bal.233.cau2: The tilaka and beads of sweat on their brows look lovely; ornaments shine on their shapely ears.
Their brows are arched, their hair curly, their eyes like fresh lotuses, tinged with red.
bal.233.cau3: Lovely are their chin, nose and cheeks; the grace of their smile buys the heart outright.
The beauty of their faces I cannot tell; seeing it, many a Kāmadeva is put to shame.
bal.233.cau4: On the chest a necklace of gems, a lovely neck like a conch; arms like the trunk of Kāmadeva's young elephant, the limit of strength.
Friend, the dark prince, a leaf-bowl of flowers in his left hand, is lovely beyond measure.
bal.233.do233: Lion-waisted, clad in yellow, the treasure-house of beauty and good nature —
seeing him, the jewel of the line of the Sun, the friends forgot themselves.
bal.234.cau1: Then one clever friend, steadying herself, took Sītā by the hand and said:
You can meditate on Gaurī later; why not look at the young princes now?
bal.234.cau2: Shyly Sītā then opened her eyes, and before her she beheld the two lions of the Raghus.
Seeing Śrī Rāma's beauty from head to foot, and remembering her father's vow, she was deeply troubled at heart.
bal.234.cau3: When her friends saw Sītā so overcome, they all said in alarm: It has grown late.
We shall come again at this same hour tomorrow. So saying, one friend smiled to herself.
bal.234.cau4: Hearing the veiled words, Sītā was abashed; it had grown late, and she was afraid of her mother.
Summoning great composure she took Śrī Rāma into her heart, and turned back, knowing herself to be under her father's authority.
bal.234.do234: On the pretext of looking at deer, birds and trees she turns round again and again,
and as she gazes and gazes on Śrī Rāma's beauty her love grows, and not a little.
bal.235.cau1: Knowing how hard Śiva's bow is, she grieved, and went, keeping that dark form in her heart.
When the Lord knew that Sītā, the mine of joy, love, beauty and virtue, was going,
bal.235.cau2: he made a soft ink of the purest love and drew her picture on the lovely wall of his heart.
Sītā went back to Bhavānī's temple and, bowing at her feet, said with joined palms:
bal.235.cau3: Glory, glory to the daughter of the king of mountains! Glory to you, cakora hen to the moon of Maheśa's face!
Glory to the mother of elephant-faced Gaṇeśa and six-faced Kārttikeya! Mother of the world, your body shines like lightning.
bal.235.cau4: You have no beginning, middle or end; your boundless power not even the Veda knows.
You bring about the birth, the flourishing and the dissolution of the world; you hold the universe spellbound and move at your own free will.
bal.235.do235: Mother, among good wives who worship their husbands as gods, your name stands first;
your boundless glory a thousand Sarasvatīs and Śeṣas could not tell.
bal.236.cau1: Those who serve you easily win the four fruits of life, O giver of boons, beloved of Śiva, the foe of Tripura.
O Goddess, by worshipping your lotus feet gods, men and sages all find happiness.
bal.236.cau2: You know well the wish of my heart, for you dwell always in the city of every heart.
That is why I have not spoken it aloud. So saying, Sītā clasped her feet.
bal.236.cau3: Bhavānī was won over by her humility and love: her garland slipped down and the image smiled.
Sītā reverently placed the blessed gift on her head, and Gaurī, her heart full of joy, said:
bal.236.cau4: Listen, Sītā: my blessing is true; your heart's desire will be fulfilled.
Nārada's words are always pure and true: the bridegroom your heart is set on will be yours.
bal.236.cha1: The one your heart is set on, that bridegroom, lovely by nature and dark, shall be yours;
a treasury of compassion and all-wise, he knows your goodness and your love.
Hearing Gaurī's blessing in these words, Sītā and her friends rejoiced at heart.
Tulasīdāsa says: worshipping Bhavānī again and again, Sītā set off for the palace with a glad heart.
bal.236.so236: Knowing Gaurī to be gracious to her, Sītā felt a joy in her heart beyond telling;
her left limbs, the root of fair good fortune, began to throb.
bal.237.cau1: Praising Sītā's loveliness in their hearts, the two brothers went to their guru.
Śrī Rāma told Viśvāmitra everything; his nature is guileless, untouched by deceit.
bal.237.cau2: Receiving the flowers, the sage performed his worship, then blessed the two brothers:
May your wishes bear fruit. Hearing this, Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were glad.
bal.237.cau3: After the meal the great sage, rich in realised knowledge, began to tell some ancient tales.
When the day was over, with their guru's leave, the two brothers went to offer the evening prayers.
bal.237.cau4: In the east the lovely moon rose; seeing it like Sītā's face, Śrī Rāma was glad.
Then he reflected in his mind: the moon is no match for Sītā's face.
bal.237.do237: Its birth is from the ocean, poison is its brother, it is pale by day and blemished;
how could the poor, wretched moon ever equal Sītā's face?
bal.238.cau1: It wanes and waxes, pains women parted from their loved ones, and Rāhu seizes it when he finds his moment.
It brings grief to the cakravāka bird and is the lotus's foe; O moon, you have many faults.
bal.238.cau2: To liken you to Sītā's face would be a grave fault, an unfitting thing to do.
Praising the beauty of Sītā's face under the guise of the moon, he went to the guru, knowing that much of the night had gone.
bal.238.cau3: The brothers bowed at the lotus feet of the sage and, with his leave, lay down to rest.
When the night had passed Śrī Rāma awoke and, looking at his brother, began to say:
bal.238.cau4: Look, dear brother, the dawn has risen, bringing joy to the lotuses, the cakravākas and the world.
Lakṣmaṇa joined his palms and spoke gentle words that pointed to the Lord's glory:
bal.238.do238: With the dawn the night-lilies have closed and the stars' light has grown dim,
just as the kings lost their strength when they heard you had come.
bal.239.cau1: The kings are all stars that shed some light, but they cannot lift the heavy darkness of the bow.
Lotuses, cakravākas, bees and birds of every kind have all rejoiced at the night's end;
bal.239.cau2: in the same way, my Lord, all your devotees will rejoice when the bow is broken.
The sun has risen and the darkness is gone without effort; the stars have hidden and radiance lights the world.
bal.239.cau3: O Lord of the Raghus, under cover of its own rising the sun has shown all the kings your glory.
It has laid bare the greatness of the strength of your arms, and the way the bow will be broken stands revealed.
bal.239.cau4: Hearing his brother's words the Lord smiled; holy by nature, he cleansed himself and bathed.
His daily rites done, he came to the guru and bowed his head at his lovely lotus feet.
bal.239.cau5: Then Janaka summoned Śatānanda and sent him at once to the sage Viśvāmitra.
He came and delivered Janaka's request; the sage, delighted, called the two brothers to him.
bal.239.do239: Bowing at Śatānanda's feet, the Lord went and sat beside the guru.
Then the sage said: Come, my son; Janaka has sent for us.
bal.240.cau1: Let us go and see Sītā's svayaṃvara; who knows to whom God will give the honour.
Lakṣmaṇa said: My lord, he on whom your grace rests, he alone will be the vessel of glory.
bal.240.cau2: All the sages rejoiced to hear those fine words, and gladly gave their blessings.
Then the compassionate Lord, with the company of sages, set out to see the hall of the bow-sacrifice.
bal.240.cau3: News reached all the townspeople that the two brothers had come to the arena,
and all set out, forgetting their household tasks: children, the young and the old, men and women.
bal.240.cau4: Janaka saw that a great crowd had gathered; he summoned all his faithful servants and said:
Go at once to all the people, and give everyone a seat that befits them.
bal.240.do240: With soft and courteous words they seated the men and women,
those of high, middle, lower and humble rank, each in the place that suited them.
bal.241.cau1: At that moment the princes arrived, as if charm itself were spread over their bodies:
oceans of virtue, refined, the finest of heroes, handsome, one dark and one fair of body.
bal.241.cau2: In the gathering of kings they shine in splendour, like two full moons among the stars.
As each one's feeling was, so each saw the form of the Lord.
bal.241.cau3: The great warriors, steadfast in battle, see his form as though the heroic mood itself had taken a body.
The crooked kings took fright at the sight of the Lord, as if at a huge and terrible form.
bal.241.cau4: The demons who were there disguised by guile as kings saw the Lord as Death made manifest.
The townspeople saw the two brothers as the jewels of mankind, a delight to the eyes.
bal.241.do241: The women look on with joy in their hearts, each after her own liking,
as though the mood of love itself had taken a supremely peerless form and shone there.
bal.242.cau1: The learned saw the Lord as the cosmic form: many-faced, with many hands, feet, eyes and heads.
And how do Janaka's kin see him? As dear as their own close relations.
bal.242.cau2: The queens, with Videha, look on him with a love as for their own child, beyond all telling.
To the yogīs he appeared as the supreme reality: serene, pure, unvarying and self-luminous.
bal.242.cau3: The devotees of Hari saw the two brothers as their own chosen deity, the giver of every joy.
The feeling with which Sītā looks at Śrī Rāma, that love and that joy, are beyond words.
bal.242.cau4: She feels it in her heart, yet even she cannot tell it; how then could any poet?
Thus each saw the Lord of Kosala according to the feeling that each held.
bal.242.do242: In the gathering of kings the young sons of the king of Kosala shine,
lovely of body, one dark and one fair, stealers of the eyes of the whole world.
bal.243.cau1: Both their forms are charming by nature; even a comparison with millions of Kāmadevas falls short of them.
Their lovely faces put the autumn moon to shame, and their lotus eyes are dear to the heart.
bal.243.cau2: Their lovely glance steals the heart even of Kāmadeva; it delights the heart, yet cannot be described.
Fair cheeks, earrings swaying in their ears, lovely chin and lips, and gentle speech.
bal.243.cau3: Their smile puts to shame the moon's rays; their brows are arched, their noses charming.
Tilakas gleam on their broad foreheads; seeing their hair, rows of bees are put to shame.
bal.243.cau4: Yellow four-cornered caps look lovely on their heads, worked here and there with flower buds.
On their lovely conch-like necks are graceful lines, as if marking the limit of the beauty of the three worlds.
bal.243.do243: On their chests are lovely necklaces of elephant-pearls and garlands of tulasī;
their shoulders are like a bull's, their bearing is a lion's, and their long arms are treasuries of strength.
bal.244.cau1: Quivers and yellow cloth are tied at their waists; arrows are in their hands, bows on their fine left shoulders.
Yellow sacred threads adorn them; from toe-nail to crown they are lovely, overspread with surpassing beauty.
bal.244.cau2: Seeing them, all the people were glad; their eyes were fixed, the pupils not moving.
Janaka rejoiced to see the two brothers; then he went up and clasped the lotus feet of the sage.
bal.244.cau3: Humbly he told the sage his own account, and showed him the whole arena.
Wherever the two fine princes go, everyone there looks at them in wonder.
bal.244.cau4: Each one saw Śrī Rāma turned towards himself; no one knew anything of the deeper secret of it.
The sage remarked to the king that the arrangements were fine; delighted, the king felt great joy.
bal.244.do244: Of all the platforms one was lovely, bright and spacious;
and there, with the sage, the king seated the two brothers.
bal.245.cau1: Seeing the Lord, all the kings lost heart, as the stars fade when the full moon rises.
Everyone was sure in his mind that Śrī Rāma would break the bow, beyond any doubt,
bal.245.cau2: and that even without the breaking of Śiva's great bow, Sītā would lay the garland on Śrī Rāma's breast.
The kings said to one another: Thinking this over, brothers, go home, your fame, glory, strength and lustre lost.
bal.245.cau3: Hearing these words, the other kings laughed, those blind with want of discernment and full of pride.
They said: Even if the bow is broken, the marriage is hard to win; and without breaking it, who could wed the princess?
bal.245.cau4: Let Death himself come for once, we shall defeat him too in battle for Sītā.
Hearing this, other kings smiled: righteous men, devotees of Śrī Hari, and wise.
bal.245.so245: They said: Śrī Rāma will wed Sītā, humbling the pride of the kings.
Who can defeat in battle the sons of Daśaratha, heroes of the battlefield?
bal.246.cau1: Do not die for nothing, boasting. Is hunger ever eased by sweets eaten in the mind?
Hear our most holy counsel: know Sītā in your heart as the Mother of the world,
bal.246.cau2: think of Śrī Rāma as the Father of the world, and fill your eyes with the sight of his beauty.
Lovely, bringers of joy, a treasury of every virtue, these two brothers dwell in Śiva's heart.
bal.246.cau3: Why leave the ocean of nectar close at hand and, seeing a mirage, run after it to your death?
Go, and let each do what pleases him; we, today, have won the fruit of our birth.
bal.246.cau4: With these words the good kings, filled with love, began to gaze at that matchless beauty.
The gods, riding their aerial cars in the sky, look on, rain flowers and sing sweetly.
bal.246.do246: Then, knowing the moment was right, Janaka sent for Sītā.
Her friends, all clever and lovely, brought her along with due respect.
bal.247.cau1: Sītā's beauty cannot be told; she is the Mother of the world, a mine of beauty and virtue.
Every comparison seems small to me, for they all cling to the limbs of mortal women.
bal.247.cau2: Who would describe Sītā with those same comparisons, to be called a poor poet and earn disgrace?
If Sītā is likened to a woman, where in the world is a young woman so lovely?
bal.247.cau3: Sarasvatī, goddess of speech, is talkative; Bhavānī has but half a body; Rati is sorrowful, knowing her husband bodiless;
and Lakṣmī's dear brothers are poison and wine: how can Vaidehī be called her equal?
bal.247.cau4: If beauty were the ocean of nectar, and supreme loveliness the tortoise,
splendour the rope, adornment itself Mount Mandara, and Kāma churned it with his own lotus hands,
bal.247.do247: and when, in this way, a Lakṣmī was born who was the root of beauty and joy,
even then poets would call her Sītā's equal only with hesitation.
bal.248.cau1: Her wise friends set off with her, singing songs in charming voices.
A lovely sari graces her youthful body; the beauty of the Mother of the world is vast and beyond compare.
bal.248.cau2: Every ornament is in its fitting place and lovely, set with care on each limb by her friends.
When Sītā set foot in the arena, men and women were enchanted at the sight of her beauty.
bal.248.cau3: The gods in delight beat their drums; the apsarases rained flowers and sang.
The victory garland shines in her lotus hand; all the kings turned to look at her with a start.
bal.248.cau4: Sītā, startled at heart, looks for Śrī Rāma; all the kings are overcome with infatuation.
She saw the two brothers near the sage, and her eyes fastened on them eagerly, as on a treasure found.
bal.248.do248: Seeing her elders and the great gathering, Sītā shrank back in modesty,
and, bringing Śrī Rāma into her heart, turned her eyes towards her friends.
bal.249.cau1: At the sight of Śrī Rāma's beauty and Sītā's loveliness, the men and women ceased to blink.
All are anxious but shrink from saying so; in their hearts they pray to the Creator:
bal.249.cau2: O Creator, take away Janaka's stubborn folly quickly, and grant him a good mind like ours,
so that, without more thought, the king may give up his vow and marry Sītā to Śrī Rāma.
bal.249.cau3: The world will praise it, and it pleases everyone; holding fast to obstinacy brings a burning heart in the end.
All the people are lost in this one longing: the dark bridegroom is the match for Jānakī.
bal.249.cau4: Then Janaka summoned the heralds; they came, chanting the praises of his house.
The king said: Go and announce my vow. The bards set out, their hearts full of joy.
bal.249.do249: The heralds spoke these fine words: Hear, all you kings.
Raising our long arms, we proclaim the vow of the king of Videha.
bal.250.cau1: The kings' might of arm is the moon, Śiva's bow is Rāhu; heavy and hard it is, as all know.
Even Rāvaṇa and Bāṇa, mighty warriors, took one look at the bow and quietly slipped away.
bal.250.cau2: Whoever in this royal assembly today breaks that same hard bow of Śiva, the foe of Tripura,
him Vaidehī will choose, without a second thought and resolutely, and with her the victory over the three worlds.
bal.250.cau3: Hearing the vow, all the kings were filled with longing; those vain of their valour burned with anger at heart.
They girded their loins, rose in haste, bowed their heads to their chosen deities and went forward.
bal.250.cau4: In their heat they glare at Śiva's bow, fix their eyes on it and seize it; they strain in countless ways, but it does not rise.
Those kings who have some sense in their minds do not go near the bow.
bal.250.do250: Foolish kings seize the bow in their heat, and when it will not rise, go off in shame,
as though, taking in each warrior's strength of arm, it grows heavier and heavier.
bal.251.cau1: Ten thousand kings at once began to lift it, but it would not move however they tried.
Śiva's bow no more stirs than a faithful wife's mind at a lustful man's words.
bal.251.cau2: All the kings became a laughing-stock, like a renunciant without dispassion.
Their fame, their victories and their great valour they lost perforce to the bow, and went away.
bal.251.cau3: Defeated at heart and robbed of their lustre, the kings went and sat down, each among his own company.
Seeing the kings, Janaka was troubled, and spoke words that seemed steeped in anger:
bal.251.cau4: Hearing of the vow I had made, kings of every continent came, many of them.
Gods and demons came in human form; many heroes came, steadfast in battle.
bal.251.do251: A lovely princess, a great victory, a fame most splendid:
it seems Brahmā never made the one who could win them by mastering the bow.
bal.252.cau1: Tell me, whom did this prize not please? Yet no one strung Śaṅkara's bow.
Never mind stringing or breaking it, brothers: no one could shift it from the ground by so much as a sesame seed's breadth.
bal.252.cau2: Now let no one proud of his valour take offence: I have learnt that the earth is empty of heroes.
Give up hope and go, each of you, to your own homes; the Creator has not written a marriage in Vaidehī's fate.
bal.252.cau3: If I abandon the vow, my merit is lost; let the princess stay unmarried, what can I do?
Had I known, brothers, that the earth was without heroes, I would not have made the vow and made myself a laughing-stock.
bal.252.cau4: Hearing Janaka's words, all the men and women looked at Jānakī and were grieved.
Lakṣmaṇa was incensed: his brows knitted, his lips quivered, his eyes were full of anger.
bal.252.do252: He could not speak for fear of Śrī Rāma, though the words struck him like arrows;
then he bowed his head at the lotus feet of Śrī Rāma and spoke words true and weighty:
bal.253.cau1: Where any one of the Raghus is present, no one in that company says such things
as the improper words Janaka has spoken, knowing that the jewel of the Raghu line is here.
bal.253.cau2: Listen, O sun to the lotus of the Solar race: I tell you my nature, with no pride in it at all.
If I have your command, I would lift the universe like a ball
bal.253.cau3: and smash it like an unbaked pot; I could snap Mount Meru like a radish.
Before the glory of your might, Lord, what is this wretched old Pināka (Śiva's bow)?
bal.253.cau4: Knowing this, my Lord, give the command and I will show you a feat; watch it:
I will string the bow like a lotus stalk and run with it a hundred yojanas.
bal.253.do253: By the power of your might, my Lord, I would break it like the stalk of a mushroom.
If I do not, I swear by my Lord's feet, I will never take bow and quiver in hand.
bal.254.cau1: At the angry words Lakṣmaṇa spoke, the earth reeled and the elephants of the quarters shook.
All the people and all the kings were afraid; Sītā's heart was glad, and Janaka was abashed.
bal.254.cau2: The guru, Śrī Rāma and all the sages rejoiced inwardly, thrilling again and again.
Śrī Rāma restrained Lakṣmaṇa by a sign and lovingly made him sit near him.
bal.254.cau3: Viśvāmitra, seeing that the time was auspicious, spoke words full of affection:
Rise, Rāma, break Śiva's bow, and, dear son, end Janaka's anguish.
bal.254.cau4: Śrī Rāma laid his head at the guru's feet on hearing his words; neither joy nor sorrow entered his heart.
He rose and stood up with natural ease, in a bearing that put a young lion to shame.
bal.254.do254: On the platform, as on the eastern mountain of sunrise, Śrī Rāma rose like the young sun;
all the lotuses that were the saints blossomed, and the bees that were their eyes rejoiced.
bal.255.cau1: The night of the kings' hopes was gone, and the cluster of stars that was their talk shone no more.
The proud kings closed up like night lotuses, and the deceitful kings hid like owls.
bal.255.cau2: The sages and gods, like cakravāka birds, were freed from sorrow; they rain down flowers and show their service.
Śrī Rāma bowed with love at the guru's feet and sought the sages' leave.
bal.255.cau3: The Lord of all the world moved off with natural ease, with the gait of a fine, noble elephant in rut.
As Śrī Rāma went, all the men and women of the city thrilled from head to foot and were glad.
bal.255.cau4: Bowing to their forefathers and the gods, they called to mind their merits: If our merits have any power at all,
then, lord Gaṇeśa, may Śrī Rāma break Śiva's bow like a lotus stalk.
bal.255.do255: Gazing at Śrī Rāma with love and calling her friends to her side,
Sītā's mother, overcome with affection, speaks in distress:
bal.256.cau1: Friend, they are all mere onlookers at a show, even those who are called our well-wishers.
No one reasons with the guru and tells him: These are boys; such insistence is not good.
bal.256.cau2: The bow that Rāvaṇa and Bāṇa did not even touch, and before which all the kings, for all their pride, were beaten —
that bow they are putting into the prince's hands. Can a young swan lift Mount Mandara?
bal.256.cau3: The king's good sense has all run out. Friend, the ways of the Creator cannot be known at all.
A clever friend spoke in gentle words: Queen, one who has glory and power is not to be counted small.
bal.256.cau4: How small the pot-born Agastya, and how boundless the ocean! Yet he dried it up, and his fair fame filled the whole world.
The orb of the sun looks small to the eye, yet at its rising the darkness of the three worlds flees.
bal.256.do256: A mantra is very small, yet Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva and all the gods are under its sway.
A little goad brings under control a mighty elephant maddened in rut.
bal.257.cau1: Kāmadeva, holding a bow and arrows of flowers, has brought all the worlds under his sway.
Lady, knowing this, give up your doubt. Listen, queen: Śrī Rāma will break the bow.
bal.257.cau2: Hearing her friend's words, the queen believed her; her grief was gone and her love grew greatly.
Then Vaidehī, looking at Śrī Rāma, fearful at heart, prays to one god after another.
bal.257.cau3: Distressed, she prays within her mind: Maheśa and Bhavānī, be gracious.
Make my service of you bear fruit; be kind to me and take away the heaviness of the bow.
bal.257.cau4: Gaṇeśa, lord of the gaṇas, giver of boons, I have served you to this day.
Hearing my prayer, made again and again, make the heaviness of the bow very slight.
bal.257.do257: Looking again and again towards Śrī Rāma, she holds herself steady and prays to the gods.
Her eyes are filled with tears of love, and her body thrills all over.
bal.258.cau1: Gazing her fill and filling her eyes with his beauty, she then remembered her father's vow, and her mind was shaken.
Alas, my father has set himself on a cruel obstinacy; he sees neither gain nor loss.
bal.258.cau2: The ministers are afraid and no one gives him counsel; in an assembly of the wise a great wrong is being done.
On one side a bow harder even than the thunderbolt, on the other this dark youth of tender limbs!
bal.258.cau3: O Creator, how can I keep my heart steady? Can a diamond be pierced with a speck of a śirīṣa flower?
The mind of the whole assembly has grown simple; now, bow of Śiva, my hope rests in you.
bal.258.cau4: Cast your own dull weight upon the people, and grow light as you look on Śrī Rāma.
Sītā's mind is in great anguish; each instant, each twinkling of an eye, passes like a hundred ages.
bal.258.do258: She looks at the Lord, then looks down at the ground; her restless eyes are lovely,
as if Kāmadeva's two fish were at play in a swing that is the orb of the moon.
bal.259.cau1: Her speech, a bee, is held fast in the lotus of her face; seeing the night of modesty, it does not come out.
The tears of her eyes stay in the corners of her eyes, as a great miser's gold stays where it is.
bal.259.cau2: She grew shy, knowing how great her agitation was, and gathering her courage brought faith into her heart:
If my vow is true in body, mind and speech, and my mind is given to the lotus feet of Śrī Rāma,
bal.259.cau3: then the Lord who dwells in every heart will make me the handmaid of Śrī Rāma.
Whoever bears true love for another is sure to meet that one; of this there is no doubt.
bal.259.cau4: Looking towards the Lord, she resolved on love with her very body; all this was known to Śrī Rāma, the treasury of compassion.
Having looked at Sītā, how did he look at the bow? As Garuḍa looks at a little snake.
bal.259.do259: Lakṣmaṇa saw that Śrī Rāma, the jewel of Raghu's line, had looked at Śiva's bow;
thrilling all over, pressing the universe down under his feet, he spoke these words:
bal.260.cau1: Elephants of the quarters, Tortoise, Serpent and Boar, hold the earth steady and firm so that it does not shake.
Śrī Rāma wishes to break Śaṅkara's bow; hear my command and be on your guard.
bal.260.cau2: When Śrī Rāma came near the bow, the men and women called on the gods and on their own merits.
The doubt and ignorance of all, the pride of the foolish kings,
bal.260.cau3: the weight of the pride of Paraśurāma, lord of the Bhṛgus, the faint-heartedness of the gods and the great sages,
Sītā's anxiety, Janaka's remorse, and the fierce fire of the queens' grief —
bal.260.cau4: all these found in Śiva's bow a great ship, and went aboard it in company.
They long to reach the far shore of the boundless sea that is the strength of Śrī Rāma's arms, but no boatman is there.
bal.260.do260: Śrī Rāma looked at all the people and saw them as still as figures drawn in a picture;
then the abode of compassion looked at Sītā and knew her to be distressed above all.
bal.261.cau1: He saw Vaidehī deeply distressed; to her each twinkling of an eye was passing like a kalpa.
If one who thirsts has given up the body for lack of water, what can a pool of nectar do once he is dead?
bal.261.cau2: What good is rain when all the crops have withered? What use is regret once the moment is missed?
Thinking thus in his heart, the Lord looked at Jānakī, and seeing her great love, he thrilled.
bal.261.cau3: In his mind he bowed to the guru, and with great swiftness he lifted the bow and took it up.
As he took it, it flashed like lightning; then the bow became like a ring in the sky.
bal.261.cau4: No one saw him take it, string it or draw it hard; all saw only that he stood there.
At that moment Śrī Rāma broke the bow in the middle; a terrible, harsh sound filled the worlds.
bal.261.cha1: The terrible, harsh sound filled the worlds; the horses of the sun left their path and strayed.
The elephants of the quarters trumpeted, the earth swayed, and the Serpent, the Boar and the Tortoise writhed.
Gods, demons and sages put their hands over their ears, and all, in distress, began to wonder.
Knowing that Śrī Rāma had broken the bow, says Tulasīdāsa, they raised cries of victory.
bal.261.so261: Śaṅkara's bow was the ship, and the strength of Śrī Rāma's arms the ocean;
the whole company that had boarded it first, under delusion, was drowned.
bal.262.cau1: The Lord threw both pieces of the bow down on the ground, and at the sight all the people were glad.
Kauśika (Viśvāmitra) is a holy ocean, whose water of love is deep and lovely;
bal.262.cau2: gazing on the full moon of Śrī Rāma's form, it swells with high waves of rapture.
Kettledrums boomed in the sky, and the celestial women danced and sang.
bal.262.cau3: Brahmā and the other gods, the siddhas and the great sages praise the Lord and give their blessings.
They rain down flowers and garlands of many colours; the kinnaras sing sweet songs.
bal.262.cau4: Cries of victory, victory filled all the worlds; the sound of the bow's breaking could not be made out.
Everywhere men and women say with joy: Śrī Rāma has broken Śiva's mighty bow.
bal.262.do262: Bards, Māgadhas and sūtas, steady of mind, proclaim songs of glory.
All the people lavish horses, elephants, wealth, gems and garments as offerings.
bal.263.cau1: Cymbals, mṛdaṅgas, conches, shehnais, bherīs, dhols and fine kettledrums —
many lovely instruments are sounding, and young women everywhere sang auspicious songs.
bal.263.cau2: The queen and her friends were overjoyed, as if water had fallen on withering paddy.
Janaka, his anxiety gone, found happiness, like a swimmer who, worn out, finds his footing.
bal.263.cau3: With the bow broken the kings lost their lustre, as a lamp loses its brightness by day.
How can Sītā's joy be told? It was as if a cātaka hen had found the water of Svāti.
bal.263.cau4: How does Lakṣmaṇa gaze at Śrī Rāma? As a young cakora gazes at the moon.
Then Śatānanda gave the word, and Sītā went towards Śrī Rāma.
bal.263.do263: With her went her lovely, clever friends, singing auspicious songs.
She moved with the gait of a young swan, her limbs boundless in beauty.
bal.264.cau1: Among her friends Sītā shines as Beauty supreme shines among a host of beauties.
In her lotus hand is the lovely garland of victory, over which the splendour of victory over the world is spread.
bal.264.cau2: Her body is shy, her heart full of eager joy; her deep love is seen by no one.
Going near, she beheld Śrī Rāma's beauty, and the princess stood still as though painted in a picture.
bal.264.cau3: Seeing this, a clever friend prompted her: Put the lovely garland on him.
At this she raised the garland with both hands, but overcome by love she could not put it on him.
bal.264.cau4: Her hands holding it look like two lotuses on their stalks, timidly offering a garland of victory to the moon.
Seeing the beauty of it her friends sing, and Sītā laid the garland on Śrī Rāma's breast.
bal.264.so264: Seeing the garland on Śrī Rāma's breast, the gods rain down flowers.
All the kings shrank, as a cluster of water-lilies closes at the sight of the sun.
bal.265.cau1: Music sounded in the city and in the sky; the wicked grew gloomy and all the good rejoiced.
Gods, kinnaras, men, nāgas and great sages give their blessings, crying victory, victory, victory.
bal.265.cau2: The wives of the gods dance and sing, and handfuls of flowers are showered again and again.
Here and there Brahmins chant the Vedas, and heralds recite songs of praise.
bal.265.cau3: The fame went abroad through earth, the nether world and heaven: Śrī Rāma has won Sītā, he has broken the bow.
The men and women of the city perform āratī and, forgetting their wealth, lavish offerings.
bal.265.cau4: The pair of Sītā and Śrī Rāma is so lovely, as if Beauty and Śṛṅgāra, the spirit of love, had come together in one place.
Her friends say: Sītā, clasp the Lord's feet; but, greatly afraid, she does not touch his feet.
bal.265.do265: Remembering what befell the wife of Gautama, she does not touch his feet with her hands.
Knowing her love to be beyond this world, Śrī Rāma, jewel of the Raghu line, smiled within.
bal.266.cau1: Then, seeing Sītā, kings were filled with longing, and the cruel, base and foolish were incensed at heart.
Rising one after another and putting on armour, the luckless men began to boast here and there.
bal.266.cau2: One says: Carry Sītā off, and seize the two princes and bind them.
Breaking the bow does not win him his purpose; who can wed the princess while we live?
bal.266.cau3: If Videha lends them any help, defeat him in battle along with the two brothers.
Hearing this, the good kings said: Shame itself is put to shame by this assembly of kings.
bal.266.cau4: Your strength, glory, valour, greatness and honour went away with the bow Pināka.
Is this that same valour, or have you now found some somewhere? Such is your mind, and so the Creator has blackened your faces.
bal.266.do266: Put away envy, pride and anger, and look at Śrī Rāma to your eyes' content.
Know Lakṣmaṇa's wrath to be a raging fire, and do not be moths to it.
bal.267.cau1: As a crow wants the share of Garuḍa, as a hare wants the share of the lion, foe of elephants;
as one angry without cause wants well-being, and one hostile to Śiva wants every kind of wealth;
bal.267.cau2: as the greedy and grasping want fair fame — can the lustful ever be free of stain? —
and as one turned away from Hari's feet wants the supreme state: such, O kings, is your greed.
bal.267.cau3: Hearing the uproar Sītā grew afraid, and her friends took her to where the queen was.
Śrī Rāma, unconcerned, went to his guru, praising Sītā's love in his heart.
bal.267.cau4: Sītā and the queens are filled with anxiety: what can the Creator mean to do now?
Hearing the kings' words, Lakṣmaṇa looks this way and that, but for fear of Śrī Rāma he cannot speak.
bal.267.do267: Eyes red and brows knit, he looks at the kings in anger,
like a lion cub roused to eagerness at the sight of a herd of rutting elephants.
bal.268.cau1: Seeing the commotion, the women of the city were distressed, and together they all revile the kings.
At that moment, hearing that Śiva's bow was broken, there came Paraśurāma, the sun to the lotus of Bhṛgu's line.
bal.268.cau2: Seeing him all the kings shrank, like quails hiding from the swoop of a hawk.
Sacred ash shone well on his fair body, and the tripuṇḍra, the triple mark, on his broad forehead.
bal.268.cau3: Matted locks on his head, his lovely moon-like face flushed a little red with anger;
brows knit and eyes red with wrath, even his natural glance seems angry.
bal.268.cau4: Shoulders like a bull's, a broad chest and mighty arms; a fair sacred thread, a rosary and a deerskin;
an ascetic's garment at his waist, with two quivers tied on; bow and arrows in his hands and a fine axe on his shoulder.
bal.268.do268: His garb is tranquil but his deeds are harsh; his form is past describing.
It is as though the heroic mood itself had taken a sage's body and come where all the kings were.
bal.269.cau1: At the sight of the fearsome guise of Paraśurāma, lord of the Bhṛgus, all the kings rose, distraught with fear;
each telling his own name with his father's, they all began to fall prostrate before him.
bal.269.cau2: Anyone at whom he glances in his natural way, meaning him well, feels that his days have run out.
Then Janaka came and bowed his head, and called Sītā and had her bow to him.
bal.269.cau3: He gave his blessing; the friends were glad, and wisely took her back to her own company.
Then Viśvāmitra came and met him, and laid both brothers at his lotus feet.
bal.269.cau4: Seeing the fine pair, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the sons of Daśaratha, he gave them his blessing.
His eyes fell on Śrī Rāma and stayed there, held by a boundless beauty that strips Kāma of his pride.
bal.269.do269: Then, looking about, he said to Videha: Tell me, why this great crowd?
He asks as one who does not know, though he knows; anger has spread through his whole frame.
bal.270.cau1: Janaka told him all that had happened, and why all the kings had come.
Hearing this he turned and looked elsewhere, and saw the pieces of the bow lying on the ground.
bal.270.cau2: In great anger he spoke harsh words: Tell me, dull Janaka, who broke the bow?
Show him to me at once, fool, or today I will overturn the earth as far as your kingdom reaches.
bal.270.cau3: In great fear the king gives no answer, and the crooked kings rejoiced at heart.
Gods, sages, nāgas and the men and women of the city are all anxious, with heavy dread in their hearts.
bal.270.cau4: Sītā's mother grieves at heart: Now the Creator has spoiled all that had come right.
Hearing of the nature of Paraśurāma, lord of the Bhṛgus, Sītā felt half a moment pass like an aeon.
bal.270.do270: Seeing all the people afraid, and knowing Jānakī to be frightened,
Śrī Rāma, with neither joy nor sorrow in his heart, spoke:
bal.271.cau1: My lord, the one who broke Śiva's bow must be some servant of yours.
What is your command? Why not tell me? Hearing this, the wrathful sage spoke in anger:
bal.271.cau2: A servant is one who serves; one who does what an enemy does must then fight.
Listen, Rāma: whoever broke Śiva's bow is my enemy, as Sahasrabāhu was.
bal.271.cau3: Let him leave this gathering and stand apart, or else all the kings will be slain.
At the sage's words Lakṣmaṇa smiled, and spoke to Paraśurāma slightingly:
bal.271.cau4: Master, we broke many little bows in our boyhood, yet you never showed such anger.
Why this fondness for this one bow? Hearing this, Paraśurāma, the banner of Bhṛgu's line, said in anger:
bal.271.do271: You prince, in the grip of death, you take no care of what you say!
Is the bow of Śiva, Tripura's foe, famed through all the world, like a little bow?
bal.272.cau1: Lakṣmaṇa said with a laugh: Listen, my lord: to our mind all bows are alike.
What loss or gain is there in breaking an old bow? Śrī Rāma looked at it with eyes deceived, taking it for new.
bal.272.cau2: It broke at a touch; Śrī Rāma is not to blame either. Sage, why be angry for no cause?
Looking towards his axe, Paraśurāma said: You wicked fool, have you not heard what I am like?
bal.272.cau3: Because you are a boy I do not kill you; fool, you take me for a mere sage.
I have been celibate from boyhood and am quick to wrath, known to the whole world as the foe of the Kṣatriya race.
bal.272.cau4: By the might of my arms I rid the earth of kings, and many times gave it to the Brahmins.
Look, prince, at this axe that cut off the arms of Sahasrabāhu.
bal.272.do272: Young prince, do not plunge your mother and father in grief.
My axe, which destroys the unborn in the womb, is terrible indeed.
bal.273.cau1: Lakṣmaṇa smiled and said in gentle words: Ah, the great sage thinks himself a mighty warrior!
Again and again he shows me his axe; he wants to blow a mountain away with a puff.
bal.273.cau2: There is no baby gourd here, to die at the sight of a pointed finger.
It was on seeing your axe, bow and arrows that I said something with pride.
bal.273.cau3: Knowing you to be of Bhṛgu's line and seeing your sacred thread, whatever you say I bear, holding back my anger.
Gods, Brahmins, devotees of Hari and cows: against these our family does not show its valour.
bal.273.cau4: To kill them is sin and to lose to them is disgrace; so even if you strike, one should fall at your feet.
Your word is like ten million thunderbolts; you carry bow, arrows and axe for nothing.
bal.273.do273: If, seeing them, I have said anything unfitting, forgive me, steadfast great sage.
Hearing this, Paraśurāma, the jewel of Bhṛgu's line, spoke angrily in a deep voice:
bal.274.cau1: Kauśika, listen: this boy is a fool; in the grip of cruel fate he is the ruin of his own line.
He is a stain on the full moon of the solar race, utterly unruly, senseless and reckless.
bal.274.cau2: In a moment he will be a morsel for Death. I say it aloud: the fault will not be mine.
If you wish to save him, restrain him by telling him of my glory, my strength and my wrath.
bal.274.cau3: Lakṣmaṇa said: Sage, while you are here, who else could tell the whole of your fair fame?
With your own mouth you have told of your deeds many times over, in many ways.
bal.274.cau4: If you are still not satisfied, say something more; do not hold back your anger and suffer unbearable pain.
You are sworn to valour, steadfast and unshaken; hurling abuse does not become you.
bal.274.do274: Heroes do their deeds in battle; they do not make themselves known by talk.
Cowards, faced with the enemy on the field of battle, talk of their own prowess.
bal.275.cau1: You, it seems, have raised a shout to Death and call him again and again for me.
On hearing Lakṣmaṇa's harsh words, Paraśurāma readied his terrible axe and gripped it in his hand.
bal.275.cau2: Paraśurāma said: Now let no one blame me; this harsh-tongued boy deserves to be killed.
Seeing he was a child, I have spared him much; now he is truly bound to die.
bal.275.cau3: Viśvāmitra said: Forgive the offence; the good do not count a child's faults and merits.
Paraśurāma said: The axe is sharp, I am merciless and wrathful, and before me stands an offender, an enemy of my guru;
bal.275.cau4: yet he answers back and I let him go unharmed, Kauśika, only out of regard for your kindness.
Otherwise I would have cut him down with this hard axe and freed myself of my debt to my guru with little effort.
bal.275.do275: Viśvāmitra, son of Gādhi, laughed in his heart and said: The sage sees nothing but green.
This blade is made of iron, not of sugarcane; the senseless one still does not see it.
bal.276.cau1: Lakṣmaṇa said: Sage, who does not know your goodness? It is famous throughout the world.
You have repaid your debt to mother and father handsomely; the debt to your guru remains, and it weighs heavily on your mind.
bal.276.cau2: That debt, it seems, you had charged to my account alone; many days have gone by and the interest has grown large.
Now send for the money-lender, and I will open my purse and pay at once.
bal.276.cau3: Hearing the bitter words, Paraśurāma made ready his axe, and the whole assembly cried out, Alas, alas!
Lakṣmaṇa said: Best of the Bhṛgus, you show me your axe? Enemy of kings, I spare you because I count you a Brahmin.
bal.276.cau4: You have never met stout warriors in battle; Brahmin god, you have grown great only at home.
Everyone cried out that this was wrong, and Śrī Rāma checked Lakṣmaṇa with a sign.
bal.276.do276: Lakṣmaṇa's answers were like oblations, and the anger of Paraśurāma, best of the Bhṛgus, like fire.
Seeing that fire blaze up, Śrī Rāma spoke words like water:
bal.277.cau1: My Lord, be kind to the boy; do not be angry with a simple child still at the breast.
Had he known anything of your power, my Lord, would the ignorant boy set himself up as your equal?
bal.277.cau2: When children are a little naughty, their guru, father and mother are filled with delight.
Be gracious, knowing him a child and your servant; you are even-minded, gentle, steadfast, a sage and wise.
bal.277.cau3: Śrī Rāma's words calmed Paraśurāma a little; Lakṣmaṇa said something and smiled again.
Seeing him laugh, Paraśurāma was filled with rage from toe to crown and said: Rāma, your brother is very wicked.
bal.277.cau4: Fair of body, he is dark at heart; his is a mouth of deadly poison, not of milk.
Crooked by nature, he is nothing like you; the base one does not see me as his death.
bal.277.do277: Lakṣmaṇa laughed and said: Listen, sage: anger is the root of sin.
In its grip people do what is wrong and set themselves against all the world.
bal.278.cau1: Chief of sages, I am your follower; give up your anger now and be kind.
The broken bow will not mend through anger. Do sit down; your feet must be aching.
bal.278.cau2: If it is so dear to you, find a remedy: call some great craftsman and have it mended.
As Lakṣmaṇa speaks, Janaka grows afraid and says: Be quiet; what is improper is not good.
bal.278.cau3: The men and women of the city tremble and think: The little prince is a great mischief-maker.
Hearing Lakṣmaṇa's fearless words again and again, Paraśurāma burns with anger in his body, and his strength wanes.
bal.278.cau4: Paraśurāma said to Śrī Rāma, making him feel the favour: I spare him because I think of him as your younger brother.
Foul in mind and fair in body — like what? Like a golden pot filled with poison.
bal.278.do278: Hearing this Lakṣmaṇa laughed again, and Śrī Rāma gave him a stern look.
Abashed, Lakṣmaṇa left off his contrary words and went to his guru's side.
bal.279.cau1: With joined palms, Śrī Rāma spoke in words most humble, gentle and cool:
Listen, my Lord: you are wise by nature; pay no heed to what a child says.
bal.279.cau2: A wasp and a child share one nature; the saints never hold it against them.
He has spoiled nothing; it is I who have wronged you, my Lord.
bal.279.cau3: Grace or anger, death or bonds, my master: deal them to me as to your servant.
Tell me quickly, chief of sages, how your anger may pass, and I will do just that.
bal.279.cau4: The sage said: Rāma, how can my anger pass? Even now your younger brother eyes me with ill will.
If I have not put my axe to his throat, what has my anger achieved?
bal.279.do279: Hearing of my axe's terrible work, the wives of kings miscarry.
And yet, while that axe is still in my hand, I see this enemy prince alive.
bal.280.cau1: My hand will not strike, rage burns in my breast, and the king-slaying axe has grown blunt.
The Creator has turned against me and my nature has changed; when was there ever mercy in my heart?
bal.280.cau2: Today mercy has made me bear unbearable pain. Hearing this, Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, smiled, bowed his head and said:
The breeze of your grace well befits your form: when you speak, it is as if flowers were falling.
bal.280.cau3: If mercy makes the sage's limbs burn, may the Creator protect his body when he is angry!
Paraśurāma said: Look, Janaka: this foolish boy is bent on making his home in the city of Yama.
bal.280.cau4: Why do you not quickly take him out of my sight? This king's son looks small, but he is wicked.
Lakṣmaṇa laughed and said to himself: Shut your eyes, and there is no one anywhere.
bal.280.do280: Then Paraśurāma, his heart full of fury, said to Śrī Rāma:
Wretch, you break Śiva's bow and then try to talk me round!
bal.281.cau1: Your brother speaks bitterly with your consent, while you fold your hands and feign humility.
Satisfy me in battle, or else stop calling yourself Rāma.
bal.281.cau2: Enemy of Śiva, drop your deceit and fight, or I will kill you along with your brother.
Paraśurāma raves with his axe raised, while Śrī Rāma, head bowed, smiles inwardly.
bal.281.cau3: He thinks: The fault is Lakṣmaṇa's, and the anger falls on me; at times even straightness is a great failing.
Knowing someone to be crooked, everyone bows to him; Rāhu does not swallow the crooked moon.
bal.281.cau4: Śrī Rāma said: Lord of sages, give up your anger; your hand holds the axe, and here before you is this head.
Do whatever will rid you of your anger, master; know me as your follower.
bal.281.do281: How can master and servant fight? Best of Brahmins, give up your anger.
The boy said something on seeing your garb; the fault is not even the boy's.
bal.282.cau1: Seeing you bearing an axe, arrows and a bow, the boy thought you a warrior, and anger rose in him.
He knew your name but did not recognise you, and answered as his lineage is wont to.
bal.282.cau2: Had you come as a sage, my master, the child would have placed on his head the dust of your feet.
Pardon a slip made in ignorance; a Brahmin's heart should hold abundant mercy.
bal.282.cau3: My Lord, how can we be your equals? Tell me, where are the feet and where the head?
My name is just Rāma, a short one; yours is the long one, with the axe joined to it: Paraśurāma.
bal.282.cau4: Revered one, we have but one guṇa, the single string of a bow; you have nine guṇas, supremely holy.
In every way we are beaten by you; Brahmin, forgive our offences.
bal.282.do282: Again and again Śrī Rāma addressed him as sage and best of Brahmins.
Then Paraśurāma, lord of the Bhṛgus, said angrily: You too are as perverse as your brother.
bal.283.cau1: You take me for a mere Brahmin; let me tell you what kind of Brahmin I am.
Know the bow to be my sacrificial ladle, the arrows my oblations, and my most terrible anger the fire.
bal.283.cau2: The splendid fourfold army is the kindling; great kings came and became the sacrificial beasts.
With this axe I cut them down and offered them up; I have performed millions of battle-sacrifices, with their japa.
bal.283.cau3: You do not know my power; you speak in contempt, mistaking me for a mere Brahmin.
You broke a bow and your pride has swollen; you stand there in your conceit as if you had conquered the world.
bal.283.cau4: Śrī Rāma said: Sage, weigh your words; your anger is very great and our fault is small.
The old Pināka broke at a touch; what cause have I for pride?
bal.283.do283: If we slight you by calling you a Brahmin, then hear the truth, lord of the Bhṛgus:
who in the world is so great a warrior that we should bow our heads to him in fear?
bal.284.cau1: Gods, demons, kings or warriors of every kind, whether our equal in strength or mightier:
if anyone challenges us to battle, we fight him gladly, even if he is Death himself.
bal.284.cau2: Whoever, born in a Kṣatriya's body, shrinks from battle, that wretch has brought a stain upon his lineage.
I say it as our nature is, not to praise our clan: the sons of Raghu do not fear even Death in battle.
bal.284.cau3: Such is the greatness of the Brahmin line that whoever fears you becomes free from fear.
Hearing Śrī Rāma's gentle and deep words, the veils over Paraśurāma's understanding were lifted.
bal.284.cau4: Paraśurāma said: Rāma, take in your hand this bow of Viṣṇu, the lord of Lakṣmī, and draw it, so that my doubt may be removed.
As he offered the bow, it went over to Śrī Rāma of its own accord, and Paraśurāma was filled with wonder.
bal.284.do284: Then he knew Śrī Rāma's power, and his body thrilled and glowed with joy.
Joining his palms he spoke, his heart unable to hold its love.
bal.285.cau1: Glory to you, sun to the lotus-forest of Raghu's line, fire that burns the dense forest of the demon race.
Glory to you, who do good to gods, Brahmins and cows; glory to you, who dispel pride, delusion, anger and error.
bal.285.cau2: Ocean of humility, good conduct, compassion and every virtue, glory to you, most skilled in the art of speech.
Giver of joy to your servants, lovely in every limb, glory to you, whose body has the beauty of countless Kāmadevas.
bal.285.cau3: What praise can I offer with a single mouth? Glory to you, swan of the Mānasa lake of Śiva's mind.
Unknowing, I said much that was improper; forgive me, you two brothers, homes of forgiveness.
bal.285.cau4: Crying: Glory, glory, glory to you, banner of Raghu's race, Paraśurāma went away to the forest for austerity.
The scheming kings were seized by a groundless fear of their own; the cowards slipped away and fled in all directions.
bal.285.do285: The gods struck up their kettledrums and showered the Lord with flowers.
All the men and women of the city rejoiced; the pain of their delusion was gone.
bal.286.cau1: Instruments struck up with a great joyful din, and everyone set out lovely auspicious things.
Women with fair faces, lovely eyes and voices like the cuckoo's gathered in groups and sang sweet songs.
bal.286.cau2: The joy of Janaka, king of Videha, is beyond words, as if one poor from birth had found a treasure.
Her fear gone, Sītā was as happy as a young cakora bird when the moon rises.
bal.286.cau3: Janaka bowed to Viśvāmitra and said: My lord, it is by your grace that Śrī Rāma has broken the bow.
The two brothers have fulfilled my every aim; tell me now, master, what is proper to do.
bal.286.cau4: The sage said: Listen, wise king: the marriage rested on the bow.
The moment the bow broke, the marriage was made; gods, men and nāgas all know it.
bal.286.do286: Still, go now and do what the custom of your line requires,
asking the Brahmins, the elders of the family and the gurus, and following the practice the Vedas make known.
bal.287.cau1: Go and send messengers to Ayodhyā, to invite King Daśaratha and bring him here.
The king gladly said: Very well, gracious one; and at that very hour he called messengers and sent them off.
bal.287.cau2: Then he called all the leading citizens; they came and bowed their heads with respect.
The king said: Adorn the city on all four sides: the markets, the roads, the houses and the temples.
bal.287.cau3: They left in joy and went each to his own home. Then the king sent for his attendants
and said: Make a wondrous canopy, and make it well. Taking the order upon their heads, they went off gladly.
bal.287.cau4: They sent for craftsmen of many kinds, skilled and expert in the art of building canopies.
Bowing to the Creator, the craftsmen began, and made plantain pillars of gold.
bal.287.do287: Their leaves and fruit were of green gems, their flowers of rubies.
Seeing the work, so very wonderful, even Brahmā's mind was bewildered.
bal.288.cau1: All the bamboos were made of green gems, straight and jointed, and no one could tell they were not real.
A betel creeper was made, adorned with gold; lovely with its leaves, it passed for a living one.
bal.288.cau2: Of that creeper, with great care and labour, they made the ties, with lovely strings of pearls between them here and there.
Cutting, carving and inlaying rubies, emeralds, diamonds and turquoise, they made lotuses.
bal.288.cau3: Bees and birds of many colours were made, which hummed and warbled whenever the wind touched them.
Images of the gods were carved out on the pillars, all standing with auspicious offerings in their hands.
bal.288.cau4: Auspicious squares of many kinds were filled in, made of elephant-pearls and naturally lovely.
bal.288.do288: Mango leaves of great beauty were carved from sapphire;
the blossoms were of gold and the clusters of fruit of emerald, and silken cords shone among them.
bal.289.cau1: Fine and beautiful festoons were made, as though Kāmadeva had laid out his snares.
Many auspicious pitchers were made, and flags, pennants, hangings and fly-whisks made a lovely show.
bal.289.cau2: There were many charming lamps made of gems; the wondrous canopy is beyond description.
The pavilion in which Vaidehī is the bride: what poet has the wit to describe it?
bal.289.cau3: Where Śrī Rāma, ocean of beauty and virtue, is the bridegroom, that canopy is renowned in all three worlds.
The splendour seen in Janaka's palace was seen in every house of the city.
bal.289.cau4: Whoever beheld Tirhut at that time found the fourteen worlds small beside it.
The wealth that graced even a humble house entranced Indra, king of the gods, when he saw it.
bal.289.do289: The city where Lakṣmī herself dwells, disguised as a beautiful woman:
Sarasvatī and Śeṣa shrink from telling its beauty.
bal.290.cau1: The messengers reached Śrī Rāma's holy city and rejoiced to see how lovely it was.
At the king's gate they sent word of their coming; hearing it, King Daśaratha had them called in.
bal.290.cau2: They bowed and gave the letter; the delighted king rose himself to take it.
As he read it his eyes filled with tears, his body thrilled and his heart overflowed.
bal.290.cau3: Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in his heart and the precious letter in his hand, he stayed so, unable to say a word, sour or sweet.
Then, steadying himself, he read the letter, and the whole court rejoiced at the true news.
bal.290.cau4: Bharata was at play with his friends and his brother; hearing the news there, they came.
With great love and some shyness he asked: Father, where has the letter come from?
bal.290.do290: Are the two brothers, dear as life, well? Tell us, in what land are they?
At these love-steeped words, the king read the letter once more.
bal.291.cau1: Hearing the letter, both brothers thrilled; their love was more than their bodies could hold.
Seeing Bharata's pure love, the whole court felt a special joy.
bal.291.cau2: Then the king seated the messengers beside him and spoke sweet and charming words:
Tell me, brothers, are the two boys well? Did you see them clearly with your own eyes?
bal.291.cau3: One dark, one fair, bearing bow and quiver, in their early youth, with the sage Viśvāmitra:
do you know them? Tell me what they are like. Overcome by love, the king said it again and again.
bal.291.cau4: From the day the sage took them away, today is the first true news of them I have had.
Tell me, how did the king of Videha come to know them? Hearing these fond words, the messengers smiled.
bal.291.do291: The messengers said: Listen, crest-jewel of kings: no one is as blessed as you,
whose sons are Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the two ornaments of the world.
bal.292.cau1: Your sons are not ones to be asked about; they are lions among men, the light of the three worlds,
before whose fame the moon looks dim and before whose glory the sun seems cool.
bal.292.cau2: My lord, how can one say how they came to be known? Does anyone look for the sun with a lamp in his hand?
At Sītā's svayaṃvara many kings had gathered, warriors each mightier than the last.
bal.292.cau3: No one could so much as move Śiva's bow; all the mighty heroes were beaten.
All in the three worlds who prided themselves on their valour had their strength broken by Śiva's bow.
bal.292.cau4: Bāṇāsura, who can lift Mount Meru, also lost heart, walked round the bow and went away.
He who lifted Śiva's mountain, Kailāsa, in sport also met defeat in that assembly.
bal.292.do292: There, hear it, great king, Śrī Rāma, the jewel of Raghu's line,
broke the bow without effort, as an elephant breaks the stalk of a lotus.
bal.293.cau1: Hearing of it, Paraśurāma, chief of the Bhṛgus, came in a rage and glared at them in many ways.
Then, seeing Śrī Rāma's strength, he gave him his own bow, and after much humble entreaty went away to the forest.
bal.293.cau2: O king, as Śrī Rāma is of matchless strength, so too is Lakṣmaṇa, that treasury of splendour;
kings tremble at his glance as elephants do when a lion cub looks at them.
bal.293.cau3: Your Majesty, after seeing your two boys, no one else seems anything in our eyes.
The messengers' well-wrought words, steeped in love, glory and the heroic mood, delighted all who heard.
bal.293.cau4: The king and his court were moved with love and began to shower gifts on the messengers.
Saying it would be wrong, the messengers stopped their ears; seeing their regard for dharma, everyone was pleased.
bal.293.do293: Then the king rose, went to Vasiṣṭha and gave him the letter,
and, calling the messengers in with respect, told the guru the whole story.
bal.294.cau1: Hearing this, the guru Vasiṣṭha was overjoyed and said: For a man of merit the whole earth is filled with happiness.
Just as rivers flow into the ocean, though the ocean has no desire for them,
bal.294.cau2: so happiness and prosperity go unbidden, of their own accord, to one who lives by dharma.
You serve the guru, Brahmins, cows and the gods, and Queen Kausalyā is just as holy.
bal.294.cau3: No one in the world as blessed with merit as you has ever been, is now, or ever will be.
Whose merit is greater than yours, O king, when you have a son like Śrī Rāma?
bal.294.cau4: Your four fine boys are heroic and humble, steadfast in dharma and in their vows, and oceans of virtue.
For you every time is a time of good fortune. Have the kettledrums sounded and make ready the wedding procession,
bal.294.do294: and set out quickly. Hearing this from the guru, the king bowed his head and replied: Very well, my lord.
Then, having had lodgings given to the messengers, the king went to the palace.
bal.295.cau1: The king called together all the women of the palace and read Janaka's letter aloud to them.
Hearing the message, they all rejoiced, and the king told them the rest of the story as well.
bal.295.cau2: The queens, thrilling with love, glow like peahens on hearing the voice of the clouds.
The elders' wives give their blessings with joy, and the mothers are lost in great delight.
bal.295.cau3: They pass the beloved letter from hand to hand, press it to their hearts and soothe their breasts.
Again and again the great king told of the fame and the deeds of Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
bal.295.cau4: Saying it was all the sage's grace, the king went out to the gate. Then the queens summoned the Brahmins
and joyfully gave them gifts, and the noble Brahmins went their way pronouncing blessings.
bal.295.so295: Then the supplicants were summoned, and gifts were lavished on them in countless ways.
May the four sons of the emperor Daśaratha live long —
bal.296.cau1: so saying they went, clad in garments of many kinds. In joy the kettledrums were beaten with a resounding din.
Everyone heard the news, and in house after house the festive rejoicing began.
bal.296.cau2: The fourteen worlds were filled with joy: Janaka's daughter and Śrī Rāma are to be wed.
Hearing the happy news, the people were filled with love and set about adorning the roads, houses and lanes.
bal.296.cau3: Though Avadh is always lovely, being Śrī Rāma's city, auspicious and purifying,
yet love delights in love, and so auspicious adornments were devised and set out with care.
bal.296.cau4: With flags, pennants, hangings and lovely fly-whisks the market was decked most wonderfully.
With golden pitchers, festal arches, nets of gems, turmeric, dūrvā grass, curd, unbroken rice and garlands
bal.296.do296: the people adorned their own houses and made each one auspicious;
they sprinkled the streets with catuḥsama, a blend of four fragrances, and drew lovely auspicious squares on the ground.
bal.297.cau1: Here and there fair women have gathered in groups, decked in all the sixteen adornments, all radiant as lightning,
moon-faced, with eyes like a fawn's, whose own beauty would rid Rati of her pride.
bal.297.cau2: They sing auspicious songs in lovely voices; hearing their sweet notes, the cuckoos are put to shame.
How can the king's palace be described? A canopy that would enchant the whole world has been raised there.
bal.297.cau3: Charming auspicious articles of many kinds are set out in splendour, and many kettledrums are sounding.
In one place heralds proclaim panegyrics; in another, Brahmins chant the Vedas.
bal.297.cau4: Fair women sing auspicious songs, naming Śrī Rāma and Sītā again and again.
The joy is so great and the palace so small that it seems to overflow and spill out on every side.
bal.297.do297: What poet could describe the splendour of Daśaratha's palace to its end,
